budget-50-30-20.text: Targets: needs 50%, wants 30%, savings and debt repayment 20% of after-tax income. Zero-based check: income - needs - wants - savings should equal 0
budget-50-30-20.when: Use it to check whether spending is balanced. The 50/30/20 split is a starting rule, not a law: in a high-rent city needs may take 60%, and the goal is then to shift the other two. Zero-based budgeting goes further and gives every unit of income a job, so the unassigned amount should end at zero.

abs-excess-spread.mathml: Excess spread=Pool interest−Note interest−Fees−Losses,OC=Pool−NotesPool\text{Excess spread}=\text{Pool interest}-\text{Note interest}-\text{Fees}-\text{Losses},\quad OC=\frac{\text{Pool}-\text{Notes}}{\text{Pool}}
abs-excess-spread.text: Excess spread = Interest earned on the pool - Interest paid on the notes - Fees - Credit losses; Overcollateralization = (Pool balance - Notes outstanding) / Pool balance
abs-excess-spread.when: Use it to judge how much protection an asset-backed security has. Credit enhancement comes from two sources: the pool being bigger than the notes (overcollateralization) and the extra interest the pool earns (excess spread).

accretion-dilution.text: Pro forma EPS = (Acquirer NI + Target NI) / (Acquirer shares + New shares), where New shares = Price paid / Acquirer share price
accretion-dilution.when: Use it to see whether paying for a target with shares raises (accretive) or lowers (dilutive) the buyer's earnings per share. EPS impact is not the same as value created, but the market watches it.

accrual-ratio.text: Accrual ratio = (Net income - Cash flow from operations) / Average total assets
accrual-ratio.when: Use it to test how much of profit is backed by cash. Profit that exceeds operating cash flow rests on accruals, such as unpaid sales and capitalized costs. High, rising accruals tend to come before lower future earnings, so analysts treat them as a warning.

accrued-interest-dirty-price.text: Accrued interest = Coupon payment x Days since last coupon / Days in the coupon period; Dirty (full) price = Clean (quoted) price + Accrued interest
accrued-interest-dirty-price.when: Use it when you buy a government bond between coupon dates. Quoted prices are clean, without accrued interest. The buyer pays the clean price plus the interest earned since the last coupon, which the seller is owed.

afn-external-financing.text: Additional funds needed = (Assets/Sales) x Change in sales - (Spontaneous liabilities/Sales) x Change in sales - Net margin x New sales x (1 - Payout ratio)
afn-external-financing.when: Use it to forecast how much outside money a growing company will need. Assets grow with sales and need funding. Part of it is funded by liabilities that grow automatically and by profit kept in the business. What remains must come from new debt or equity, and this is the plug in a model.

adjusted-leverage-off-balance.text: Adjusted debt = Reported debt + Capitalized operating leases + Pension deficit + Probability x Guarantees; Adjusted leverage = Adjusted debt / EBITDAR
adjusted-leverage-off-balance.when: Use it to include debt-like obligations that the balance sheet leaves out. Rating agencies and lenders do the same. If you add lease debt, add the rent back to earnings so both sides treat leases the same way.

after-tax-cost-of-debt.text: After-tax cost of debt = Pre-tax cost of debt x (1 - Tax rate)
after-tax-cost-of-debt.when: Use it in WACC. Interest is tax deductible, so debt costs the company less than its stated rate. Use today's borrowing rate, not the coupon on old debt.

after-tax-return-tey.text: After-tax return = Pre-tax return x (1 - tax rate); Tax-equivalent yield = Tax-free yield / (1 - tax rate)
after-tax-return-tey.when: Use it to compare taxable and tax-free investments on the same footing. The higher your tax rate, the more a tax-free yield is worth.

after-tax-salvage.text: After-tax salvage = Sale price - T x (Sale price - Book value)
after-tax-salvage.when: Use it for the cash you really receive when a project ends and its assets are sold. A sale above book value is taxed. A sale below book value gives a tax saving.

age-based-allocation.text: Equity share = (base number - age) / 100, kept between 0% and 100%; Portfolio return = equity share x equity return + (1 - equity share) x bond return; Portfolio risk uses the two-asset variance formula
age-based-allocation.when: Use it to turn a rule of thumb into numbers. The idea is that you hold less in equities as retirement nears, because there is less time to recover from a fall. The rule is a starting point, not advice: your goals, other income, risk tolerance and time horizon matter more than age. The return and risk inputs are assumptions you should set yourself.

ai-fraud-model-value.text: Fraud stopped = true alerts x average loss per fraud; Review cost = all alerts (true + false) x cost to review one alert; Net value = fraud stopped - review cost; Missed fraud = missed cases x average loss; Precision = true alerts / all alerts; Recall = true alerts / all frauds
ai-fraud-model-value.when: Use it to judge a machine-learning model by money, not accuracy alone. A model that flags many harmless transactions costs analyst time and annoys customers; one that is too cautious lets fraud through. Choose the alert threshold where the net value is highest. The same logic applies to credit models and trading signals, with their own cost of an error.

all-in-loan-cost.text: All-in cost = (Interest + Fees) / Net proceeds, for a one-year loan
all-in-loan-cost.when: Use it to compare loans with different rates and fees on one basis. The cost to the borrower is higher than the stated rate when fees are taken up front. For loans longer than a year use IRR on the cash flows.

altman-z-score.text: Z = 1.2 x Working capital/Total assets + 1.4 x Retained earnings/Total assets + 3.3 x EBIT/Total assets + 0.6 x Market value of equity/Total liabilities + 1.0 x Sales/Total assets
altman-z-score.when: Use it as a quick screen of a listed manufacturing company's chance of failing within about two years. This is the original 1968 version for public manufacturers. Other versions exist for private firms and services. Treat the result as a signal to investigate, not a verdict.

aml-customer-risk-score.mathml: S=∑iwisi,Rating={HighS≥3.5Medium2.5≤S<3.5LowS<2.5S=\sum_{i}w_{i}s_{i},\quad \text{Rating}=\begin{cases}\text{High}&S\ge 3.5\\\text{Medium}&2.5\le S<3.5\\\text{Low}&S<2.5\end{cases}
aml-customer-risk-score.text: Customer risk score = sum of (weight x score) over factors such as country, product, customer type, delivery channel and transaction pattern, each scored 1 (low) to 5 (high), weights adding up to 1; Rating bands set by the firm (here: 3.5 or more is high risk and gets enhanced due diligence)
aml-customer-risk-score.when: Use it to see how a bank applies a risk-based approach under anti-money-laundering rules. Higher-risk customers get more checks (source of funds, senior approval, closer monitoring). The factors, weights and cut-offs are set by each firm and approved by its regulator, so the numbers here are illustrative.

anchoring-adjustment-bias.mathml: x^=a+θ (x−a),Bias=x^−x=−(1−θ)(x−a)\hat{x}=a+\theta\,(x-a),\quad \text{Bias}=\hat{x}-x=-(1-\theta)(x-a)
anchoring-adjustment-bias.text: Estimate = anchor + adjustment share x (true value - anchor); Bias = estimate - true value = - (1 - adjustment share) x (true value - anchor). An adjustment share below 1 means the estimate stays too close to the anchor
anchoring-adjustment-bias.when: Use it to see how a starting number pulls judgment. A 52-week high, a purchase price or an analyst's target price can act as an anchor, so valuations end up too close to it. Framing is related: the same facts described as gains or losses lead to different choices. Counter anchoring by forming an estimate before seeing others' numbers.

annual-report-scorecard.mathml: ROE=NIE,Interest cover=EBITInterest,FCF=CFO−CapEx,Conversion=FCFNIROE=\frac{NI}{E},\quad \text{Interest cover}=\frac{EBIT}{\text{Interest}},\quad FCF=CFO-CapEx,\quad \text{Conversion}=\frac{FCF}{NI}
annual-report-scorecard.text: Operating margin = operating profit / revenue; Net margin = net income / revenue; ROE = net income / equity; ROA = net income / assets; Net debt / EBITDA is common but needs depreciation, so net debt / operating profit is used here; Net debt = debt - cash; Interest cover = operating profit / interest; Free cash flow = operating cash flow - capital spending; Cash conversion = free cash flow / net income
annual-report-scorecard.when: Use it as the first pass through an annual report. Pull seven numbers from the statements, compute the ratios, then read the notes to find out why they are what they are. No ratio stands alone; compare each with the company's earlier years and with its peers.

annualized-loss-expectancy.text: Annualized loss expectancy = Single loss expectancy x Annual rate of occurrence; Single loss expectancy = Asset value x Exposure factor
annualized-loss-expectancy.when: Use it to put a money value on a cyber risk and decide whether a control is worth buying. A control is worth it if the drop in expected yearly loss exceeds its yearly cost.

annualized-hpr.when: Use it to compare investments held for different lengths of time, by restating each return as a yearly figure. It assumes the same return could be earned again and again.

annualized-volatility.text: Annual volatility = period volatility x square root of m
annualized-volatility.when: Use it to put the volatility of daily or monthly returns on a yearly basis, so different investments can be compared. It assumes returns in each period are independent.

apt-expected-return.text: Expected return = rf + beta1 x premium1 + beta2 x premium2 + ...
apt-expected-return.when: Use it when several economic factors drive returns, not just the market. The CAPM is the special case with one factor, the market.

arithmetic-mean-return.when: Use it to estimate the typical return in a single period. It is not the right measure of long-run growth when returns vary, which is what the geometric mean is for.

asian-option-payoff.mathml: Payoff=max⁡(Sˉ−K,0),Sˉ=1n∑Si\text{Payoff}=\max(\bar{S}-K,0),\quad \bar{S}=\frac{1}{n}\sum S_{i}
asian-option-payoff.text: Asian call payoff = max(Average price over the period - Strike, 0); the average of the prices recorded on set dates
asian-option-payoff.when: Use it to see the payoff of an option on the average price. Averaging smooths out price spikes, so the option has lower volatility and is cheaper than a standard option. It is popular with commodity buyers who purchase evenly through the year.

asset-manager-economics.text: Ending AUM = starting AUM x (1 + market return) + net flows; Revenue = average AUM x fee rate; Operating profit = revenue x operating margin
asset-manager-economics.when: Use it to see what drives an asset manager's earnings. Revenue rises with markets and net inflows, and falls with fee cuts, since costs are largely fixed, so profit moves more than revenue. The shift to cheaper passive funds has been compressing fee rates for years, so the fee sensitivity is worth checking.

strategy-backtest-metrics.mathml: Rann=(∏(1+rt))12/N−1,  Sharpe=12rˉ−rfσ12,  MDD=max⁡Peak−ValuePeak,  Calmar=RannMDDR_{ann}=\left(\prod(1+r_{t})\right)^{12/N}-1,\; Sharpe=\frac{12\bar{r}-r_{f}}{\sigma\sqrt{12}},\; MDD=\max\frac{Peak-Value}{Peak},\; Calmar=\frac{R_{ann}}{MDD}
strategy-backtest-metrics.text: Annual return = (product of (1 + monthly return))^(12 / months) - 1; Sharpe = (average monthly return x 12 - risk-free rate) / (monthly sd x sqrt 12); Maximum drawdown = largest fall from a previous peak; Calmar = annual return / maximum drawdown
strategy-backtest-metrics.when: Use it to summarize a backtest in a few numbers. Return and Sharpe show reward per unit of risk, drawdown shows the worst pain an investor would have lived through, and hit rate shows how often the strategy made money. A good backtest result is not proof of a good strategy: look for overfitting, look-ahead bias, survivorship bias and costs before trusting it.

backtest-performance-summary.mathml: CAGR=WT12/n−1,σ=s12,Sharpe=12(rˉ−rf)σ,IR=12 (r−b)‾TECAGR=W_{T}^{12/n}-1,\quad \sigma=s\sqrt{12},\quad Sharpe=\frac{12(\bar{r}-r_{f})}{\sigma},\quad IR=\frac{12\,\overline{(r-b)}}{TE}
backtest-performance-summary.text: Growth of 1 = product of (1 + monthly return); Annualized return (CAGR) = growth^(12 / months) - 1; Volatility = monthly standard deviation x square root of 12; Sharpe = 12 x (average monthly return - monthly risk-free rate) / volatility; Maximum drawdown = largest fall from a previous peak; Tracking error = standard deviation of monthly excess returns x square root of 12; Information ratio = annualized average excess return / tracking error
backtest-performance-summary.when: Use it to report a backtest in full rather than just the return. A good result must beat a simple benchmark after costs, in data the rule was not tuned on. Two years of monthly data, as here, is too short to say much; use many years and different market conditions, and keep the test free of look-ahead.

balance-of-payments-identity.text: Current account = trade balance + primary income (investment income, wages) + secondary income (transfers and remittances); Current account + capital account + financial account + errors = 0, where the financial account is net inflows (+) of capital; Current account = national saving - domestic investment
balance-of-payments-identity.when: Use it to see how a country pays for its overseas spending. A current account deficit means the country spends more than it earns abroad and must attract capital inflows of the same size, from borrowing or from foreign investors buying assets. The saving-investment version gives the same message: a deficit means domestic investment exceeds national saving. Persistent deficits are not harmful by themselves, but depend on investor confidence.

bank-balance-sheet-ratios.text: Loan-to-deposit ratio = loans / deposits; Equity ratio = equity / assets; Deposit funding share = deposits / total funding; The balance sheet balances: assets = deposits + wholesale funding + equity
bank-balance-sheet-ratios.when: Use it to judge funding and liquidity. A loan-to-deposit ratio well above 100% means the bank relies on wholesale funding, which is less stable than deposits. A thin equity ratio means a small fall in asset values can wipe out equity. Compare ratios across banks of the same type.

bank-profitability-dupont.text: Net interest income = interest income - interest expense; Revenue = NII + fee income; Net income = (revenue - non-interest expense - loan loss provisions) x (1 - tax rate); Efficiency ratio = non-interest expense / revenue (lower is better); ROE = ROA x (assets / equity)
bank-profitability-dupont.when: Use it to read a bank's results. Banks earn mostly from the spread between lending and funding rates, plus fees. Because assets are far larger than equity, a small ROA becomes a decent ROE, but the same leverage multiplies losses. Compare the efficiency ratio across banks to see who runs more cheaply.

bank-run-liquidity-shortfall.mathml: Shortfall=wD−L,Loss=h1−h Shortfall,w∗=L+E(1−h)/hD\text{Shortfall}=wD-L,\quad \text{Loss}=\frac{h}{1-h}\,\text{Shortfall},\quad w^{*}=\frac{L+E(1-h)/h}{D}
bank-run-liquidity-shortfall.text: Cash needed = withdrawal fraction x deposits; Shortfall = cash needed - liquid assets; Assets to sell (at book value) = shortfall / (1 - haircut); Fire-sale loss = book value sold - shortfall; Withdrawal fraction that wipes out equity = (liquid assets + equity x (1 - h) / h) / deposits
bank-run-liquidity-shortfall.when: Use it to see why a solvent bank can fail in a run. Deposits can leave at once while loans cannot be sold quickly, so a run forces sales at a discount, which eats equity and justifies more fear. The model has two thresholds: the withdrawal level the liquid assets cover, and the level at which fire-sale losses exceed equity. Central bank lending and deposit insurance work by removing the need to sell.

irrbb-eve-nii.mathml: ΔEVE≈−(DAA−DLL)Δy1+y,ΔNII=(RSA−RSL) Δr\Delta EVE\approx-(D_{A}A-D_{L}L)\frac{\Delta y}{1+y},\quad \Delta NII=(RSA-RSL)\,\Delta r
irrbb-eve-nii.text: Change in economic value of equity = -(Asset duration x Assets - Liability duration x Liabilities) x Rate change / (1 + yield); Change in net interest income = (Rate-sensitive assets - Rate-sensitive liabilities) x Rate change
irrbb-eve-nii.when: Use it to see how a bank's earnings and value react to rates. A bank that funds long assets with short liabilities loses value when rates rise (duration gap) and loses earnings if liabilities reprice before assets (repricing gap). Regulators call this IRRBB.

barrier-option-payoff.mathml: Up-and-out call={0max⁡(St)≥Bmax⁡(ST−K,0)otherwise\text{Up-and-out call}=\begin{cases}0 & \max(S_{t})\ge B\\ \max(S_{T}-K,0) & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
barrier-option-payoff.text: An up-and-out call pays max(ST - K, 0) only if the price never touched the barrier B; an up-and-in call pays it only if the barrier was touched
barrier-option-payoff.when: Use it to see how a barrier changes a call's payoff. Knock-out options are cheaper than standard options because they can disappear. A knock-in plus a knock-out with the same barrier and strike equals one ordinary option.

basel-capital-buffers.text: Required CET1 ratio = 4.5% minimum + capital conservation buffer (2.5%) + countercyclical buffer (set by the country, 0% to 2.5%) + surcharge for global systemically important banks (1% to 3.5%); Headroom = actual CET1 ratio - requirement (this is the loss the bank can absorb before restrictions); Capital needed = shortfall x risk-weighted assets; Banks inside the buffers face limits on dividends and bonuses
basel-capital-buffers.when: Use it to see how much loss a bank can bear before it faces limits on payouts. The minimum is not the real constraint; the buffers on top are. Supervisors raise the countercyclical buffer in booms, so the requirement can change. It ignores other requirements such as leverage ratio, liquidity and bank-specific add-ons.

basel-output-floor.text: Risk-weighted assets used for the capital ratio = the larger of (assets as measured by the bank's own models) and (72.5% of assets as measured by the standardized approach); The floor binds when internal models give less than 72.5% of the standardized amount; Capital ratio = CET1 / floored RWA
basel-output-floor.when: Use it to see how the floor stops internal models from producing capital that is too low. A bank with sophisticated models can report much lower risk-weighted assets than the standard method gives. The floor puts a lower bound at 72.5% of the standard figure. It is most important for banks with low-risk mortgage and corporate books under internal models.

lcr-nsfr.text: LCR = High-quality liquid assets / (30-day outflows - min(30-day inflows, 75% of outflows)); NSFR = Available stable funding / Required stable funding; both must be at least 100%
lcr-nsfr.when: Use it to check a bank against the two main Basel III liquidity rules. The LCR is short-term: can liquid assets cover 30 days of stress outflows? The NSFR is long-term: is the balance sheet funded with stable sources over one year? Regulators require both at 100% or above. The Level 2 cap (40% of HQLA) is ignored here for simplicity.

baumol-cash-model.text: Optimal cash transfer C = square root of (2 x Fixed cost per transaction x Annual cash needs / Interest rate)
baumol-cash-model.when: Use it to decide how much cash to hold and how often to top it up. Holding more cash costs interest you could have earned, while topping up often costs transaction fees.

bayes-theorem.mathml: P(A∣B)=P(B∣A) P(A)P(B∣A) P(A)+P(B∣¬A) P(¬A)P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)+P(B\mid \neg A)\,P(\neg A)}
bayes-theorem.text: P(A given B) = P(B given A) x P(A) / (P(B given A) x P(A) + P(B given not A) x P(not A))
bayes-theorem.when: Use it to revise a probability when new evidence arrives, for example how likely a borrower is to default after a warning signal. It shows why a rare event stays unlikely even after a fairly accurate warning.

beneish-m-score.text: M = -4.84 + 0.920 x DSRI + 0.528 x GMI + 0.404 x AQI + 0.892 x SGI + 0.115 x DEPI - 0.172 x SGAI + 4.679 x TATA - 0.327 x LVGI. A score above about -1.78 flags a likely manipulator
beneish-m-score.when: Use it as a screen for earnings manipulation. Eight ratios, mostly comparing this year with last year, are combined into one score. It is a statistical flag, not proof of fraud, and gives false alarms, especially for fast-growing firms. Use it to decide where to look harder.

best-execution-price-improvement.text: For a buy order: price improvement = (best offer at order time - price paid) x shares; Execution cost vs mid-point = (price paid - mid-point) x shares; Effective half-spread paid = (price paid - mid-point) / mid-point; Firms under MiFID II must show they took steps to get the best result for clients, including price, costs, speed and likelihood of execution
best-execution-price-improvement.when: Use it to check execution quality, which MiFID II requires firms to monitor and publish. Getting a price better than the best quote means the client gained; paying above the mid-point is the normal cost of trading. It ignores fees, market impact for large orders and the speed of the fill.

beta.when: Use it to measure how much a stock tends to move when the market moves. A beta above 1 means the stock swings more than the market, and below 1 means it swings less.

bid-ask-spread.text: Spread = Ask - Bid; Relative spread = Spread / Mid price
bid-ask-spread.when: Use it to measure the cost of trading. A market maker earns the spread by buying at the bid and selling at the ask. A buyer who sells straight away loses the whole spread.

binomial-option-two-step.mathml: u=eσΔt, d=1u, q=erΔt−du−d, V=e−rΔt[qVu+(1−q)Vd]u=e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}},\ d=\frac{1}{u},\ q=\frac{e^{r\Delta t}-d}{u-d},\ V=e^{-r\Delta t}\left[qV_{u}+(1-q)V_{d}\right]
binomial-option-two-step.text: u = e^(sigma x sqrt(dt)); d = 1/u; risk-neutral probability q = (e^(r x dt) - d) / (u - d); Option value = e^(-r x dt) x [q x Value if up + (1 - q) x Value if down], worked back from expiry
binomial-option-two-step.when: Use it to price an option by building a tree of possible stock prices, finding the payoff at the end and discounting back at the risk-free rate using risk-neutral probabilities. More steps give prices closer to Black-Scholes. This is a European option. For an American option you would also check early exercise at each node.

miner-breakeven-price.mathml: BTC/day=hH B (R+F),P∗=kW×24×cBTC/dayBTC/day=\frac{h}{H}\,B\,(R+F),\quad P^{*}=\frac{kW\times 24\times c}{BTC/day}
miner-breakeven-price.text: Share of the network = miner hash rate / network hash rate; Coins won per day = share x blocks per day (144) x (block reward + average fees per block); Daily electricity cost = power in kW x 24 x price per kWh; Break-even price = daily cost / coins won per day
miner-breakeven-price.when: Use it to see the price at which a mining machine stops paying for its power. Mining is a competition: when more computing power joins, each machine wins a smaller share. Costs of the machine, hosting and pool fees are left out here, so the true break-even is higher.

bitcoin-supply-schedule.mathml: Rk=502k,Sh=210,000∑k=0h−1Rk,SF=Syearly issuanceR_{k}=\frac{50}{2^{k}},\quad S_{h}=210{,}000\sum_{k=0}^{h-1}R_{k},\quad SF=\frac{S}{\text{yearly issuance}}
bitcoin-supply-schedule.text: Block reward after k halvings = 50 / 2^k coins; Each halving period lasts 210,000 blocks; Total supply after h halvings = 210,000 x sum of the rewards over those periods (the limit is 21 million); Yearly issuance = reward x 6 blocks an hour x 24 x 365 (about 52,560 blocks); Annual supply growth = yearly issuance / supply; Stock-to-flow = supply / yearly issuance
bitcoin-supply-schedule.when: Use it to see how Bitcoin's fixed schedule works: issuance halves about every four years until it approaches 21 million. Stock-to-flow is a ratio that some analysts use to compare scarcity, though it has no proven link to price. The 2024 halving cut the reward to 3.125 coins.

black-76-option.mathml: Payer=N A [F N(d1)−K N(d2)], Receiver=N A [K N(−d2)−F N(−d1)], d1=ln⁡(F/K)+σ2T/2σT\text{Payer}=N\,A\,[F\,N(d_{1})-K\,N(d_{2})],\ \text{Receiver}=N\,A\,[K\,N(-d_{2})-F\,N(-d_{1})],\ d_{1}=\frac{\ln(F/K)+\sigma^{2}T/2}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}
black-76-option.text: Payer option (caplet, or payer swaption) = Notional x Annuity x [F x N(d1) - K x N(d2)]; Receiver option = Notional x Annuity x [K x N(-d2) - F x N(-d1)]; d1 = [ln(F/K) + sigma^2 x T / 2] / (sigma x sqrt(T)); d2 = d1 - sigma x sqrt(T)
black-76-option.when: Use it to price options on interest rates, which are quoted market-standard with Black's model: caplets, floorlets and swaptions. It treats the forward rate as lognormal, and the annuity converts the result into present-value money.

black-litterman-one-asset.text: Blended return = (Equilibrium / (tau x s^2) + View / w) / (1 / (tau x s^2) + 1 / w)
black-litterman-one-asset.when: Use it to combine the return implied by the market with your own opinion, weighting each by how confident it is. The full model uses matrices for many assets. This is the one-asset case, which shows the idea.

bs-pde-check.text: Theta + r x S x Delta + 0.5 x sigma^2 x S^2 x Gamma - r x V = 0 for any option price V that follows from Black-Scholes
bs-pde-check.when: Use it to see how Black-Scholes is derived. A portfolio long one option and short Delta shares has no random shocks, so by no-arbitrage it must earn the risk-free rate. That condition gives this equation. The check shows that the formula's price satisfies it: the terms add to zero.

black-scholes-merton.mathml: C=Se−qTN(d1)−Ke−rTN(d2), P=Ke−rTN(−d2)−Se−qTN(−d1), d1=ln⁡(S/K)+(r−q+σ2/2)TσT, d2=d1−σTC=S e^{-qT}N(d_{1})-K e^{-rT}N(d_{2}),\ P=K e^{-rT}N(-d_{2})-S e^{-qT}N(-d_{1}),\ d_{1}=\frac{\ln(S/K)+(r-q+\sigma^{2}/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}},\ d_{2}=d_{1}-\sigma\sqrt{T}
black-scholes-merton.text: Call = S x e^(-qT) x N(d1) - K x e^(-rT) x N(d2); Put = K x e^(-rT) x N(-d2) - S x e^(-qT) x N(-d1); d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r - q + sigma^2 / 2) x T] / (sigma x sqrt(T)); d2 = d1 - sigma x sqrt(T)
black-scholes-merton.when: Use it to price European options on a share, index or currency when volatility is steady. It assumes continuous trading, constant volatility and interest rates, and no jumps, so it is a benchmark and not a perfect model. It does not handle early exercise of American options.

double-spend-probability.text: Let q be the attacker's share of total computing power and p = 1 - q the honest share. After z confirmations, the chance the attacker can still catch up and replace the chain = 1 - sum for k = 0 to z of Poisson(k; lambda) x (1 - (q/p)^(z-k)), with lambda = z x q / p; If q is 50% or more the attacker eventually succeeds
double-spend-probability.when: Use it to see why waiting for more confirmations makes a payment safer. The chance of reversal falls very fast as confirmations rise when the attacker has a small share, which is why the number of confirmations a merchant demands should match the amount at risk. It assumes a pure proof-of-work chain and a simple attacker.

bollinger-bands.text: Bands = Simple moving average of the last n prices plus and minus k standard deviations (k is usually 2)
bollinger-bands.when: Use it to see whether a price is high or low compared with its own recent range. Bands widen when the market is volatile and narrow when it is calm. A price near the upper band is only "high" relative to recent history, not necessarily overvalued.

bond-features-cash-flows.text: Coupon payment = Coupon rate x Face value / Payments per year; Number of payments = Years x Payments per year
bond-features-cash-flows.when: Use it to lay out what a bond will pay. The coupon rate is fixed on the face value and does not change with the market price. The bond repays the face value on the maturity date along with the last coupon.

convexity.text: Convexity = [sum over each period k of k x (k + 1) x PV of cash flow k] / [Price x (1 + y/m)^2 x m^2]
convexity.when: Use it to refine the duration estimate. Convexity is the curve in the price-yield relationship. It is good for the holder, because the price rises more when yields fall than it drops when they rise by the same amount. Zero-coupon and long bonds have more of it.

bond-futures-invoice.text: Invoice price = Futures price x Conversion factor + Accrued interest; Basis = Clean price of the bond - Futures price x Conversion factor
bond-futures-invoice.when: Use it to see what the short side of a Treasury bond future receives when delivering a bond. The short chooses which bond to deliver and picks the one with the smallest basis, the cheapest to deliver.

bond-price.text: Price = Coupon x [1 - (1 + r)^-N] / r + Face value / (1 + r)^N, where r = yield / payments per year and N = number of payments
bond-price.when: Use it to find what a bond is worth at a given market yield. When the market yield is above the coupon rate the bond sells at a discount, and when it is below the bond sells at a premium.

bootstrap-spot-rates.text: Discount factor for year n = (1 - par yield n x sum of earlier discount factors) / (1 + par yield n); Spot rate n = DF^(-1/n) - 1
bootstrap-spot-rates.when: Use it to turn a curve of par yields, which is how bond markets quote the curve, into zero-coupon rates that can discount any single cash flow. You work from the shortest maturity to the longest, using each answer for the next step.

break-even-analysis.text: Break-even quantity = Fixed costs / (Price - Variable cost per unit)
break-even-analysis.when: Use it to find the sales volume at which the project makes neither a profit nor a loss. Compare it with your realistic sales forecast to see how much room for error there is.

brownian-motion-facts.mathml: WT∼N(0,T),P(WT>a)=1−N ⁣(aT),P(max⁡u≤TWu≥a)=2 P(WT≥a),Corr(Ws,Wt)=s/tW_{T}\sim N(0,T),\quad P(W_{T}>a)=1-N\!\left(\tfrac{a}{\sqrt{T}}\right),\quad P\left(\max_{u\le T}W_{u}\ge a\right)=2\,P(W_{T}\ge a),\quad Corr(W_{s},W_{t})=\sqrt{s/t}
brownian-motion-facts.text: W_T is normal with mean 0 and variance T; P(W_T > a) = 1 - N(a / sqrt(T)); P(the path touches a before T) = 2 x P(W_T >= a); Correlation of W at times s < t = sqrt(s / t)
brownian-motion-facts.when: Use it for the basic facts about the random process behind most continuous-time models. It has independent, normally distributed increments, with variance equal to elapsed time. The reflection principle gives the chance that a path ever touches a level, which matters for barrier options and stop-losses.

bull-call-spread.mathml: Max profit=(K2−K1)−(C1−C2),Max loss=C1−C2\text{Max profit}=(K_{2}-K_{1})-(C_{1}-C_{2}),\quad \text{Max loss}=C_{1}-C_{2}
bull-call-spread.text: Buy a call at the lower strike K1 and sell a call at the higher strike K2. Net cost = C1 - C2; Max profit = (K2 - K1) - net cost; Breakeven = K1 + net cost
bull-call-spread.when: Use it when you expect a moderate rise. The call you sell pays for part of the call you buy, so the cost is lower, but the profit is capped at the higher strike.

bnpl-merchant-breakeven.mathml: Δπ=(1+u) (m−f)−m,u∗=fm−f\Delta\pi=(1+u)\,(m-f)-m,\quad u^{*}=\frac{f}{m-f}
bnpl-merchant-breakeven.text: Merchant profit per 100 of base sales = base sales x margin; with BNPL: sales x (1 + lift) x (margin - fee); Break-even lift u* = fee / (margin - fee); Customer pays nothing extra when paid on time, so the lender earns from merchant fees and late fees
bnpl-merchant-breakeven.when: Use it to decide whether a merchant gains from offering pay-in-installments. The fee is typically higher than a card fee, so sales must rise enough to pay it. For the lender, the merchant fee must cover credit losses, funding and late-payment risk. The calculation counts only merchant profit and ignores returns and repeat purchases.

buyout-value-creation.mathml: MOIC=EexitEentry,IRR=MOIC1/n−1,ΔE=(EBITDA1−EBITDA0)m0⏟growth+(m1−m0)EBITDA1⏟multiple+(D0−D1)⏟deleveragingMOIC=\frac{E_{exit}}{E_{entry}},\quad IRR=MOIC^{1/n}-1,\quad \Delta E=\underbrace{(EBITDA_{1}-EBITDA_{0})m_{0}}_{growth}+\underbrace{(m_{1}-m_{0})EBITDA_{1}}_{multiple}+\underbrace{(D_{0}-D_{1})}_{deleveraging}
buyout-value-creation.text: Entry equity = EBITDA x entry multiple x (1 - debt share); Exit equity = EBITDA at exit x exit multiple - remaining debt; MOIC = exit equity / entry equity; IRR = MOIC^(1/years) - 1 when there are no interim payouts; Gain splits into EBITDA growth x entry multiple, multiple change x exit EBITDA, and debt paid down
buyout-value-creation.when: Use it to see where a buyout return comes from. A fund buys with a lot of debt, grows earnings, pays debt down with cash flow and sells. Splitting the gain into growth, multiple change and deleveraging shows how much was skill and how much was luck in the exit price. It assumes no payouts between entry and exit.

option-payoffs.mathml: Call payoff=max⁡(ST−K,0),Put payoff=max⁡(K−ST,0)\text{Call payoff}=\max(S_{T}-K,0),\quad \text{Put payoff}=\max(K-S_{T},0)
option-payoffs.text: Call payoff = max(Spot at expiry - Strike, 0); Put payoff = max(Strike - Spot at expiry, 0); Profit = Payoff - Premium paid (a seller's profit is the opposite)
option-payoffs.when: Use it to draw or calculate the result of holding an option to expiry. The buyer's loss is limited to the premium. The seller's loss on a call is unlimited, and on a put it is limited to the strike minus the premium. The breakeven is where profit crosses zero.

callable-bond-value.text: Callable bond price = Straight bond price - Value of the call option; Putable bond price = Straight bond price + Value of the put option
callable-bond-value.when: Use it to price a bond with an embedded option. The issuer owns a call option, so the holder gets a lower price. The holder owns a put option, so the bond is worth more. The option value comes from an interest rate model such as a binomial tree.

capital-allocation-line.mathml: E(Rc)=rf+y [E(Rp)−rf],σc=y σp,y∗=E(Rp)−rfAσp2E(R_{c})=r_{f}+y\,[E(R_{p})-r_{f}],\quad \sigma_{c}=y\,\sigma_{p},\quad y^{*}=\frac{E(R_{p})-r_{f}}{A\sigma_{p}^{2}}
capital-allocation-line.text: Complete portfolio return = rf + y x (E(Rp) - rf); risk = y x sp; optimal y = (E(Rp) - rf) / (A x sp^2)
capital-allocation-line.when: Use it to split money between a risky portfolio and a risk-free asset. The line shows every risk and return combination you can reach, and the optimal y picks the point that suits your risk aversion.

urr-implicit-tax.text: Implicit tax of an unremunerated reserve requirement (annualized) = interest rate x share of the inflow that must be deposited x (years the deposit is held / years of the loan); Transaction tax annualized = tax per transaction x 365 / holding days
urr-implicit-tax.when: Use it to see why short-term capital is hit hardest by controls. A requirement to deposit part of an inflow for a year is the same as a fixed fee, and that fee is far heavier per year on a 3-month loan than on a 3-year one. A small transaction tax works in the same way. These measures aim to discourage hot money but can also raise costs for firms, and they tend to be evaded over time.

capital-gains-tax.text: Capital gain = sale proceeds - cost basis; Taxable gain = gain minus any capital losses used against it (not below 0); Tax = capital gains rate (short-term or long-term depending on holding period) x taxable gain + dividend tax rate x dividends
capital-gains-tax.when: Use it to estimate the tax cost of selling or of holding income-paying investments. Holding past the long-term threshold often cuts the rate, and losses can offset gains. Rules differ widely by country (some have no capital gains tax, others tax gains as ordinary income), so enter the rates and thresholds from your own tax rules. The rates below are illustrative.

capital-market-line.text: Expected return = rf + (E(Rm) - rf) / sm x sp
capital-market-line.when: Use it to find the best expected return available for a given level of total risk, by mixing the market portfolio with the risk-free asset. It applies to efficient, well-diversified portfolios only.

carbon-abatement-decision.mathml: Abate if MACj<P,C=∑abatedqjMACj+P×(Need−∑qj)\text{Abate if } MAC_{j}<P,\quad C=\sum_{abated}q_{j}MAC_{j}+P\times(\text{Need}-\sum q_{j})
carbon-abatement-decision.text: Shortfall = emissions - permits held; Abate each metric ton whose marginal abatement cost (MAC) is below the permit price, cheapest first, until the shortfall is closed; Cost of abatement = sum of (metric tons x MAC) over measures used; Permits to buy = shortfall not abated; Total cost = abatement cost + permits bought x price; Compare with buying permits for the whole shortfall
carbon-abatement-decision.when: Use it to see why a carbon price makes cuts happen where they are cheapest. A firm facing a permit price compares each abatement option with the price of simply buying permits. Trading lets the total cut be done at the lowest overall cost. This sketch takes the price as given and measures as separate, which real markets do not.

carhart-model.text: Expected return = rf + b_mkt x MKT + b_smb x SMB + b_hml x HML + b_wml x WML
carhart-model.when: Use it to add momentum to the Fama-French model. Stocks that have recently risen tend to keep rising for a while, and this factor captures that.

carry-trade-return.mathml: R=(1+ih)(1+Δs)−(1+il),Δs∗=1+il1+ih−1R=(1+i_{h})(1+\Delta s)-(1+i_{l}),\quad \Delta s^{*}=\frac{1+i_{l}}{1+i_{h}}-1
carry-trade-return.text: Return per unit borrowed = (1 + high-yield rate) x (1 + change in the high-yield currency) - (1 + funding rate); Break-even currency move = (1 + funding rate) / (1 + high rate) - 1; Levered return = leverage x return per unit
carry-trade-return.when: Use it to size the risk of a carry trade: borrow in a low-rate currency and lend in a high-rate one. The trade earns the rate gap if the exchange rate holds, and loses if the high-yield currency falls by more than the break-even. Returns are small and steady, with rare sharp losses when the funding currency surges in a crisis, and leverage multiplies both sides.

cash-conversion-cycle.text: Cash conversion cycle = Days inventory + Days sales outstanding - Days payables
cash-conversion-cycle.when: Use it to see how long cash is tied up in the business. A shorter cycle means the company needs less financing for its working capital.

cash-conversion-from-statements.text: DIO = Average inventory / COGS x 365; DSO = Average receivables / Revenue x 365; DPO = Average payables / COGS x 365; Cash conversion cycle = DIO + DSO - DPO
cash-conversion-from-statements.when: Use it to see how long cash is tied up between paying suppliers and collecting from customers. A shorter cycle frees cash. A negative cycle means suppliers fund the business. This version builds each part from the statements, where the Corporate Finance entry takes the day counts as inputs.

cash-flow-quality.text: CFO / Net income; CFO / EBITDA; Cash flow adequacy = CFO / (Capex + Dividends + Debt repayments)
cash-flow-quality.when: Use it to judge whether operations pay for themselves. CFO well above net income is usually a sign of good quality (but check for working capital being squeezed). Adequacy above 1 means operating cash covers investment, dividends and debt repayment without outside funding.

cash-ratio-defensive-interval.mathml: Cash ratio=Cash+SecuritiesCurrent liabilities,DIM=Cash+Securities+ReceivablesDaily cash expenses\text{Cash ratio}=\frac{\text{Cash}+\text{Securities}}{\text{Current liabilities}},\quad DIM=\frac{\text{Cash}+\text{Securities}+\text{Receivables}}{\text{Daily cash expenses}}
cash-ratio-defensive-interval.text: Cash ratio = (Cash + Marketable securities) / Current liabilities; Defensive interval = (Cash + Securities + Receivables) / Daily cash operating expenses
cash-ratio-defensive-interval.when: Use it as the strictest liquidity test, ahead of the current and quick ratios. The cash ratio asks whether cash alone covers short-term debts. The defensive interval asks how many days the company could operate with no new sales.

cash-runway.text: Runway (months) = Cash balance / Net monthly cash burn
cash-runway.when: Use it to plan liquidity, especially for startups and firms that spend more than they earn. A short runway means funding must be raised soon, or costs cut.

cat-bond-expected-loss.mathml: EL=pa×s,Multiple=SpreadEL,E[R]=rf+Spread−ELEL=p_{a}\times s,\quad \text{Multiple}=\frac{\text{Spread}}{EL},\quad E[R]=r_{f}+\text{Spread}-EL
cat-bond-expected-loss.text: Expected loss = probability of attachment (the event hits the bond) x average share of principal lost when it does; Multiple = spread / expected loss; Expected return = risk-free rate + spread - expected loss; Probability of losing money in a year = probability of attachment
cat-bond-expected-loss.when: Use it to price and compare catastrophe bonds. A bond pays a high coupon, but investors lose principal if a defined event (a hurricane or earthquake) occurs. Because disaster risk is little related to the stock market, the spread is paid for risk that diversifies other holdings. The expected loss estimate comes from modeling firms, so model error is the main risk.

cdo-equity-return.text: Equity return = (Interest earned on the assets - Interest paid on each debt tranche - Fees - Credit losses) / Equity invested
cdo-equity-return.when: Use it to see how a CDO magnifies returns for its equity holders. The equity tranche borrows cheaply from the debt tranches, so it keeps the spread between the asset yield and the liability costs, and also takes the first losses. That makes it high-return and high-risk.

ccp-initial-margin.text: Initial margin = z-score x Daily volatility x Square root of margin period of risk (days) x Position size
ccp-initial-margin.when: Use it to see how a clearing house sets collateral. The central counterparty stands between buyers and sellers. It asks for margin big enough to cover a large loss over the days it would take to close a defaulting member's position. Longer close-out periods, more volatile markets and bigger positions mean more margin.

cet1-ratio.mathml: RWA=∑wiEi,CET1 ratio=CET1RWA,Leverage ratio=Tier 1Total exposureRWA=\sum w_{i}E_{i},\quad CET1\ ratio=\frac{CET1}{RWA},\quad \text{Leverage ratio}=\frac{\text{Tier 1}}{\text{Total exposure}}
cet1-ratio.text: Risk-weighted assets = sum of (risk weight x exposure); CET1 ratio = common equity tier 1 capital / RWA; Tier 1 ratio = (CET1 + additional tier 1) / RWA; Total capital ratio = (Tier 1 + Tier 2) / RWA; Leverage ratio = Tier 1 / total (unweighted) exposure
cet1-ratio.when: Use it to judge whether a bank has enough capital for the risk it takes. Regulators set minimums (under Basel III, 4.5% CET1 plus buffers, 7% with the conservation buffer) and a separate leverage ratio, which does not depend on risk weights. The headroom shows how much a bank can lose or lend before it hits a limit. Local requirements differ, so enter your own.

classification-metrics.mathml: Precision=TPTP+FP,  Recall=TPTP+FN,  F1=2 P RP+R,  Accuracy=TP+TNTP+FP+FN+TNPrecision=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\; Recall=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\; F_{1}=\frac{2\,P\,R}{P+R},\; Accuracy=\frac{TP+TN}{TP+FP+FN+TN}
classification-metrics.text: Precision = TP / (TP + FP); Recall = TP / (TP + FN); F1 = 2 x Precision x Recall / (Precision + Recall); Accuracy = (TP + TN) / total
classification-metrics.when: Use it to judge a model that sorts cases into classes, such as default or no default, or fraud or genuine. When the event is rare, accuracy misleads: a model that never flags anything can be 98% accurate. Precision tells you how many flags are real, recall how many real cases were caught, and F1 balances the two.

weighted-average-carbon-intensity.text: Weighted average carbon intensity = sum of (portfolio weight x company emissions / company revenue), in metric tons of CO2 equivalent per million of revenue; Financed emissions = sum of (amount invested or lent / company enterprise value including cash) x company emissions; Portfolio footprint per million invested = financed emissions / total invested
weighted-average-carbon-intensity.when: Use it to report climate exposure of a portfolio or loan book in the way supported by TCFD and ISSB. WACI shows how carbon-intensive the holdings are relative to their sales; financed emissions assigns a share of each company's emissions to the investor in proportion to its stake. Data quality varies, since many companies report estimates.

clo-oc-test.text: OC ratio for class k = Collateral par value / (Total of the notes in class k and every class senior to it)
clo-oc-test.when: Use it to check the cushion each CLO note class has. Each class is tested against its own trigger. If the ratio falls below the trigger, interest that would go to junior holders is used to repay senior notes instead, which protects the senior investors.

coefficient-of-variation.when: Use it to compare the risk of investments that have different average returns. A lower CV means less risk for each unit of return.

cointegration-half-life.mathml: β=Cov(Y,X)Var(X),  st=Yt−βXt−α,  st=ϕst−1+ε,  t1/2=−ln⁡2ln⁡ϕ\beta=\frac{Cov(Y,X)}{Var(X)},\; s_{t}=Y_{t}-\beta X_{t}-\alpha,\; s_{t}=\phi s_{t-1}+\varepsilon,\; t_{1/2}=\frac{-\ln 2}{\ln\phi}
cointegration-half-life.text: Hedge ratio beta = Covariance(Y, X) / Variance(X); Spread = Y - beta x X - alpha; Fit spread today = phi x spread yesterday; Half-life = -ln 2 / ln(phi)
cointegration-half-life.when: Use it to test whether two prices share a long-run link. Each price may wander, but if a mix of them is stable the pair is cointegrated and the gap tends to close. The half-life says how fast. A full test also needs a unit-root test on the spread (Engle-Granger), which this calculator does not run, so treat the result as a screen and not proof.

collar-payoff.text: Collar value at expiry = min( max(Price at expiry, Put strike), Call strike ); Profit = Value - Stock price paid - Net premium
collar-payoff.when: Use it to protect a share you own at low cost. The put sets a floor under the value, and selling a call pays for the put but caps the upside. A collar with a net premium near zero is called a zero-cost collar.

collectible-net-return.text: Annual return before holding costs = [ (sale price x (1 - seller cost)) / (purchase price x (1 + buyer cost)) ] ^ (1 / years) - 1; Net return = that return - insurance rate - storage rate; Break-even sale price = purchase price x (1 + buyer cost) x (1 + hurdle)^years / (1 - seller cost)
collectible-net-return.when: Use it before buying art, wine, watches or other collectibles. They pay no income, trade rarely and cost a lot to buy and sell, so the price has to rise a good deal just to break even. Compare the net result with what a stock index would have returned. Reported auction results show only the items that sold, so published returns can look better than a typical buyer's experience.

combined-ratio.text: Combined ratio = (Claims paid + Operating expenses) / Premiums earned
combined-ratio.when: Use it to judge whether an insurer makes money from underwriting alone. Below 100% it makes an underwriting profit. Above 100% it relies on investment income to make a profit.

commercial-paper-yield.text: Price = Face x (1 - discount rate x days / 360); Yield = (Face - Price) / Price x 365 / days
commercial-paper-yield.when: Use it for discount instruments such as commercial paper, which are issued below face value and repaid at face value. The quoted discount rate understates the true cost of borrowing.

commodity-roll-yield.mathml: Basis=S−F,Roll yield per roll=FnearFfar−1\text{Basis}=S-F,\quad \text{Roll yield per roll}=\frac{F_{near}}{F_{far}}-1
commodity-roll-yield.text: Basis = Spot - Futures; Roll yield = Near futures price / Next futures price - 1 (negative in contango, positive in backwardation)
commodity-roll-yield.when: Use it to see what rolling a futures position costs or earns. In contango (the futures curve slopes up) a long investor sells the cheaper near contract and buys the dearer far one, losing roll yield. In backwardation the curve slopes down and the long investor gains.

commodity-futures-total-return.text: Roll yield per roll = (near futures price - next futures price) / near futures price (negative in contango, positive in backwardation); Annualized roll = (1 + roll)^(12 / months between contracts) - 1; Total return of a futures investment = spot price change + roll yield + interest on the cash collateral; Implied convenience yield y = interest rate + storage cost - (1/T) x ln(F / S)
commodity-futures-total-return.when: Use it to see why returns on a commodity futures fund can differ from the spot price. A futures investor sells the contract that is expiring and buys the next one. When the curve slopes up (contango), each roll costs money; when it slopes down (backwardation), each roll adds money. Over years roll yield can matter as much as the price change.

commodity-hedge-effective-price.text: Effective price = Spot at sale + Futures gain = Initial futures price + Final basis; Optimal hedge ratio = Correlation x Std dev of spot changes / Std dev of futures changes
commodity-hedge-effective-price.when: Use it to see what a hedger really receives. A producer sells futures to lock in a price, but the basis (spot minus futures) can move, which is basis risk. The hedge ratio finds the quantity to hedge when spot and futures are not perfectly correlated.

common-size-statement.text: Common-size percentage = Line item / Base, where the base is revenue for an income statement and total assets for a balance sheet
common-size-statement.when: Use it to compare companies of different size, or one company over time, by turning every line into a percentage of one base. Changes in the percentages show where costs or assets have grown faster than the business.

comparative-advantage.text: Opportunity cost of one unit of wine, in cloth = hours per wine / hours per cloth. The country with the lower opportunity cost has the comparative advantage. Both gain if they trade at a price (terms of trade) between the two opportunity costs
comparative-advantage.when: Use it to see why trade benefits both sides even when one country is better at everything. What counts is the relative cost, not the absolute cost. Each country should specialize where its opportunity cost is lower and trade for the rest. Real trade also faces transport costs, tariffs, and supply-chain risk, which can outweigh small gains.

cagr.when: Use it to describe growth over several years as one smooth yearly rate, for example the growth of an investment, sales or a population.

conditional-probability.text: P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B)
conditional-probability.when: Use it when you have extra information and want to update a probability, for example the chance a company defaults given that the economy is in recession.

confidence-interval-mean.when: Use it to give a range that is likely to contain the true average, based on a sample. It works best when the sample is reasonably large.

conflict-of-interest-cost.text: Value with a fiduciary adviser who charges f = V0 x (1 + r - f)^n; Value with a product that also pays the adviser a yearly commission c = V0 x (1 + r - f - c)^n; Cost of the conflict = difference between the two; Share of ending value lost = 1 - (1 + r - f - c)^n / (1 + r - f)^n
conflict-of-interest-cost.when: Use it to see why fiduciary duty (acting in the client's best interest) matters. A suitability standard allows an adviser to sell a product that is suitable but pays them more. A one-percentage-point difference in yearly cost looks small but compounds into a large share of the final amount over many years.

laspeyres-cpi.text: Laspeyres (CPI style) = cost of the OLD basket at new prices / cost of the old basket at old prices x 100; Paasche = cost of the NEW basket at new prices / cost of the new basket at old prices x 100; Fisher = square root of (Laspeyres x Paasche)
laspeyres-cpi.when: Use it to see how a price index is built and why measures differ. A fixed basket (CPI style) overstates inflation when people switch to cheaper items. An index using current quantities (Paasche) tends to understate it. PCE and chain-weighted measures update the weights to reduce this gap. Headline inflation is the change in the index over time.

short-term-fee-apr.text: Simple annualized rate = (fee / amount borrowed) x (365 / days borrowed); Effective annual rate if the loan is rolled over again and again = (1 + fee / amount)^(365 / days) - 1; Consumer rules require firms to disclose the annual percentage rate so short-term products can be compared with other credit
short-term-fee-apr.when: Use it to see the true cost of an overdraft fee or a payday loan. A fee that looks small becomes a very high rate once it is expressed per year, which is why laws require the rate to be shown (Truth in Lending in the US) and why some places cap it. Use the rolled-over rate only if the borrower really renews every time.

continuous-compounding.text: FV = PV x e^(r x t)
continuous-compounding.when: Use it when interest is added at every instant, as a limit of ever more frequent compounding. It is common in derivatives pricing and in theory.

convertible-bond-value.mathml: CR=ParConversion price,CV=CR×Pshare,Premium=Bond priceCV−1CR=\frac{\text{Par}}{\text{Conversion price}},\quad CV=CR\times P_{share},\quad \text{Premium}=\frac{\text{Bond price}}{CV}-1
convertible-bond-value.text: Conversion ratio = Par / Conversion price; Conversion value = Conversion ratio x Share price; Premium = Bond price / Conversion value - 1
convertible-bond-value.when: Use it to see what a convertible bond is worth if converted into shares, and how much extra investors pay for the bond's downside protection.

convertible-premium.mathml: Conversion value=CR×S,Conversion price=FCR,Premium=PconvCR×S−1\text{Conversion value}=CR\times S,\quad \text{Conversion price}=\frac{F}{CR},\quad \text{Premium}=\frac{P_{conv}}{CR\times S}-1
convertible-premium.text: Conversion value = Conversion ratio x Share price; Conversion price = Face value / Conversion ratio; Premium over conversion value = Bond price / Conversion value - 1; Floor = higher of conversion value and straight bond value
convertible-premium.when: Use it to judge a convertible bond. Its value is at least the larger of its straight bond value (the bond floor) and what it would be worth if converted. The market pays a premium above both because the holder keeps the upside of the shares while having the safety of the bond.

ear-to-apr.text: Periodic rate = (1 + EAR)^(1/m) - 1, and APR = m x periodic rate
ear-to-apr.when: Use it to work backwards from a known true yearly rate, for example to find the monthly rate that equals a 12.68% effective annual rate.

corporate-bond-yield.text: Corporate bond yield = Government yield for the same maturity + Credit spread + Liquidity premium
corporate-bond-yield.when: Use it to understand what makes up a corporate bond yield, or to price a new corporate bond from the government curve. The price then follows from the bond price formula at that yield.

correlation.when: Use it to measure how closely two returns move together on a scale from -1 to +1. A value near +1 means they move together, near 0 means no linear link, and near -1 means they move in opposite directions.

capm-cost-of-equity.text: Cost of equity = Risk-free rate + Beta x Equity risk premium
capm-cost-of-equity.when: Use it to estimate the return shareholders expect for the risk they take, which becomes the discount rate for equity cash flows and an input to WACC.

dividend-growth-cost-of-equity.text: Cost of equity = Next dividend / Current price + Growth rate
dividend-growth-cost-of-equity.when: Use it for a stable dividend-paying company as a cross-check on CAPM. It rests on the Gordon growth model, so it only suits companies with steady dividend growth.

mm-cost-of-equity.text: Cost of equity = r0 + (r0 - rd) x D/E x (1 - T)
mm-cost-of-equity.when: Use it to see why shareholders demand a higher return as a firm borrows more: the debt makes their returns riskier. It shows that cheap debt does not make the firm cheaper to finance in a no-tax world.

fee-drag.text: Final value = Amount invested x (1 + gross return - annual fee)^years
fee-drag.when: Use it to see what fees cost over time. Because fees come out of the balance each year, they compound too. An active fund must earn more than its passive rival, by at least the fee difference, just to match it.

cost-of-goods-sold.text: COGS = Beginning inventory + Purchases - Ending inventory
cost-of-goods-sold.when: Use it to work out the cost of the goods that were sold. The method you use to value inventory (FIFO, LIFO or weighted average) changes the ending inventory figure, and so changes COGS.

flotation-adjusted-cost-of-equity.text: Cost of new equity = Next dividend / (Price x (1 - flotation cost)) + Growth rate
flotation-adjusted-cost-of-equity.when: Use it when the company raises money by selling new shares. Underwriting and issue fees reduce the proceeds, so new equity costs more than retained earnings.

cost-of-preferred.text: Cost of preferred = Preferred dividend / (Price x (1 - flotation cost))
cost-of-preferred.when: Use it for the preferred part of WACC. Preferred dividends are fixed and paid forever, so the share is valued like a perpetuity.

cost-of-trade-credit.text: Effective annual cost = (1 + d / (1 - d))^(365 / (Final due day - Discount day)) - 1
cost-of-trade-credit.when: Use it to decide whether to pay early. A "2/10 net 30" term gives 2% off if paid within 10 days, otherwise the full amount is due in 30. Skipping the discount is like borrowing at a very high rate.

regulation-cost-benefit.mathml: NB=Δp×L−C,Δp∗=CLNB=\Delta p\times L-C,\quad \Delta p^{*}=\frac{C}{L}
regulation-cost-benefit.text: Expected yearly benefit = reduction in the yearly chance of a crisis x cost of a crisis to the economy; Net benefit = expected benefit - yearly cost of complying; Break-even reduction in crisis chance = compliance cost / crisis cost
regulation-cost-benefit.when: Use it to see why rules can be worth their cost even when firms dislike them. A failure of a bank or market costs people who are not party to the contract (an externality), so private choices alone may be too risky. A rule is worth having if the reduction in the expected crisis loss exceeds the cost of compliance. The inputs are estimates with wide uncertainty.

counterparty-exposure-netting.mathml: Gross=∑max⁡(MtMi,0),Net=max⁡(∑MtMi,0),PFE=z σt×N\text{Gross}=\sum\max(MtM_{i},0),\quad \text{Net}=\max\left(\sum MtM_{i},0\right),\quad PFE=z\,\sigma\sqrt{t}\times N
counterparty-exposure-netting.text: Gross exposure = sum of the positive trade values; Net exposure = max(sum of all trade values, 0); Potential future exposure = z-score x volatility x sqrt(time) x Notional
counterparty-exposure-netting.when: Use it to measure what you would lose if a counterparty defaulted today, and how that might grow. Under a netting agreement the trades are added together, so gains on some offset losses on others, which cuts the exposure. CVA (priced in the Derivatives section) turns the exposure profile into a money charge.

country-risk-premium.text: CRP = Sovereign default spread x (Equity volatility / Bond volatility); Cost of equity = rf + beta x ERP + CRP
country-risk-premium.when: Use it to add a premium for political and economic risk when valuing a company in a riskier country. The volatility ratio scales a bond spread up to an equity-sized premium.

covariance.text: Cov(X,Y) = sum of (xi - mean x)(yi - mean y) / (n - 1)
covariance.when: Use it to see whether two returns tend to move in the same direction (positive) or in opposite directions (negative). Its size is hard to interpret, so it is usually converted to correlation.

covered-bond-overcollateralization.text: Overcollateralization = Cover pool value / Covered bonds outstanding - 1
covered-bond-overcollateralization.when: Use it to see how much protection a covered bond holder has. Holders have a claim on the issuing bank and a first claim on the cover pool, which stays on the bank's balance sheet. The pool must exceed the bonds by a set margin.

covered-interest-arbitrage.text: Parity says the forward rate F = S x (1 + domestic rate T) / (1 + foreign rate T). If the market forward differs, borrow where it is cheaper, convert at spot, invest abroad, and sell the proceeds forward: profit = foreign proceeds at the market forward - domestic proceeds. Compare: invest K in domestic currency = K x (1 + r_d T)
covered-interest-arbitrage.when: Use it to test whether the forward rate is in line with interest rates. If the market forward is higher than parity, buying the foreign currency spot, investing it and selling it forward locks in more than the domestic deposit pays, a risk-free profit. In real markets the gap is usually smaller than costs, except in stress, when funding frictions can open a persistent gap (the cross-currency basis).

cir-moments-feller.text: Expected rate = theta + (r0 - theta) x e^(-kappa t); Variance = r0 x sigma^2 / kappa x (e^(-kappa t) - e^(-2 kappa t)) + theta x sigma^2 / (2 kappa) x (1 - e^(-kappa t))^2; the rate stays above zero if 2 x kappa x theta >= sigma^2
cir-moments-feller.when: Use it for a mean-reverting rate that cannot go negative. Shocks shrink as the rate nears zero, which keeps it positive when the Feller condition holds. If the condition fails, the rate can touch zero (it still never goes below). The same process is used for variance in the Heston model.

credit-card-payoff.text: Months to pay off = -ln(1 - i x Balance / Payment) / ln(1 + i), where i is the monthly rate (APR / 12); Payment needed to clear in n months = i x Balance / (1 - (1 + i)^(-n))
credit-card-payoff.when: Use it to see the real cost of carrying a balance. If the payment is no more than one month of interest (i x B) the balance never falls. Paying only the minimum, which shrinks as the balance falls, takes far longer than a fixed payment. This assumes no new purchases and a constant rate; promotional rates change that.

cds-spread-upfront.mathml: s≈h (1−R),Upfront=(s−c)×RPV01×N,Payout=N(1−R)s\approx h\,(1-R),\quad \text{Upfront}=(s-c)\times RPV01\times N,\quad \text{Payout}=N(1-R)
cds-spread-upfront.text: CDS spread = Hazard rate (annual default probability) x (1 - Recovery); Upfront = (Spread - Standard coupon) x Risky annuity x Notional; Payout on default = Notional x (1 - Recovery)
cds-spread-upfront.when: Use it to price protection against default. The buyer pays a yearly premium and receives the notional less the recovery if the borrower defaults. Contracts have a standard coupon, so the difference from the fair spread is settled with an upfront payment.

credit-scoring-logit.text: Probability of default = 1 / (1 + e^-(intercept + b1 x x1 + b2 x x2 + ...))
credit-scoring-logit.when: Use it to turn borrower characteristics into a default probability. The coefficients come from fitting a logistic regression on historical loans, with default as the outcome. The result is always between 0 and 1. Banks use it for scorecards on retail and small business loans.

credit-spread.text: Credit spread = Corporate yield - Government yield; Percentage price change = -Spread duration x Change in spread
credit-spread.when: Use it to measure the extra yield for credit risk and what a change in that spread does to price. A widening spread (worse credit conditions) lowers the bond price even if government yields do not move.

credit-union-member-benefit.mathml: Benefit=(ibank−icu)L+(dcu−dbank)S,Net worth ratio=Net worthAssets\text{Benefit}=(i_{bank}-i_{cu})L+(d_{cu}-d_{bank})S,\quad \text{Net worth ratio}=\frac{\text{Net worth}}{\text{Assets}}
credit-union-member-benefit.text: Yearly member benefit = (bank loan rate - credit union loan rate) x loans + (credit union savings rate - bank savings rate) x savings; Net worth ratio = net worth / total assets (7% or more counts as well capitalized in the US)
credit-union-member-benefit.when: Use it to see what member ownership is worth. A credit union is owned by its members and not by outside shareholders, so profits go back as lower loan rates and higher savings rates. The net worth ratio shows whether it has enough capital, which it can build only by retaining earnings, since it cannot sell shares. Membership rules, product range and branch access also matter.

credit-utilization.text: Credit utilization = total revolving balances / total credit limits. A common guideline is to keep it under 30%, and lower is better
credit-utilization.when: Use it to see one of the factors that scoring models weigh heavily. Scores also reward paying on time and a long history, and penalize many new applications, so utilization is only part of the picture. Scoring details vary by country and provider, so treat 30% as a guideline, not a rule.

cva-approximation.text: CVA = (1 - Recovery) x Sum over each year of [Expected positive exposure x Probability of default in that year x Discount factor]
cva-approximation.when: Use it to price the risk that the other side of an over-the-counter derivative fails to pay. CVA is the expected loss from counterparty default, and banks deduct it from the value of their derivatives. Central clearing reduces this risk by guaranteeing the trades.

triangular-arbitrage.text: Implied cross rate = EUR/USD rate x USD/JPY rate. Triangular arbitrage trades around the three currencies at the dealer's prices (buy at the ask, sell at the bid) and profits if the quoted cross differs from the implied cross by more than the spread; Spread in pips = (ask - bid) / pip size
triangular-arbitrage.when: Use it to see how the three prices in a currency triangle stay in line. Dealers quote a bid and ask, so you always buy dearer and sell cheaper, and the gap is their spread and your trading cost. Arbitrage profits are tiny and vanish quickly in liquid markets, and a profit only exists if it exceeds the spreads, which is what the calculator tests.

cross-border-payment-cost.text: Amount received = (amount sent - sender fee - correspondent fee) x bank exchange rate - receiving bank fee; All-in cost = 1 - amount received / (amount sent x mid-market exchange rate)
cross-border-payment-cost.when: Use it to see what a payment really costs. A transfer over SWIFT may pass through one or more correspondent banks that each take a fee, and the exchange-rate margin is often the largest cost but is not shown as a fee. Compare the amount received with what you would get at the mid-market rate. Fees and rates differ by route and provider.

crowdfunding-net-proceeds.text: Net proceeds = money raised x (1 - platform fee - payment fee) - fixed fee per backer x number of backers; Raise needed to receive a target G = (G + fixed fees) / (1 - platform fee - payment fee)
crowdfunding-net-proceeds.when: Use it to set a campaign goal. Fees and failed payments mean you receive less than the headline total, and you still have to pay for rewards and delivery. Set the goal from the amount you need after fees and costs, not from the amount you hope to see on the page.

crypto-etf-fee-drag.text: Value of an ETF after n years = start value x (1 + coin return - fee) multiplied over the years; Value of holding the coin directly = start value x (1 + coin return) multiplied over the years, less custody and trading costs paid; Fee drag = (direct value - ETF value) / direct value; Break-even yearly cost of self-custody = ETF fee
crypto-etf-fee-drag.when: Use it to compare buying a spot crypto ETF with holding the coin yourself. The ETF fee compounds against you every year but removes the need for wallets and keys, and it can be held in ordinary brokerage and retirement accounts. The right choice depends on size, time held and how much you value the convenience.

abnormal-return-event-window.mathml: ARt=Rt−(α+βRm,t),CAR=∑tARt,z=CARσNAR_{t}=R_{t}-(\alpha+\beta R_{m,t}),\quad CAR=\sum_{t}AR_{t},\quad z=\frac{CAR}{\sigma\sqrt{N}}
abnormal-return-event-window.text: Abnormal return on day t = stock return - (alpha + beta x market return); Cumulative abnormal return = sum of abnormal returns over the window before the announcement; z-score = CAR / (daily residual volatility x square root of the number of days); Large unexplained run-ups before news can prompt an investigation
abnormal-return-event-window.when: Use it to see how surveillance teams flag possible trading on secret information. A stock that rises well beyond what the market explains in the days before a takeover announcement is a warning sign, not proof. Other news, rumors or analysis can explain the move. The test compares the run-up with normal day-to-day noise.

cumulative-voting.text: Shares needed = rounded down (Total shares x Seats wanted / (Seats up for election + 1)) + 1
cumulative-voting.when: Use it to see how many shares a minority shareholder needs to win board seats under cumulative voting. This system lets each holder put all their votes on one candidate, which helps minorities.

currency-swap-cash-flows.text: Foreign notional = Home notional / Exchange rate at the start; Value to the party paying USD and receiving EUR = Exchange rate now x Value of the EUR leg - Value of the USD leg
currency-swap-cash-flows.when: Use it to lay out a currency swap. The parties exchange principal at the start, pay interest on it in the other currency each year, and swap the principal back at the end at the original rate. The value changes with both currencies' interest rates and the exchange rate.

current-ratio.text: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities
current-ratio.when: Use it to judge whether a company can pay its short-term bills. A ratio above 1 means current assets cover current liabilities.

current-yield-ytc.mathml: CY=Annual couponP,P=∑C(1+y/m)k+Call price(1+y/m)Ncall solved for yCY=\frac{\text{Annual coupon}}{P},\quad P=\sum\frac{C}{(1+y/m)^{k}}+\frac{\text{Call price}}{(1+y/m)^{N_{call}}}\ \text{solved for }y
current-yield-ytc.text: Current yield = Annual coupon / Price; Yield to call = the yield that makes the coupons up to the call date plus the call price worth today's price
current-yield-ytc.when: Use the current yield for a quick income figure. Use the yield to call when a bond trades above its call price, because the issuer is then likely to redeem it early. The lowest of the yield to maturity and the yield to call is the yield to worst.

ltv-to-cac.text: LTV = Yearly revenue per customer x Gross margin / Yearly churn rate; LTV:CAC = LTV / Cost to acquire a customer
ltv-to-cac.when: Use it to judge whether a growth business earns back what it spends to win customers. A ratio of about 3 or more is often seen as healthy.

security-control-rosi.text: Expected yearly loss (ALE) = loss per incident x incidents per year, summed over threats; Risk reduction = ALE before - ALE after the control; Return on security investment = (risk reduction - cost of the control) / cost of the control; Break-even reduction = cost of the control / ALE before
security-control-rosi.when: Use it to compare security spending with the loss it prevents. Estimate the yearly expected loss before and after a control (such as multi-factor authentication or staff training). A positive return means the control pays for itself in expected terms, though rare severe events are hard to estimate and one breach can threaten a firm.

days-sales-outstanding.text: DSO = Receivables / Sales x 365; Receivables turnover = Sales / Receivables
days-sales-outstanding.when: Use it to see how quickly customers pay. A rising DSO means customers are paying more slowly, which ties up cash and can signal credit problems.

dcf-capstone-bridge.text: Enterprise value = present value of five forecast free cash flows + present value of terminal value; Terminal value = last cash flow x (1 + growth) / (WACC - growth); Equity value = enterprise value - net debt; Value per share = equity value / shares; Share of value in the terminal value = PV of terminal value / enterprise value
dcf-capstone-bridge.when: Use it as the last step after forecasting a real company's cash flows from its statements. Show the answer as a range, since the terminal value usually carries most of the value and small changes in WACC and growth move the answer a lot. Compare the implied multiple with peers as a sense check.

dcf-enterprise-value.text: EV = sum of FCFF_t / (1 + WACC)^t for t = 1 to n, plus Terminal value / (1 + WACC)^n
dcf-enterprise-value.when: Use it to value a business from its forecast cash flows. Check what share of the value comes from the terminal value, because a very high share means the answer rests on a distant guess.

trial-balance.when: Use it as the basic check on bookkeeping. After recording every transaction, total debits must equal total credits. If they do not, there is an error to find.

debt-ratio.mathml: Debt ratio=Total liabilitiesTotal assets\text{Debt ratio} = \frac{\text{Total liabilities}}{\text{Total assets}}
debt-ratio.text: Debt ratio = Total liabilities / Total assets
debt-ratio.when: Use it to see what share of a company's assets is financed by debt. A ratio of 0.4 means 40% of the assets are funded by what the company owes.

debt-to-equity.when: Use it to see how much a company relies on borrowing compared with its owners' money. A higher ratio means more leverage and usually more risk.

dti-ratios.text: Front-end ratio = housing payment / gross monthly income; Back-end ratio = (housing payment + other debt payments) / gross monthly income; Maximum housing payment = the smaller of 28% of income and 36% of income - other debt payments
dti-ratios.when: Use it to see how lenders judge affordability. The 28% and 36% limits are a traditional guideline; lenders vary and some allow higher. The result is the most you could be approved for, not what is comfortable, so budget below it. Convert the maximum payment to a loan size using the loan payment formula.

default-enrollment-effect.mathml: ΔN=N (pout−pin),ΔFV=ΔN×C (1+r)n−1r\Delta N=N\,(p_{out}-p_{in}),\quad \Delta FV=\Delta N\times C\,\frac{(1+r)^{n}-1}{r}
default-enrollment-effect.text: Extra participants = workers x (participation with automatic enrollment - participation with opt-in); Extra savings per year = extra participants x salary x contribution rate; Extra retirement balance = extra participants x yearly contribution x ((1 + r)^n - 1) / r
default-enrollment-effect.when: Use it to see the size of a "nudge". Making saving the default, and leaving people free to opt out, raises participation sharply because inertia works in favor of saving. The calculation values a change in how a choice is presented without any change in incentives. Real programs also set default contribution rates and investments, and some people lower their own contributions when the default is low, so net effects can be smaller.

default-probability-from-spread.text: Annual default probability = Spread / (1 - Recovery rate); Cumulative default probability over n years = 1 - (1 - PD)^n; Expected loss = PD x (1 - R) x Exposure
default-probability-from-spread.when: Use it to turn a credit spread into a rough default probability, or to estimate expected loss on a loan or bond. It treats the whole spread as compensation for default, ignoring liquidity and risk premiums, so it overstates default risk.

deferred-tax.mathml: Tax expense=t×PBT,Current tax=t×(PBT−Extra tax depreciation),Deferred tax=Expense−Current\text{Tax expense}=t\times PBT,\quad \text{Current tax}=t\times(PBT-\text{Extra tax depreciation}),\quad \text{Deferred tax}=\text{Expense}-\text{Current}
deferred-tax.text: Tax expense = Tax rate x Pre-tax book profit; Current tax payable = Tax rate x (Pre-tax profit - Extra depreciation allowed for tax); Deferred tax = Tax expense - Current tax
deferred-tax.when: Use it to see why the tax expense in the income statement differs from the tax actually paid. When the tax authority allows faster depreciation than the accounts use, tax paid now is lower and a deferred tax liability builds up, which reverses later. Analysts treat a growing deferred tax liability on a growing business as close to permanent.

amm-constant-product-swap.mathml: x y=k,Δy=y−kx+Δx(1−ϕ),Slippage=1−Δy/Δxy/xx\,y=k,\quad \Delta y=y-\frac{k}{x+\Delta x(1-\phi)},\quad \text{Slippage}=1-\frac{\Delta y/\Delta x}{y/x}
amm-constant-product-swap.text: A pool holds x of token A and y of token B and keeps x times y constant; Selling dx of A (after a fee share phi) pays out dy = y - x y / (x + dx x (1 - phi)); Pool price before = y / x; Average price paid = dy / dx; Slippage = 1 - average price / pool price
amm-constant-product-swap.when: Use it to understand how a decentralized exchange sets prices without an order book. The price moves with every trade along a curve, so a large trade relative to the pool gets a worse average price. Liquidity providers earn the fee but face the loss shown in the next entry.

db-vs-dc-pension.text: Defined benefit pension = accrual rate x years of service x final salary; Its value at retirement = pension x annuity factor, where annuity factor = (1 - (1 + r)^(-n)) / r; Defined contribution pot = yearly contribution x ((1 + g)^N - 1) / g; Income the pot can buy = pot / annuity factor
db-vs-dc-pension.when: Use it to compare who bears the risk. In a defined benefit plan the employer promises the income and bears the investment and longevity risk. In a defined contribution plan the worker gets whatever the pot buys, so the worker bears the risk. The comparison shows what contribution would be needed to match a promised pension. Real plans have indexation, tax rules and survivor benefits.

degree-of-combined-leverage.when: Use it to see the total effect of fixed operating costs and borrowing together. A firm with both high fixed costs and high debt has very volatile earnings.

degree-of-financial-leverage.when: Use it to see how much borrowing magnifies swings in profit available to shareholders. A firm with no debt has a DFL of 1.

degree-of-operating-leverage.text: DOL = Contribution margin / EBIT = Q x (P - VC) / (Q x (P - VC) - FC)
degree-of-operating-leverage.when: Use it to see how much a firm's operating profit swings when sales change. The higher the fixed costs, the higher the DOL, the bigger the swing in both directions.

delta-hedge-shares.mathml: Shares to hold=Δ×N×M,ΔC≈Δ ΔS+12Γ(ΔS)2\text{Shares to hold}=\Delta\times N\times M,\quad \Delta C\approx\Delta\,\Delta S+\tfrac{1}{2}\Gamma(\Delta S)^{2}
delta-hedge-shares.text: Shares held to hedge short options = Delta x Number of options x Shares per option; Option price change = Delta x Stock change + 0.5 x Gamma x Stock change^2
delta-hedge-shares.when: Use it to make a short option position insensitive to small moves in the stock by holding delta shares per option. The hedge breaks down for large moves because delta changes (gamma), so it is rebalanced as the stock moves. The leftover loss from gamma is the hedging error.

deposit-insurance-coverage.text: Insured amount = sum over depositors of the smaller of their balance and the coverage limit; Uninsured = total deposits - insured; Premium = premium rate x assessment base (often insured deposits or total liabilities, depending on the scheme)
deposit-insurance-coverage.when: Use it to see how much of a bank's deposits are protected. Insured depositors have little reason to run, so a high insured share lowers run risk.
