Large uninsured balances are the flighty part. Coverage rules (limits, account categories, premium base) differ by country, so enter your own scheme's numbers. Limits here are per depositor per bank.

disability-coverage-gap.text: Monthly benefit = replacement % x monthly income; Monthly gap = monthly expenses - benefit; Cash needed for the waiting period = months waiting x monthly expenses
disability-coverage-gap.when: Use it to see whether disability cover would keep you afloat. A policy usually replaces only part of income and pays only after a waiting period, so you need savings to bridge that wait. Whether the benefit is taxed depends on who pays the premiums and on local rules, so this uses the benefit as received.

illiquidity-discount.text: Private company value = Marketable minority value x (1 - Discount for lack of marketability)
illiquidity-discount.when: Use it to value a private company from public comparables. Private shares are harder to sell, so they are worth less than similar listed ones. A control premium may be added back if the buyer gets control.

discounted-payback.mathml: Discounted payback: use CFt(1+r)t in the payback calculation\text{Discounted payback: use }\frac{CF_{t}}{(1+r)^{t}}\text{ in the payback calculation}
discounted-payback.text: Discounted payback = payback calculated on each cash flow divided by (1 + r)^t
discounted-payback.when: Use it when you want payback that respects the time value of money. It is always longer than the simple payback, and it ignores cash flows after the payback point.

disposition-effect-pgr-plr.text: Proportion of gains realized = realized gains / (realized gains + paper gains); Proportion of losses realized = realized losses / (realized losses + paper losses); Disposition effect = PGR - PLR (positive means winners are sold more readily than losers)
disposition-effect-pgr-plr.when: Use it to check your own selling behavior. Investors tend to sell winners to lock in gains and hold losers hoping to break even, which is the reverse of what tax rules favor. A PGR well above PLR is a sign. Count positions on days when you sold something, as in the original study, so you do not mix in days with no decision.

diversification-n-assets.text: Variance of n equal-weighted assets = s^2 / n + (1 - 1/n) x rho x s^2
diversification-n-assets.when: Use it to see how adding assets cuts risk. The first term (the risk specific to each asset) shrinks as n grows. The second term (the risk common to all assets) does not, and it is the part you cannot diversify away.

gordon-growth-model.text: Price = D0 x (1 + g) / (r - g) = D1 / (r - g)
gordon-growth-model.when: Use it to value a stable, mature company that pays dividends growing at a steady rate. It is very sensitive to g and r, and it fails when g is close to or above r.

dividend-payout-ratio.text: Payout ratio = Dividends / Net income, and Retention ratio b = 1 - Payout ratio
dividend-payout-ratio.when: Use it to see how much of its profit a company pays out and how much it keeps to reinvest. Mature firms tend to pay out more and growth firms less.

drip-shares.text: New shares = (Shares held x Dividend per share) / Reinvestment price
drip-shares.when: Use it to see how reinvesting dividends grows your holding. Each reinvestment buys more shares, which pay more dividends, so the effect compounds.

dividend-yield.text: Dividend yield = Dividend per share / Price; Buyback yield = Buybacks / Market capitalization; Total shareholder yield = the sum
dividend-yield.when: Use it to compare the cash a company returns to owners, counting both dividends and buybacks. A company that only pays dividends can look less generous than one that also repurchases shares.

yield-on-cost.text: Yield on cost = Dividend now / Price you originally paid, where dividend now = starting dividend x (1 + growth)^years
yield-on-cost.when: Use it to see how a growing dividend compares with what you paid. It is a way of showing income growth. It ignores whether you could have earned more elsewhere, so use it alongside the current yield.

dollar-cost-averaging.text: Average cost per share = total invested / total shares bought = n / (sum of 1 / price). It is the harmonic mean of the prices, which is never above the plain average price
dollar-cost-averaging.when: Use it to see what regular fixed-amount investing does to your average cost. Because the same money buys more shares when prices are low, your average cost is below the average price whenever prices vary. This does not mean DCA beats investing a lump sum at once: if prices rise on average, the lump sum usually wins. Its main benefit is behavioral and matches investing from pay.

double-declining-balance.text: Depreciation in year t = (2 / L) x book value at the start of the year
double-declining-balance.when: Use it when an asset loses value faster in its early years, such as a vehicle or technology. It gives larger expenses early and smaller ones later, and never takes the book value below salvage value.

dual-class-voting-power.text: Voting power = A shares x A votes / (A shares x A votes + B shares x B votes); Economic share = A shares / (A shares + B shares)
dual-class-voting-power.when: Use it to see how a founder can control a company with a small share of its value. The gap between voting power and economic ownership is a governance risk that investors watch.

dupont-analysis.text: ROE = Net margin x Asset turnover x Equity multiplier. Five-step: ROE = Tax burden x Interest burden x EBIT margin x Asset turnover x Equity multiplier
dupont-analysis.when: Use it to find out why ROE is high or low. It splits ROE into profitability, efficiency and leverage. Two companies with the same ROE can be very different: one a high-margin business and the other a thin-margin business using lots of debt.

duration-gap.text: Duration gap = duration of assets - (liabilities / assets) x duration of liabilities; Change in equity value = - duration gap x assets x (change in yield) / (1 + yield)
duration-gap.when: Use it to see how a rise in rates changes a bank's equity. A bank that funds long assets with short deposits has a positive duration gap, so higher rates cut asset values by more than they cut liabilities and equity falls. It shows value risk, whereas the repricing gap shows effects on income. It assumes a parallel yield shift and uses approximations that are less accurate for large moves.

dv01.text: DV01 = Modified duration x Price x 0.0001 (the money change in price for a 1 basis-point change in yield)
dv01.when: Use it to express interest rate risk in money. Traders set limits and hedge in DV01. To hedge, trade an instrument with an offsetting DV01. Key rate duration breaks the same risk down by maturity point on the curve, so you can see exposure to the 2-year rate separately from the 10-year rate.

supply-chain-finance-return.text: Annualized return = d / (1 - d) x 365 / Days paid early
supply-chain-finance-return.when: Use it to compare an early-payment discount with the return you would earn elsewhere. A buyer with spare cash earns this return by paying a supplier early, and a supplier should compare it with the cost of its other funding.

eps.text: EPS = (Net income - Preferred dividends) / Weighted average shares
eps.when: Use it to see the profit that belongs to each ordinary share. It is the "E" in the P/E ratio.

ebitda-and-its-limits.text: EBITDA = Net income + Tax + Interest + Depreciation and amortization; Cash proxy = EBITDA - Cash tax - Capex - Increase in working capital - Interest
ebitda-and-its-limits.when: Use it to see what EBITDA leaves out. EBITDA ignores the cost of replacing assets, tax, interest and working capital, so it overstates the cash a business generates. A large gap between EBITDA and the cash proxy is a limit on its usefulness.

economic-order-quantity.text: EOQ = square root of (2 x Annual demand x Cost per order / Holding cost per unit)
economic-order-quantity.when: Use it to choose how much stock to order at a time. Larger orders mean fewer order costs but more holding costs, and EOQ balances the two.

economic-value-added.text: EVA = NOPAT - WACC x Invested capital
economic-value-added.when: Use it to see whether a business earns more than the cost of the capital it uses. A positive EVA creates value, and a negative EVA destroys it even when accounting profit is positive.

ear.when: Use it to compare accounts or loans that compound at different frequencies, by converting each quoted rate to the true yearly rate.

effective-duration-convexity.mathml: Deff=P−−P+2P0Δy,Ceff=P−+P+−2P0P0(Δy)2D_{eff}=\frac{P_{-}-P_{+}}{2P_{0}\Delta y},\quad C_{eff}=\frac{P_{-}+P_{+}-2P_{0}}{P_{0}(\Delta y)^{2}}
effective-duration-convexity.text: Effective duration = (Price when yields fall - Price when yields rise) / (2 x Price now x Yield change); Effective convexity = (P- + P+ - 2 x P0) / (P0 x Yield change^2)
effective-duration-convexity.when: Use it for bonds whose cash flows change when rates change, such as callable, putable and mortgage bonds. Ordinary duration formulas assume fixed cash flows, so you reprice the bond with a model after shifting yields down and up and use the results.

effective-spread.text: Effective spread = 2 x D x (Trade price - Mid price before the trade); Realized spread uses the mid price some minutes later; D = +1 for a buy and -1 for a sell
effective-spread.when: Use it to measure what a trade really cost, since many trades happen inside or outside the quoted spread. The realized spread is what the liquidity provider keeps. The rest is the price impact, the permanent move caused by the information in the trade.

efficiency-turnover-ratios.text: Asset turnover = Revenue / Average total assets; Fixed asset turnover = Revenue / Average net fixed assets; Inventory turnover = COGS / Average inventory; Receivables turnover = Revenue / Average receivables; Payables turnover = COGS / Average payables
efficiency-turnover-ratios.when: Use it to see how hard a company works its assets. A rising turnover means more sales or cost per unit of the balance sheet item. Compare with past years and with peers, since normal levels vary by industry.

embedded-finance-revenue.mathml: R=G×a×t,Π=G a (t−k)−FR=G\times a\times t,\quad \Pi=G\,a\,(t-k)-F
embedded-finance-revenue.text: Revenue = platform sales volume x share of sales that use the financial product (attach rate) x take rate; Profit = volume x attach rate x (take rate - partner cost rate) - fixed cost; Break-even attach rate = fixed cost / (volume x (take rate - cost rate))
embedded-finance-revenue.when: Use it to size what a non-bank platform (a marketplace or software firm) can earn by offering payments, loans or insurance inside its own product. The bank partner holds the license and takes a share. Growth depends on how many customers use the product, which is the attach rate.

emergency-fund-target.text: Target = months of cover x monthly essential spending; Monthly saving = (Target - current fund x (1 + i)^n) / [((1 + i)^n - 1) / i], where i is the monthly interest rate and n is the number of months
emergency-fund-target.when: Use it to set a savings goal for the cash that covers a job loss or a big bill. Base it on essential spending only, since wants can be cut in an emergency. Keep it in an easy-access account, so the return is low, and do not count investments that can fall when you need the money.

unhedged-foreign-return.text: Dollar return unhedged = (1 + local return) x (1 + change in the local currency against the dollar) - 1; Dollar return hedged with a forward = (1 + local return) x (1 + dollar interest rate) / (1 + local interest rate) - 1. Hedging cost is roughly the local rate minus the dollar rate
unhedged-foreign-return.when: Use it to split an emerging market return into the asset and the currency. High local returns are often offset by currency depreciation, especially where inflation is high. Hedging removes the currency move but costs the interest differential, which is large when local rates are high, so the hedged return is lower when the currency would otherwise have held. Choose by comparing the hedging cost with the depreciation you fear.

employer-match-vesting.mathml: Match=m×min⁡(c, cap)×S,Vested match=Match×v\text{Match}=m\times\min(c,\,cap)\times S,\quad \text{Vested match}=\text{Match}\times v
employer-match-vesting.text: Employer match = match rate x min(your contribution %, match cap %) x salary; Vested share v rises with years of service (0 before the start year, 1 after the full year, in between linear for a graded schedule); Vested match = match x v
employer-match-vesting.when: Use it to see how much employer money you earn and how much is yours if you leave. Your own contributions are always yours, while the employer's part vests over time. A match is an immediate return on your contribution, so contributing at least up to the cap is usually the first priority. Schedules differ: enter the start and full years for your plan (equal values give a cliff schedule).

endowment-spending-rule.text: Spending this year = rho x Last year's spending + (1 - rho) x Target spending rate x Last year's market value
endowment-spending-rule.when: Use it to set a steady spending amount for an endowment. The rule blends last year's spending with a share of the fund's current value, so spending moves slowly when markets move quickly.

erm-risk-aggregation.text: Total capital = square root of the sum over all pairs of (Correlation between risks i and j x Capital for risk i x Capital for risk j)
erm-risk-aggregation.when: Use it to combine capital for different risks into one figure. Simply adding them assumes all risks go wrong together. If risks are not perfectly correlated, the total is lower, and the gap is the diversification benefit. The correlations are the most uncertain input and rise in crises.

ev-to-equity-value.text: Equity value = Enterprise value - Debt + Cash - Minority interest - Preferred stock
ev-to-equity-value.when: Use it to turn the value of the business into the value that belongs to ordinary shareholders, and then into a value per share. Subtract claims ahead of the shareholders and add cash they own.

equity-multiplier.mathml: Equity multiplier=Total assetsTotal equity\text{Equity multiplier} = \frac{\text{Total assets}}{\text{Total equity}}
equity-multiplier.text: Equity multiplier = Total assets / Total equity
equity-multiplier.when: Use it to see how many dollars of assets the company holds for each dollar of owners' money. A higher number means more borrowing.

research-pitch-risk-reward.mathml: Ptarget=EPS×PE,E[P]=∑psPs,RR=Pbull−P0P0−PbearP_{target}=EPS\times PE,\quad E[P]=\sum p_{s}P_{s},\quad RR=\frac{P_{bull}-P_{0}}{P_{0}-P_{bear}}
research-pitch-risk-reward.text: Base target price = forecast earnings per share x target price-to-earnings multiple; Expected value = sum of probability x price over bull, base and bear; Upside to expected value = expected price / current price - 1; Risk/reward = (bull price - current price) / (current price - bear price); Implied multiple at the current price = price / forecast EPS
research-pitch-risk-reward.when: Use it to put a recommendation on a few clear numbers. State what you expect earnings to be, what multiple you think is fair, and what happens in good and bad cases. A pitch should say what would make it wrong. The probabilities are your judgment, so say why you chose them.

equivalent-annual-annuity.when: Use it to compare projects with different lives. Comparing raw NPVs favors the longer project, so convert each to a yearly equivalent and pick the higher one.

esg-rating-divergence.text: Correlation between two providers' scores = covariance of the scores / (standard deviation of A x standard deviation of B); Mean absolute gap = average of |score A - score B|; Share of companies on which the providers rank in opposite halves = count of firms above the median on one and below on the other / number of firms. Credit rating agencies tend to have correlations near 0.99, ESG raters much lower (studies report about 0.5 to 0.6)
esg-rating-divergence.when: Use it to see one reason ESG ratings are criticized: different providers disagree about the same company, because they measure different things, weight them differently and treat missing data differently. If two ratings correlate weakly, a choice of provider can change which companies a fund holds. Use the score as one input, not as a fact.

estate-tax-basic.text: Taxable estate = gross estate - debts and expenses - charitable gifts; Tax = tax rate x the part of the taxable estate above the exemption threshold
estate-tax-basic.when: Use it for a rough idea of whether an estate might be taxed. Many estates fall below the threshold and owe nothing. Rules vary a great deal between countries and states, and some places tax the heirs (inheritance tax) and not the estate, so the exemption and rate here are illustrative inputs that you should replace. Planning tools such as wills, trusts and gifts should be set up with a qualified professional.

etf-premium-tracking.text: Premium (or discount) = (Market price - NAV) / NAV; Tracking difference = ETF return - Index return
etf-premium-tracking.when: Use the premium to check whether an ETF trades near the value of its holdings. Large gaps get closed by authorized participants, who create or redeem shares. Use the tracking difference to see what fees and frictions cost compared with the index.

gas-fee-cost.text: Fee in ETH = gas used x (base fee + priority tip) in gwei x 0.000000001; Fee in money = fee in ETH x price of ETH; The base fee is burned, so burned part = gas used x base fee; Simple transfers use 21,000 gas and smart-contract calls use much more
gas-fee-cost.when: Use it to see what a transaction or smart-contract call costs. Fees rise when the network is busy and depend on how much computation the contract uses, not on the amount of money sent. A swap in a decentralized exchange may use five to ten times the gas of a plain transfer.

event-study-car.mathml: ARt=Rt−(α+βRm,t),CAR=∑ARt,t=CARσεNAR_{t}=R_{t}-(\alpha+\beta R_{m,t}),\quad CAR=\sum AR_{t},\quad t=\frac{CAR}{\sigma_{\varepsilon}\sqrt{N}}
event-study-car.text: Abnormal return = actual return - (alpha + beta x market return); CAR = sum of the abnormal returns; t = CAR / (s x sqrt(N))
event-study-car.when: Use it to measure how much a news event, such as an earnings release or a merger announcement, moved a stock beyond what the market did that day. Under efficient markets the effect shows up at once and does not drift afterward.

ewma-volatility.text: Variance today = lambda x yesterday's variance + (1 - lambda) x yesterday's return squared. RiskMetrics uses lambda = 0.94 for daily data
ewma-volatility.when: Use it for a quick volatility estimate that reacts to recent returns more than old ones. It is GARCH with omega = 0 and alpha + beta = 1, so it has no long-run level and its forecast is flat. It needs only one parameter, which is why risk systems used it as a default.

ex-dividend-price.text: Ex-dividend price = Price before the dividend - Dividend per share
ex-dividend-price.when: Use it to see the idea behind dividend irrelevance. Without taxes or costs, paying a dividend simply moves value from the company to the shareholder, so total wealth stays the same.

excess-kurtosis.text: Excess kurtosis = average of ((Ri - mean) / standard deviation)^4, minus 3
excess-kurtosis.when: Use it to check for fat tails, meaning extreme gains and losses that happen more often than a normal curve predicts. Positive excess kurtosis signals higher tail risk.

expanded-accounting-equation.text: Assets = Liabilities + Contributed capital + Beginning retained earnings + Revenues - Expenses - Dividends
expanded-accounting-equation.when: Use it to see why every transaction keeps the accounting equation in balance. Each journal entry changes both sides by the same amount, which is the idea behind double-entry bookkeeping.

expectations-theory.text: (1 + two-year spot)^2 = (1 + one-year spot) x (1 + expected one-year rate next year + liquidity premium)
expectations-theory.when: Use it to see what the yield curve says about expected future rates. Under pure expectations the long rate is the average of expected short rates (L = 0). Liquidity preference adds a premium that makes the curve slope up even if rates are not expected to rise. Segmentation theory says each maturity has its own supply and demand, so no such formula links them.

expected-unexpected-loss.text: Expected loss = PD x LGD x EAD; Unexpected loss = EAD x sqrt(PD x (LGD volatility)^2 + LGD^2 x PD x (1 - PD)); LGD = 1 - Recovery rate
expected-unexpected-loss.when: Use it to size credit losses. Expected loss is the average, which should be covered by pricing and provisions. Unexpected loss is the standard deviation around it, which should be covered by capital. Regulators use PD, LGD and EAD as the inputs of the internal-ratings approach.

high-yield-expected-return.text: Expected return = Promised yield - Probability of default x (1 - Recovery rate)
high-yield-expected-return.when: Use it to compare bonds of different credit quality. A high-yield bond promises more, but defaults take part of it back. What is left, compared with a safe rate, is the real reward for taking credit risk.

portfolio-expected-return.text: Portfolio expected return = w1 x E(R1) + w2 x E(R2) + ... + wn x E(Rn)
portfolio-expected-return.when: Use it to find the expected return of a mix of assets. It also works for a core-satellite portfolio, where a large core holding is combined with smaller satellite holdings.

expected-shortfall.mathml: ES=V(σφ(zc)1−c−μ),EShist=−V×average of returns below the (1−c) percentileES=V\left(\sigma\frac{\varphi(z_{c})}{1-c}-\mu\right),\quad ES_{hist}=-V\times\text{average of returns below the }(1-c)\text{ percentile}
expected-shortfall.text: Parametric ES = V x (sd x pdf(z) / (1 - c) - mean); Historical ES = -V x the average of the returns that fall at or below the VaR cut-off
expected-shortfall.when: Use it to answer "how bad is it when VaR is breached?". VaR gives the threshold and ES gives the average loss beyond it. ES is always larger than VaR, and regulators now prefer it (Basel FRTB uses ES at 97.5%) because it captures the shape of the tail.

expected-value.text: E(X) = p1 x x1 + p2 x x2 + ... + pn x xn
expected-value.when: Use it to find the average outcome when several results are possible, each with its own probability, such as the expected return across economic scenarios.

evpi.mathml: EVPI=E[max⁡aPayoff(a,s)]−max⁡aE[Payoff(a,s)]EVPI=E\left[\max_{a}\text{Payoff}(a,s)\right]-\max_{a}E\left[\text{Payoff}(a,s)\right]
evpi.text: Expected value of perfect information = (expected payoff if you could pick the best action after seeing the state) - (best expected payoff when you must choose before seeing it)
evpi.when: Use it to cap what research, data or advice is worth paying for. Even a perfect forecast cannot be worth more than EVPI, so if a study costs more than this, skip it. Real information is imperfect, so its true value is lower. It depends entirely on your probabilities and payoffs, so test it with other numbers.

ema-crossover.text: EMA today = alpha x Price today + (1 - alpha) x EMA yesterday, with alpha = 2 / (n + 1)
ema-crossover.when: Use it to follow a trend. A short average crossing above a long one is read as an upward trend (a "golden cross"), and crossing below as a downward trend. The EMA reacts faster than the simple average, but it also gives more false signals.

fama-french-model.text: Expected return = rf + b_mkt x MKT + b_smb x SMB + b_hml x HML (+ b_rmw x RMW + b_cma x CMA for five factors)
fama-french-model.when: Use it to explain or predict a stock's return from its exposure to market, size and value factors, and from profitability and investment too in the five-factor version. It is the standard test of whether a manager's skill is real or just factor exposure.

family-office-breakeven.text: Break-even wealth = fixed annual cost / (fee rate of the outside alternative - variable cost rate); Cost as a share of wealth = fixed cost / wealth + variable cost rate
family-office-breakeven.when: Use it to judge when a private family office is worth running. Its cost is mostly fixed, so the cost per unit of wealth falls as wealth grows. Below the break-even size an outside provider is cheaper. Cost is not the only factor: control, privacy, and bespoke services such as tax planning and philanthropy also matter.

fi-number-4-percent.mathml: FI=Ew,n=ln⁡ ⁣[(FI r+s)/(P r+s)]ln⁡(1+r)FI=\frac{E}{w},\quad n=\frac{\ln\!\left[(FI\,r+s)/(P\,r+s)\right]}{\ln(1+r)}
fi-number-4-percent.text: Financial independence number = annual spending / safe withdrawal rate (4% gives 25 x spending); Years to get there = ln[(FI x r + s) / (current portfolio x r + s)] / ln(1 + r), where s is the yearly saving and r is the real return
fi-number-4-percent.when: Use it to estimate how large a portfolio must be to fund spending, and how long saving will take. The 4% rule comes from historical US data for a 30-year retirement; a longer retirement, lower expected returns or high fees point to a lower rate such as 3 to 3.5%. It is a guide, not a guarantee, and it does not include pensions or taxes. Working in real terms keeps the arithmetic free of inflation.

fd-explicit-step.mathml: uin+1=uin+α(ui+1n−2uin+ui−1n),α=D Δt(Δx)2≤12u_{i}^{n+1}=u_{i}^{n}+\alpha\left(u_{i+1}^{n}-2u_{i}^{n}+u_{i-1}^{n}\right),\quad \alpha=\frac{D\,\Delta t}{(\Delta x)^{2}}\le\tfrac{1}{2}
fd-explicit-step.text: New value at a grid point = Old value + alpha x (Value on the right - 2 x Old value + Value on the left), with alpha = D x time step / (grid spacing)^2; the scheme is stable only if alpha <= 0.5
fd-explicit-step.when: Use it to solve a pricing equation on a grid by stepping forward in time. Each point moves toward the average of its neighbors, which is the discrete form of the second derivative. The explicit scheme is simple but requires small time steps for stability. Implicit and Crank-Nicolson schemes remove that limit.

fiscal-multiplier.text: Spending multiplier = 1 / (1 - MPC x (1 - tax rate) + import share); Tax-cut multiplier = - MPC / (1 - MPC x (1 - tax rate) + import share). Change in GDP = multiplier x change in spending
fiscal-multiplier.when: Use it to estimate how much extra output a spending change creates. Each round of spending becomes someone's income, and part leaks into saving, tax and imports. Spending on goods has a larger multiplier than a tax cut of the same size, because part of a tax cut is saved first. Multipliers are smaller when the economy is at full capacity or interest rates rise in response.

fixed-charge-net-debt.text: Fixed charge coverage = (EBIT + Lease payments) / (Interest + Lease payments); Net debt to EBITDA = (Total debt - Cash) / EBITDA
fixed-charge-net-debt.when: Use it alongside debt-to-equity and interest coverage. Fixed charge coverage counts lease payments, which interest coverage ignores. Net debt to EBITDA shows roughly how many years of operating cash flow it takes to repay debt, and lenders use it in covenants.

mortgage-fixed-vs-arm.text: Payment = i x Loan / (1 - (1 + i)^(-n)); Balance after k payments = Loan x ((1 + i)^n - (1 + i)^k) / ((1 + i)^n - 1); after the rate resets, the new payment is the payment formula on the remaining balance over the remaining months
mortgage-fixed-vs-arm.when: Use it to compare a fixed rate with an adjustable rate that starts lower and resets. The adjustable loan wins if rates stay low or if you sell or refinance before the reset; it loses if the rate rises and you stay. Enter a stress rate for the reset, not the hoped-for one. This ignores rate caps and fees, which you should add from the loan terms.

frn-price.mathml: Coupon=(Reference rate+QM)m×F,P=∑C(1+(Ref+DM)/m)k+F(1+(Ref+DM)/m)N\text{Coupon}=\frac{(\text{Reference rate}+QM)}{m}\times F,\quad P=\sum\frac{C}{(1+(\text{Ref}+DM)/m)^{k}}+\frac{F}{(1+(\text{Ref}+DM)/m)^{N}}
frn-price.text: Coupon = (Reference rate + Quoted margin) / payments per year x Face value; Price = coupons and face value discounted at (Reference rate + Discount margin) / payments per year
frn-price.when: Use it to price a floating rate note. If the market requires the same margin as the quoted margin, the price is at par on a reset date. If investors want a higher margin because credit worsened, the price falls below par. This simple form assumes the reference rate stays flat.

forecast-calibration.text: Overconfidence = average stated probability - share of forecasts that came true; Brier score = average of (stated probability - outcome)^2, where the outcome is 1 if the event happened and 0 if not (0 is perfect and 0.25 is what always saying 50% scores)
forecast-calibration.when: Use it to test your own judgment. If you say 90% for events that happen only 70% of the time, you are overconfident. Overconfident investors trade too often and take too much risk. Keep a log of forecasts and outcomes, and check the score once you have a few dozen, as eight forecasts is too few to conclude much.

foreign-project-npv.text: Method 1: convert each foreign cash flow at its expected spot rate and discount at the home required return. Method 2: discount the foreign cash flows at the foreign required return, then convert the NPV at today's spot. Expected spot S_t = S_0 x ((1 + home inflation) / (1 + foreign inflation))^t; Foreign required return = (1 + home) x (1 + foreign inflation) / (1 + home inflation) - 1
foreign-project-npv.when: Use it to value a project abroad from the parent's point of view. The two methods give the same answer if the expected exchange rate follows the inflation gap (relative PPP) and the discount rates are linked by the Fisher relation. Differences arise when the currency is expected to move differently, and country risk must be added to the discount rate or to the cash flows, not both. Blocked funds or taxes on remittances also change the home cash flows.

forward-contract-value.text: Fair forward price = Spot x (1 + r)^T; Value of a long forward = Spot now - Delivery price / (1 + r)^(time left); Payoff to the long at expiry = Spot at expiry - Delivery price
forward-contract-value.when: Use it for a forward on an asset that pays no income and costs nothing to store. A forward is agreed with no money changing hands, so its fair delivery price makes the value zero at the start. As time passes its value to each side moves with the spot price.

fx-forward-points.text: Forward rate = spot x (1 + domestic rate x days / 360) / (1 + foreign rate x days / 360), where rates are quoted as domestic currency per 1 unit of foreign currency; Forward points = (forward - spot) x 10,000; Annualized forward premium = (F / S - 1) x 360 / days
fx-forward-points.when: Use it to price a forward exchange contract. The forward is set so that no one can profit from borrowing in one currency and lending in the other: the currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount. Forward points are the quoted difference, added to the spot. The forward is not a prediction of the future spot rate. Day-count conventions vary by currency.

forward-rate.text: Forward rate = [(1 + spot rate to t2)^t2 / (1 + spot rate to t1)^t1]^(1 / (t2 - t1)) - 1
forward-rate.when: Use it to find the interest rate implied for a future period. Locking in the long rate gives the same result as locking in the short rate and then the forward rate, so any other forward rate would let someone make a risk-free profit.

fcfe.text: FCFE = FCFF - Interest x (1 - T) + Net borrowing
fcfe.when: Use it to value equity directly, by discounting FCFE at the cost of equity. It deducts after-tax interest and adds net new borrowing.

fcff.text: FCFF = EBIT x (1 - T) + Depreciation and amortization - Capital expenditure - Increase in net working capital
fcff.when: Use it as the cash flow in a DCF that is discounted at WACC. It ignores how the firm is financed, so it can be used to value the whole business.

free-cash-flow-conversion.text: Free cash flow = Cash flow from operations - Capital expenditure; Conversion = FCF / Net income; FCF yield = FCF / Market cap
free-cash-flow-conversion.when: Use it to see how much profit is left as cash after spending needed to maintain and grow the business. A company can report profits and still burn cash if capital spending is heavy. Conversion well below 100% for several years is a concern.

fundamental-law-active.text: Information ratio (expected) = transfer coefficient x information coefficient x square root of breadth; Expected active return (alpha) = information ratio x tracking error; Information coefficient is the correlation between forecasts and outcomes; Breadth is the number of independent bets per year; Transfer coefficient is how much of the forecast makes it into the portfolio (1 = fully, below 1 with constraints); Breadth needed for a target IR = (IR / (TC x IC))^2
fundamental-law-active.when: Use it to see what is needed to add value. A small forecasting edge (IC = 0.05 is good) pays off if applied across many independent bets. Constraints such as no short selling lower the transfer coefficient. It does not prove skill: the same arithmetic applied to a manager's record needs enough data to separate skill from luck.

funded-ratio.mathml: Funded ratio=AssetsPV(Liabilities),PV(L)=∑Lt(1+r)t\text{Funded ratio}=\frac{\text{Assets}}{PV(\text{Liabilities})},\quad PV(L)=\sum\frac{L_{t}}{(1+r)^{t}}
funded-ratio.text: Funded ratio = Assets / Present value of liabilities, where each liability payment is discounted at rate r
funded-ratio.when: Use it for a pension fund or insurer, whose goal is to meet future payments, not to maximize return. A ratio below 1 means the assets would not cover the liabilities if they all fell due today.

fv-lump-sum.when: Use it when you invest one amount once, leave it alone, and want to know what it will be worth later with interest added back each period.

fv-annuity-due.text: FV(due) = PMT x ((1 + r)^n - 1) / r x (1 + r)
fv-annuity-due.when: Use it for a savings plan where each deposit is made at the start of the period, so every deposit earns one extra period of interest.

fv-ordinary-annuity.when: Use it for a savings plan with equal deposits made at the end of each period, to find how much you will have after the last deposit.

fv-compounding-m.text: FV = PV x (1 + r/m)^(m x t)
fv-compounding-m.when: Use it when interest is added more than once a year, such as monthly or daily, and the rate is quoted as a yearly figure.

futures-margin-account.mathml: Daily gain=N×M×(Ft−Ft−1),Balancet=Balancet−1+Daily gain\text{Daily gain}=N\times M\times(F_{t}-F_{t-1}),\quad \text{Balance}_{t}=\text{Balance}_{t-1}+\text{Daily gain}
futures-margin-account.text: Daily gain on a long position = Contracts x Multiplier x (Today's futures price - Yesterday's futures price); Margin balance = Previous balance + Daily gain
futures-margin-account.when: Use it to follow a futures position through daily settlement. Gains and losses are paid each day, unlike a forward. When the balance falls below the maintenance level, the holder must deposit enough to return to the initial margin.

forward-price-cost-of-carry.text: Futures price = Spot x e^((risk-free rate + storage cost - yield) x time)
forward-price-cost-of-carry.when: Use it to find the no-arbitrage futures price. Holding the asset costs interest and storage, and pays an income or convenience yield. The futures price equals the spot price grown at the net cost of carry. If the market price differs, buying the cheap one and selling the expensive one locks in a risk-free profit.

fx-forward-hedge.text: Forward rate = Spot rate x (1 + home rate x time) / (1 + foreign rate x time), with rates quoted per year and the rate quoted as home currency per unit of foreign currency
fx-forward-hedge.when: Use it to fix the home-currency value of a future foreign payment. The forward rate follows from interest rate parity, so it differs from spot by the interest difference, not by a forecast of where the currency is going. Hedging removes the risk, and the opportunity of a favorable move.

garch-forecast.text: Next-period variance = omega + alpha x (last return)^2 + beta x (last variance); Long-run variance = omega / (1 - alpha - beta); k periods ahead: long-run + (alpha + beta)^k x (next variance - long-run)
garch-forecast.when: Use it to forecast volatility that clusters: big moves are followed by big moves. A shock raises tomorrow's variance, and the effect decays at the rate alpha + beta toward the long-run level. Alpha + beta must be below 1 for a long-run level to exist; values near 1 mean shocks fade slowly.

gdp-nominal-real.mathml: Y=C+I+G+(X−M),Real GDP=Nominal GDPDeflator/100,g=RealtRealt−1−1Y=C+I+G+(X-M),\quad \text{Real GDP}=\frac{\text{Nominal GDP}}{\text{Deflator}/100},\quad g=\frac{\text{Real}_{t}}{\text{Real}_{t-1}}-1
gdp-nominal-real.text: GDP = Consumption + Investment + Government spending + (Exports - Imports); Real GDP = Nominal GDP / (GDP deflator / 100); Growth = Real GDP this year / Real GDP last year - 1
gdp-nominal-real.when: Use it to measure the size of an economy and separate real growth from price rises. Nominal GDP can rise purely because prices rose, so real GDP at constant prices is used to measure growth. Imports are subtracted because they are already inside C, I and G but were not produced at home.

gdpr-maximum-fine.mathml: Max=max⁡(20m, 4%×T) (top tier),max⁡(10m, 2%×T) (lower tier)\text{Max}=\max\left(20\text{m},\ 4\%\times T\right)\ \text{(top tier)},\quad \max\left(10\text{m},\ 2\%\times T\right)\ \text{(lower tier)}
gdpr-maximum-fine.text: Under the EU GDPR, the highest tier of fines (for breaches of core principles, consent and data-subject rights) can reach the larger of 20 million euros and 4% of the firm's total worldwide annual turnover of the previous year; The lower tier (for example, record-keeping and security duties) reaches the larger of 10 million euros and 2% of turnover; Turnover above 500 million euros makes the percentage cap the larger one
gdpr-maximum-fine.when: Use it to see the largest fine a firm could face under the GDPR. The fine is a ceiling, not a typical fine; authorities set the actual amount from the nature, length and harm of the breach, cooperation and past record. Other laws (Taiwan's PDPA, India's DPDP Act) use different fixed amounts and are not covered here.

gbm-terminal-distribution.mathml: ST=S0e(μ−σ2/2)T+σTZ,E[ST]=S0eμT,Median=S0e(μ−σ2/2)TS_{T}=S_{0}e^{(\mu-\sigma^{2}/2)T+\sigma\sqrt{T}Z},\quad E[S_{T}]=S_{0}e^{\mu T},\quad \text{Median}=S_{0}e^{(\mu-\sigma^{2}/2)T}
gbm-terminal-distribution.text: Price at T = S0 x e^((mu - sigma^2 / 2) x T + sigma x sqrt(T) x Z), where Z is a standard normal; Mean = S0 x e^(mu T); Median = S0 x e^((mu - sigma^2 / 2) T); P(S_T > K) = N([ln(S0 / K) + (mu - sigma^2 / 2) T] / (sigma sqrt(T)))
gbm-terminal-distribution.when: Use it to describe where a price following GBM is likely to be. Prices are lognormal: never negative and skewed to the upside. The mean is above the median, and the gap grows with volatility and time. A single step of the model is in the Foundations section.

geometric-mean-return.text: Geometric mean = ((1 + R1) x (1 + R2) x ... x (1 + Rn))^(1/n) - 1
geometric-mean-return.when: Use it to find the average growth rate of an investment whose returns vary from period to period. It is always at or below the arithmetic mean.

good-debt-test.text: After-tax borrowing cost = interest rate x (1 - tax rate on deductible interest); Spread = expected return of what the debt buys - after-tax borrowing cost; Annual gain = amount borrowed x spread
good-debt-test.when: Use it to compare what a loan costs with what it earns. Debt is closer to "good" when it buys something whose return is likely to exceed its cost and the downside is survivable, such as education that raises income. A card balance at 22% almost never passes. The expected return is an estimate, so a thin positive spread is not a safe margin.

purchase-price-allocation-goodwill.text: Goodwill = Purchase price - (Fair value of identifiable assets - Fair value of liabilities assumed)
purchase-price-allocation-goodwill.when: Use it in acquisition accounting. The price is spread across the target's assets and liabilities at fair value, and whatever is left over is goodwill.

goodwill-impairment-test.text: Recoverable amount = higher of (Fair value less costs of disposal) and (Value in use); Impairment loss = Carrying amount - Recoverable amount, if positive; it first reduces goodwill
goodwill-impairment-test.when: Use it to see how an impairment loss arises. Goodwill is not amortized under IFRS or US GAAP for most firms, so it is tested at least yearly. If the unit's value falls below its book value, the difference is written off, first against goodwill. A sudden impairment often signals that an acquisition was overpriced.

debt-dynamics.text: Next year's debt-to-GDP = this year's x (1 + interest rate) / (1 + GDP growth) - primary balance (as a share of GDP; a surplus is positive); The primary balance that holds debt steady = debt ratio x (r - g) / (1 + g)
debt-dynamics.when: Use it to judge whether debt is on a stable path. When the interest rate is above growth (r > g), debt keeps rising unless the government runs a primary surplus. When growth is above the rate, debt can fall even with a small primary deficit. This is why the r minus g gap matters so much. It assumes constant r and g, whereas rates are refinanced over time.

graham-number.text: Graham number = square root of (22.5 x Earnings per share x Book value per share)
graham-number.when: Use it as a rough ceiling on the price a defensive value investor might pay. A price well below it gives a margin of safety, which was Graham's idea of a cushion against error.

grant-element.text: Grant element = (face value of the loan - present value of its repayments discounted at a commercial rate) / face value. For a loan that pays interest each year and the principal at the end: PV = coupon x annuity factor + face / (1 + d)^N
grant-element.when: Use it to measure how much of a below-market loan is effectively a grant. The lower the interest rate relative to the market rate, the longer the maturity and the larger the grace period, the bigger the subsidy. Development agencies often count a loan as aid only if the grant element is above a threshold such as 25%. The discount rate is a policy choice, so results differ by lender.

greenium-and-step-up.text: Greenium = yield on a similar ordinary bond - yield on the green bond; Present value of the saving to the issuer = sum over years of (notional x greenium) discounted at the ordinary yield; For a sustainability-linked bond, extra interest if the target is missed = notional x coupon step-up x remaining years after the test date
greenium-and-step-up.when: Use it to see what labeled bonds change. A green bond ties the use of the money to eligible projects and may price slightly tighter (the greenium, often a few basis points). A sustainability-linked bond has no use-of-proceeds rule but its coupon steps up if the issuer misses a target, which is the cost of failure. A small step-up may be too weak to change behavior.

greenwashing-alignment-gap.mathml: A=∑Aligned revenueTotal revenue,Gap=C−AA=\frac{\sum \text{Aligned revenue}}{\text{Total revenue}},\quad \text{Gap}=C-A
greenwashing-alignment-gap.text: Aligned share = revenue from activities that meet an official green taxonomy criteria / total revenue; Claim gap = share claimed in marketing - aligned share; Overstatement ratio = claimed share / aligned share; Fund version: share of holdings that meet the fund's stated sustainability criteria vs share claimed
greenwashing-alignment-gap.when: Use it to compare what a firm or a fund says with what can be verified. A large gap between the claimed green share and the share that meets a recognized taxonomy is a warning of greenwashing. Regulators in several places require evidence for green claims. A small gap does not prove the claims are right, since the taxonomy has limits too.

growing-perpetuity.when: Use it for payments that go on forever and grow at a steady rate, such as a dividend expected to rise by the same percentage each year. It only works when r is larger than g.

growth-accounting.text: Productivity growth (Solow residual) = output growth - capital share x capital growth - (1 - capital share) x labor growth; Labor productivity growth = output growth - labor growth
growth-accounting.when: Use it to split growth into more inputs and better use of inputs. Long-run living standards rise mainly through productivity. The residual is whatever the inputs cannot explain, so measurement errors in capital and labor end up in it. A simple doubling-time check shows how a small growth gap compounds.

health-cost-sharing.mathml: You pay=min⁡ ⁣[M,  min⁡(B,D)+c max⁡(B−D,0)],Total cost=You pay+Premiums\text{You pay}=\min\!\left[M,\;\min(B,D)+c\,\max(B-D,0)\right],\quad \text{Total cost}=\text{You pay}+\text{Premiums}
health-cost-sharing.text: What you pay = the smaller of (out-of-pocket maximum) and [the part of the bill up to the deductible + coinsurance % x the part of the bill above the deductible]; Total yearly cost = what you pay + annual premiums
health-cost-sharing.when: Use it to compare health plans at different levels of use. A plan with high premiums and low deductibles tends to cost less in a heavy-use year, and a cheaper plan tends to win in a light year. Try your expected bills and a bad-year scenario. Real plans differ in networks and co-payments, which this simple model ignores.

hedge-fund-fees.text: Management fee = rate x starting NAV; Performance fee = performance rate x the amount by which NAV after the management fee exceeds the higher of (starting NAV x (1 + hurdle)) and the high-water mark; Net return = (NAV after both fees / starting NAV) - 1
hedge-fund-fees.when: Use it to see what investors keep. The classic "2 and 20" takes 2% of assets and 20% of profits, so fees can absorb a large part of the gross return. A hurdle and a high-water mark protect investors by requiring a minimum return and by not charging again for recovering past losses. This version uses a hard hurdle (fee only on the excess), whereas some funds use a soft hurdle where the fee is charged on all profits once the hurdle is cleared.

money-market-hedge.text: Forward hedge: dollars received = foreign amount x forward rate. Money market hedge: borrow the present value of the receivable in foreign currency (amount / (1 + foreign rate x T)), convert it at spot, and invest the dollars at the domestic rate; dollars at the due date = that amount x (1 + domestic rate x T). Unhedged: dollars = foreign amount x the spot rate at the due date
money-market-hedge.when: Use it to compare ways to lock in the value of a foreign receivable. A forward is simplest. A money market hedge borrows the foreign currency now, so the receivable repays the loan, and gives almost the same result when parity holds. The two differ if the quoted forward is off parity or if borrowing costs differ. Staying unhedged leaves the outcome to the future spot rate. Costs and credit limits can shape the choice.

information-cascade-posterior.text: If each earlier trader acted on a private signal that is right with probability q, the probability the asset is good after observing d more buys than sells = q^d / (q^d + (1 - q)^d). When d reaches 2, your own opposing signal cannot change the decision, so it is rational to follow the crowd, and the crowd stops adding information
information-cascade-posterior.when: Use it to see how herding can be rational yet fragile. Early actions are informative, but once the lead is big enough later traders ignore their own information, so a cascade rests on only a few real signals and can reverse on small news. The model assumes every earlier action reflects one independent signal, which is why it is a stylized picture.

herfindahl-index.text: HHI = sum of the squared market shares (in percent); CR4 = sum of the four largest shares
herfindahl-index.when: Use it in industry analysis to see how competitive a sector is. A concentrated industry may give firms pricing power, which supports profit margins, but it also draws the attention of regulators.

heston-variance.text: Expected average variance over T = theta + (v0 - theta) x (1 - e^(-kappa T)) / (kappa T); variance stays above zero if 2 x kappa x theta >= xi^2
heston-variance.when: Use it to understand what the Heston model says about volatility. Variance follows a CIR process: it reverts to a long-run level and is random. The expected average variance over the option's life, rather than today's variance, drives the option price level, while rho and xi shape the skew and smile.

holding-period-return.text: HPR = (End price - Start price + Income) / Start price
holding-period-return.when: Use it to measure what an investment returned over the whole time you held it, counting both the change in price and any income.

home-bias-measure.text: Home bias = (domestic weight held - domestic share of world market value) / (1 - domestic share of world market value); Portfolio risk is the two-asset formula, evaluated at the actual weight and at the market-value weight
home-bias-measure.when: Use it to measure how far a portfolio leans toward home. Investors typically hold far more of their own market than its share of the world, which gives up diversification. A market-value weight is a neutral reference, not a prescription: currency risk, costs and the cost of living in home currency are good reasons to keep some tilt.

household-cash-flow-ratios.mathml: Savings rate=SY,  Debt service=DY,  Liquidity=Liquid assetsE,  Solvency=A−LA\text{Savings rate}=\frac{S}{Y},\; \text{Debt service}=\frac{D}{Y},\; \text{Liquidity}=\frac{\text{Liquid assets}}{E},\; \text{Solvency}=\frac{A-L}{A}
household-cash-flow-ratios.text: Savings rate = monthly saving / monthly income; Debt service ratio = monthly debt payments / monthly income; Liquidity ratio = liquid assets / monthly essential spending (months of cover); Solvency ratio = (assets - liabilities) / assets
household-cash-flow-ratios.when: Use it as a quick household health check, much as analysts use ratios for a company. Common guides are a savings rate near 10 to 20% or more, debt service below about 35%, three to six months of liquidity and a rising solvency ratio. Guides depend on circumstances, so use them to spot weak areas and track progress, not as pass or fail marks.

bond-immunization-weights.text: Weight in bond 1 = (Duration of bond 2 - Duration of the liability) / (Duration of bond 2 - Duration of bond 1); weight in bond 2 = 1 - weight in bond 1
bond-immunization-weights.when: Use it to protect against interest rate changes when you must meet a payment on a known date. Set the portfolio's present value equal to the liability's and its duration equal to the liability's duration. Then a change in yields moves assets and liability by about the same amount. Rebalance as durations drift.

social-return-on-investment.text: Social return on investment = present value of social benefits (valued in money, after removing what would have happened anyway) / amount invested; Financial multiple = present value of cash returned / amount invested; Blended multiple = (PV of cash returns + PV of social benefits) / amount invested; Net social value = PV of benefits - investment
social-return-on-investment.when: Use it to compare impact investments with a common yardstick. Social benefits (jobs, health, emissions avoided) are turned into money values, which requires judgment about prices and about additionality, so the ratio is only as good as these assumptions. Show the financial and the impact parts separately so readers can see what they depend on.

impermanent-loss.text: If the price of token A relative to token B changes by a factor r, a liquidity provider's pool share is worth 2 x sqrt(r) / (1 + r) of what the same tokens would be worth if simply held, so Impermanent loss = 2 x sqrt(r) / (1 + r) - 1 (zero when r = 1, and the same for r and 1/r); Fees earned must exceed this loss for the pool to beat holding
impermanent-loss.when: Use it to see the cost to a liquidity provider when prices move. The pool sells the token that rises and buys the one that falls, so the provider ends up with less value than a holder. The loss is called impermanent because it disappears if the price returns, but it is real if the provider withdraws first.

implementation-shortfall.text: For a buy: Delay cost = (price when trading started - price at the decision) x shares; Trading cost = (average fill price - price at the start of trading) x shares; Total shortfall = delay cost + trading cost + fees; In basis points = total / (arrival price x shares) x 10,000; Typical impact model: impact as a fraction of price = k x daily volatility x square root of (shares traded / daily volume), with k about 0.5 to 1
implementation-shortfall.when: Use it to measure what a trade really cost against the price you wanted. The gap between the paper price at the decision and what you actually paid includes waiting, your own price impact and fees. Large orders move the price, and the square-root rule gives a rough guide to how much. It should be used to choose how fast to trade: faster trading costs more impact but less risk of the price drifting away.

implied-erp.text: Implied ERP = Market dividend yield + Expected growth - Risk-free rate
implied-erp.when: Use it to estimate the equity risk premium from what the market is paying now, rather than from past returns. It rests on the Gordon growth model applied to a whole market.

implied-growth.text: Implied g = (Price x r - D0) / (Price + D0)
implied-growth.when: Use it to ask what the market is assuming. It turns the Gordon growth model around, so you can judge whether the growth rate built into the price is believable.

implied-volatility.mathml: Find σimp such that BSM(S,K,r,T,σimp)=Market price\text{Find }\sigma_{imp}\text{ such that }BSM(S,K,r,T,\sigma_{imp})=\text{Market price}
implied-volatility.text: Implied volatility is the volatility that makes the Black-Scholes price equal to the price seen in the market. It has no formula and is found by trial and error.
implied-volatility.when: Use it to turn an option price into a volatility, so that options with different strikes and expiries can be compared. Plotting implied volatility against strike usually gives a smile or skew, which shows that the constant-volatility assumption of Black-Scholes does not hold.

income-driven-payment.text: Monthly payment = percentage x max(income - multiple x poverty line, 0) / 12, where the percentage, the multiple and the poverty line are set by the plan
income-driven-payment.when: Use it to estimate a payment that scales with income instead of the loan size. The percentage, the protected multiple and the poverty line all differ by plan and change over time, so enter the figures from your own plan. Remember that a low payment can leave interest unpaid, so the balance may grow, and forgiveness rules and any tax on forgiven amounts vary.

tracking-difference.text: Tracking difference each year = fund return - index return; Average tracking difference = mean of those differences; Tracking error = standard deviation of the differences; Cumulative gap = growth of the fund / growth of the index - 1
tracking-difference.when: Use it to compare index funds that follow the same index. The average gap is roughly the fund's annual cost, partly offset by income such as securities lending. The tracking error shows consistency. Between two funds on one index, the lower and steadier gap is the better one. It tells you nothing about whether the index itself is a good choice.

tips-inflation-adjustment.text: Adjusted principal = Face x CPI now / CPI at issue; Coupon = Adjusted principal x real coupon rate / payments per year; Breakeven inflation = (1 + nominal yield) / (1 + real yield) - 1
tips-inflation-adjustment.when: Use it to see what an inflation-linked bond pays. The principal is scaled up by inflation, and the coupon is a fixed rate applied to that higher principal, so both rise with prices. Breakeven inflation shows the inflation rate the market is pricing in.

information-ratio.text: Tracking error = standard deviation of (Portfolio return - Benchmark return); IR = average active return / tracking error
information-ratio.when: Use it to judge an active manager against a benchmark. Tracking error shows how far the portfolio strays from the benchmark, and the information ratio shows whether the extra risk was rewarded.

infrastructure-dscr-llcr.text: Cash flow available for debt service (CFADS) = operating cash flow after tax and capex; DSCR in year t = CFADS / (interest + principal due); LLCR = present value of CFADS over the loan life at the loan rate / debt outstanding; A project typically needs a minimum DSCR near 1.2 to 1.4 for stable assets, and pays no dividends below a lock-up level
infrastructure-dscr-llcr.when: Use it to test whether an infrastructure project (a toll road, solar farm, pipeline) can carry its debt. Lenders look at the cheapest year (minimum DSCR) and at the whole loan life (LLCR). A margin above 1 means income covers payments even if revenue falls short; a cover below 1 means equity must top up or lenders take a loss.

insider-trading-disgorgement.mathml: G=q (Pafter−Ptrade),Max civil penalty=3GG=q\,(P_{after}-P_{trade}),\quad \text{Max civil penalty}=3G
insider-trading-disgorgement.text: Profit gained (buyer) = shares x (price after the news is public - price paid); Loss avoided (seller) = shares x (price paid originally - price after bad news); Disgorgement = profit gained or loss avoided; The US civil penalty can be up to three times that amount, in addition to disgorgement, and criminal penalties may apply
insider-trading-disgorgement.when: Use it to see the scale of the money at stake in an insider trading case. Regulators ask the trader to give up the gain and may add a penalty of up to three times the gain. For a person who sold ahead of bad news, the same maths measures the loss avoided. Courts decide the actual amounts using their own rules.

insurance-float-profit.mathml: UW=P−Claims−Expenses,Cost of float=−UWFloat,Pretax profit=UW+y×FloatUW=P-Claims-Expenses,\quad \text{Cost of float}=\frac{-UW}{\text{Float}},\quad \text{Pretax profit}=UW+y\times\text{Float}
insurance-float-profit.text: Underwriting profit = premiums - claims - expenses; Cost of float = underwriting loss / float (negative if underwriting is profitable); Pretax profit = underwriting profit + investment yield x float
insurance-float-profit.when: Use it to see how insurers make money. Premiums arrive before claims are paid, so the insurer invests the float. An underwriting loss (combined ratio above 100%) can still be profitable if the float is cheap, that is, the cost of float is below what the investments earn or the risk-free rate. A long tail of liabilities, as in liability insurance, makes the float larger and longer.

insurtech-automation-savings.mathml: CR=LR+ER,ΔCR=− aLLR−aEER,UW=P(1−CR)CR=LR+ER,\quad \Delta CR=-\,a_{L}LR-a_{E}ER,\quad UW=P(1-CR)
insurtech-automation-savings.text: Combined ratio = loss ratio + expense ratio; Underwriting profit = premiums x (1 - combined ratio); New loss ratio = old x (1 - claims improvement from better pricing and fraud detection); New expense ratio = old x (1 - expense saving from automation)
insurtech-automation-savings.when: Use it to size what technology can do to an insurer's profit. Better pricing and fraud detection act on the loss ratio; automated claims and onboarding act on the expense ratio. A combined ratio below 100% is an underwriting profit. The gains are estimates from pilots and may not carry across the whole book.

loan-interest-split.text: Interest = starting balance x r, and Principal repaid = PMT - Interest
loan-interest-split.when: Use it to split one loan payment into the part that is interest and the part that reduces the debt. Repeating it row by row builds a full amortization schedule.

interest-coverage.when: Use it to judge whether a company can pay the interest on its debt. Credit rating agencies watch it closely. A ratio below about 1.5 to 2 is usually a warning sign.

circular-interest-sweep.mathml: B1=B0(1+(1−t)r2)−F1−(1−t)r2,Interest=r B0+B12B_{1}=\frac{B_{0}\left(1+\tfrac{(1-t)r}{2}\right)-F}{1-\tfrac{(1-t)r}{2}},\quad \text{Interest}=r\,\frac{B_{0}+B_{1}}{2}
circular-interest-sweep.text: Closing debt B1 = [Opening debt x (1 + (1 - t) x r / 2) - Cash available F] / [1 - (1 - t) x r / 2]; Interest = Rate x (Opening + Closing) / 2
circular-interest-sweep.when: Use it to avoid a circular reference in a model. Interest on the average balance depends on closing debt, which depends on the cash left after interest, which depends on interest. Solving the loop algebraically gives the answer in one step, with no iteration or macro, and no risk of the model breaking.

interest-rate-build-up.text: Nominal rate = real risk-free rate + expected inflation + maturity premium + default premium + liquidity premium; Exact link between real and nominal: (1 + nominal) = (1 + real) x (1 + expected inflation)
interest-rate-build-up.when: Use it to explain why different loans carry different rates and why rates move. A change in expected inflation or the real rate moves all rates, while credit and liquidity premiums widen in stress. It is a way of decomposing a quoted rate, not a forecast. A government bond has no default premium in its own currency.

cap-floor-payoffs.mathml: Caplet=N τ max⁡(L−K,0),Floorlet=N τ max⁡(K−L,0)\text{Caplet}=N\,\tau\,\max(L-K,0),\quad \text{Floorlet}=N\,\tau\,\max(K-L,0)
cap-floor-payoffs.text: Caplet payment = Notional x Accrual fraction x max(Floating rate - Cap rate, 0); Floorlet payment = Notional x Accrual fraction x max(Floor rate - Floating rate, 0); a cap or floor is the sum of its caplets or floorlets
cap-floor-payoffs.when: Use it to see what a cap or floor pays. A cap is a series of call options on a rate, so a borrower with floating-rate debt uses it to limit the interest cost. A floor is a series of put options on a rate. The payment is made at the end of each period, based on the rate set at its start.

swap-fixed-rate.text: Fair fixed rate = (1 - Discount factor for the last payment date) / Sum of all the discount factors
swap-fixed-rate.when: Use it to find the fixed rate at which a swap costs nothing to enter. In a plain vanilla swap one side pays a fixed rate and the other pays a floating rate such as SOFR on the same notional. Only the net difference is paid on each date.

swap-value.text: Value to the fixed payer (just after a floating reset) = Notional x (1 - Final discount factor - Fixed rate x Sum of discount factors)
swap-value.when: Use it to find what an existing swap is worth after rates have moved. Just after a floating reset the floating leg is worth its notional, like a par bond. The fixed leg is a fixed-coupon bond. The payer gains if market swap rates have risen above the contract rate.

day-count-interest.text: I = P x r x days / basis
day-count-interest.when: Use it for money-market loans and short-term deposits, where interest is charged on the actual number of days. Always check which basis the contract uses.

irr.text: 0 = sum of CF_t / (1 + IRR)^t, for t = 0 to n
irr.when: Use it to express a project's return as one percentage that can be compared with the cost of funding. It has no simple formula, so it is found by trial and error or with a calculator.

international-fisher.text: Fisher: nominal rate = (1 + real rate)(1 + expected inflation) - 1. International Fisher: the expected change in the exchange rate (domestic per foreign) = (1 + domestic nominal rate) / (1 + foreign nominal rate) - 1. If real rates are equal, the interest differential equals the expected inflation differential
international-fisher.when: Use it to link interest rates, inflation and currency changes. If investors demand the same real return everywhere, a country with higher nominal rates must have higher expected inflation, and its currency should depreciate by the difference. Empirically the effect appears over long horizons and across high-inflation countries, but not reliably over short periods.

change-in-nwc.text: Change in NWC = w x (Sales this year - Sales last year), where w is NWC as a share of sales
change-in-nwc.when: Use it to include the cash a growing project ties up in inventory and receivables. It is a cash outflow when sales rise, and it is recovered at the end of the project.

platform-cost-comparison.text: Total cost over n years = trades per year x fee per trade x years + percentage fee x starting balance x ((1 + growth)^n - 1) / growth (percentage fee charged on the balance at the start of each year); Break-even balance = trades x (fee A - fee B) / (percentage B - percentage A)
platform-cost-comparison.when: Use it to compare two platforms with different fee structures. A flat fee per trade favors large balances and few trades, while a percentage fee favors small balances. The break-even balance shows where the choice flips. Also compare fund costs, currency conversion fees and the range of investments available, which this does not include.

thesis-expected-return-margin.mathml: MoS=V−PV,E[R]=p(VP−1)+(1−p)(LP−1),Rann=(1+E[R])1/n−1MoS=\frac{V-P}{V},\quad E[R]=p\left(\frac{V}{P}-1\right)+(1-p)\left(\frac{L}{P}-1\right),\quad R_{ann}=(1+E[R])^{1/n}-1
thesis-expected-return-margin.text: Margin of safety = (estimated value - price) / estimated value; Expected total return = probability the thesis works x its return + probability it fails x its return (a loss); Annualized = (1 + expected return)^(1 / years) - 1; Break-even probability = loss / (gain + loss), the chance the thesis must have to just cover itself
thesis-expected-return-margin.when: Use it to test your own thesis before you commit money. Write down what you believe, the price if you are right, the price if you are wrong and your confidence. A thin margin of safety, or a break-even probability close to your confidence, means there is little room for error. Write the conditions that would make you sell (kill criteria) before you buy.

investor-sentiment-composite.text: Each indicator's z-score = sign x (current value - its average) / its standard deviation, where the sign is -1 for indicators that rise when fear rises; Composite sentiment = average of the z-scores. Above +1 reads as greed and below -1 as fear
investor-sentiment-composite.when: Use it to combine several sentiment gauges into one number. Standardizing puts different indicators on a common scale. Extreme readings have sometimes preceded low returns after greed and high returns after fear, which is why some investors use them as contrarian signals, though timing is poor and trends can persist for a long time. The choice of indicators and sample matters.

ipo-underpricing.text: Underpricing = (First-day closing price - Offer price) / Offer price
ipo-underpricing.when: Use it to measure how much value the issuing company left with first-day buyers. A large first-day jump means the company could have raised more by pricing higher.

underwriting-economics.mathml: Gross spread=s P N,Net proceeds=PN(1−s)−Costs,Left on table=(P1−P)N\text{Gross spread}=s\,P\,N,\quad \text{Net proceeds}=PN(1-s)-\text{Costs},\quad \text{Left on table}=(P_{1}-P)N
underwriting-economics.text: Gross spread = spread % x offer price x shares; Net proceeds to the issuer = price x shares x (1 - spread %) - other costs; Greenshoe adds up to 15% more shares if demand is strong; Money left on the table = (first-day close - offer price) x shares sold
underwriting-economics.when: Use it to see what an offering costs the issuer and what the banks earn. The spread pays for advisory work, risk-taking by the underwriters and selling to investors. The greenshoe lets the banks sell extra shares and cover them from the issuer if the price rises, or from the market if it falls, which supports the price. First-day pops show underpricing, a cost to the issuer.

iqr-outlier-fences.text: IQR = third quartile - first quartile; Lower fence = Q1 - k x IQR; Upper fence = Q3 + k x IQR; values outside the fences are flagged (k = 1.5 is the usual choice)
iqr-outlier-fences.when: Use it as a first pass in cleaning data, to find values that look like errors or extreme events, such as a price typed with an extra digit. Quartiles ignore extreme values, so one bad point cannot hide itself the way it can in a mean and standard deviation test. A flagged value is a prompt to investigate, not an instruction to delete: real crashes are outliers too.

ito-lemma-drift.text: If dS = mu x S dt + sigma x S dW then a function f(S, t) has drift f_t + mu x S x f_S + 0.5 x sigma^2 x S^2 x f_SS and volatility sigma x S x f_S
ito-lemma-drift.when: Use it to find how a function of a random price behaves. The extra second-derivative term appears because squared random shocks do not average to zero: dW squared is dt. For f = ln S it shows that the log price drifts at mu minus half the variance, which explains why median growth is below mean growth.

j-curve-cumulative-cash.text: Net cash flow in year t = distributions - capital called; Cumulative net cash = running total; The trough (lowest point) is the most capital an investor has out at once; Breakeven year = first year the running total is zero or more
j-curve-cumulative-cash.when: Use it to see the J-curve of a private fund. In early years fees and unrealized investments push the net position below zero; later sales bring it back and above. The trough shows the cash an investor must be ready to fund, and the breakeven year shows the wait. Carry paid to the manager (the GP) comes out of distributions, which are already net here.

jensens-alpha.text: Alpha = Portfolio return - (rf + beta x (Market return - rf))
jensens-alpha.when: Use it to measure whether a manager added value after allowing for market risk. A positive alpha means the portfolio beat what its beta predicted.

justified-price-to-book.when: Use it to value banks and other financial firms, whose book value is close to market value. A bank earning more than its cost of equity should trade above book value.

kelly-criterion.mathml: f∗=p−1−pb,g(f)=pln⁡(1+bf)+(1−p)ln⁡(1−f)f^{*}=p-\frac{1-p}{b},\quad g(f)=p\ln(1+bf)+(1-p)\ln(1-f)
kelly-criterion.text: Best fraction of capital to stake = p - (1 - p) / b, where p is the chance of winning and b is the net payoff per 1 staked; Growth rate = p x ln(1 + b x f) + (1 - p) x ln(1 - f)
kelly-criterion.when: Use it to size repeated bets when you think you have an edge. Betting more than Kelly lowers long-run growth and raises the risk of ruin; betting twice Kelly gives zero growth. Because the win probability is only an estimate, most practitioners use half Kelly or less. A zero or negative answer means there is no edge and the right stake is zero.

autocorrelation.text: Lag-1 autocorrelation = sum of (xt - mean)(x(t-1) - mean) / sum of (xt - mean)^2
autocorrelation.when: Use it to see whether a series tends to continue in the same direction (positive), or reverse (negative), from one period to the next. Values near zero mean the past does little to predict the next move.

lbo-debt-paydown-schedule.mathml: Dt=Dt−1−min⁡(Dt−1, s [EBITDAt−CapExt−rDt−1−τ (EBITDAt−CapExt−rDt−1)])D_{t}=D_{t-1}-\min\big(D_{t-1},\ s\,[EBITDA_{t}-CapEx_{t}-r D_{t-1}-\tau\,(EBITDA_{t}-CapEx_{t}-r D_{t-1})]\big)
lbo-debt-paydown-schedule.text: Interest = opening debt x rate; Cash available for repayment = EBITDA - capital spending - interest - tax, where tax = tax rate x (EBITDA - capital spending - interest) (depreciation is ignored to keep it simple); Repayment = sweep share x cash available, but no more than the debt; Closing debt = opening debt - repayment; Leverage = closing debt / EBITDA
lbo-debt-paydown-schedule.when: Use it as the debt schedule of a leveraged buyout model. Cash that is not needed goes to repay debt, so leverage falls as earnings grow and interest costs fall. This version leaves out depreciation, working capital and fees, which a full model must add.

lbo-returns.mathml: MOIC=Exit equityEntry equity,IRR=MOIC1/n−1MOIC=\frac{\text{Exit equity}}{\text{Entry equity}},\quad IRR=MOIC^{1/n}-1
lbo-returns.text: MOIC = Exit equity / Entry equity; IRR = MOIC^(1/years) - 1, when there are no interim cash flows
lbo-returns.when: Use it to judge a leveraged buyout from the sponsor's view. Debt amplifies returns, because a modest rise in enterprise value becomes a large rise in equity value.

lbo-sources-and-uses.text: Uses = Purchase EV + Fees; Debt = EBITDA x Leverage multiple; Equity check = Uses - Debt
lbo-sources-and-uses.when: Use it to set up an LBO model. Total sources must equal total uses. The debt is sized from EBITDA, and the sponsor's equity fills the gap.

lease-liability-pv.text: Lease liability = Present value of the lease payments at the discount rate; Year-1 interest = Rate x Liability; Depreciation = Right-of-use asset / Lease term; IFRS 16 expense = Interest + Depreciation
lease-liability-pv.when: Use it to see how leases appear on the balance sheet. The lessee records a liability and a right-of-use asset at the present value of the payments. Under IFRS 16 (and ASC 842 finance leases) the expense is interest plus depreciation, which is higher in early years. Under ASC 842 an operating lease keeps a single straight-line expense.

lc-discounting-cost.text: Discount = face value x discount rate x days / 360; Total cost = discount + issuance fee (% of face) + confirmation fee (% a year x days / 360 x face); Net proceeds = face - total cost; All-in annualized cost = total cost / net proceeds x 365 / days
lc-discounting-cost.when: Use it to see what a seller pays to be paid early on an export under a letter of credit. The bank pays the seller now, less a discount, and collects the buyer's bank payment later. A bank-quoted discount rate understates the true cost, since it applies to face value and not to the amount actually advanced, and fees add to it. Compare all-in rates, not quoted rates.

life-insurance-need.text: Cover needed = present value of the income to replace (first-year amount, growing at g, discounted at r for n years) + debts to clear + future goals (such as education) - existing assets and cover
life-insurance-need.when: Use it to size life insurance for people who depend on your income. It is a needs method: it asks what the family would need, not a multiple of salary. A negative result means existing assets already cover the need. The discount rate matters a lot, so test a lower one for caution. It ignores taxes and any survivor benefits, so treat it as an estimate.

arbitrage-holding-cost.text: Net profit per share from shorting an overpriced stock = gap to fundamental value - borrow fee x price x years - financing rate x margin share x price x years; Break-even holding time = gap / (price x (borrow fee + financing rate x margin share)); Loss if the price moves further away by a = a x price
arbitrage-holding-cost.when: Use it to see why obvious mispricings can last. A trader who bets against an overpriced stock pays fees every year and must post margin. If the price moves further away before it converges, losses can force the position closed at the worst time, so a mispricing can survive even when prices are wrong. The gap must be large enough to pay for time and risk.

supply-demand-equilibrium.mathml: Qd=a−bP,  Qs=c+dP  ⇒  P∗=a−cb+d,  Q∗=a−bP∗Q_{d}=a-bP,\; Q_{s}=c+dP\;\Rightarrow\; P^{*}=\frac{a-c}{b+d},\; Q^{*}=a-bP^{*}
supply-demand-equilibrium.text: Demand: Qd = a - b x P. Supply: Qs = c + d x P. Equilibrium price P* = (a - c) / (b + d); equilibrium quantity Q* = a - b x P*
supply-demand-equilibrium.when: Use it to see how a price is set where buyers and sellers agree. A rise in demand (a larger a) raises both the price and the quantity. A price ceiling below the equilibrium price creates a shortage, because buyers want more than sellers will supply. Real curves are not straight lines, so treat this as an illustration of direction and rough size.

cash-flow-statement-link.mathml: ΔCash=CFO+CFI+CFF,CFO=NI+D&A−ΔNWC\Delta Cash=CFO+CFI+CFF,\quad CFO=NI+D\&A-\Delta NWC
cash-flow-statement-link.text: Cash flow from operations = Net income + Depreciation - Increase in working capital; Cash flow from investing = -Capex; Cash flow from financing = Debt issued - Debt repaid - Dividends + Shares issued; Ending cash = Opening cash + total cash flow
cash-flow-statement-link.when: Use it to see how the three statements connect. Net income flows into the cash flow statement and retained earnings. Capex and depreciation move fixed assets. Debt and dividends change liabilities and equity. Ending cash goes back to the balance sheet, and the balance sheet must still balance, which is the check at the bottom.

liquidity-adjusted-var.text: Liquidity-adjusted VaR = VaR + 0.5 x Position value x Relative bid-ask spread
liquidity-adjusted-var.when: Use it when positions cannot be sold at the mid price. VaR assumes you can trade at the quoted price, but selling costs half the spread. In a crisis spreads widen, so the liquidity cost can be a large part of the total. This is the simple version with a fixed spread.

loan-payment.when: Use it to find the fixed payment on a loan that is repaid in equal installments, such as a mortgage or a car loan.

long-short-factor-return.text: Factor return = Return of the long portfolio - Return of the short portfolio
long-short-factor-return.when: Use it to measure a factor such as value, size or momentum. A factor return is what you earn by buying one group of stocks and selling short the other, so it is independent of the market's direction.

long-short-fund-net-return.mathml: Gross=wL+wS, Net=wL−wS,Rg=wLrL−wSrS+wSrreb,Rnet=Rg−f−pmax⁡(Rg−f−h,0)\text{Gross}=w_{L}+w_{S},\ \text{Net}=w_{L}-w_{S},\quad R_{g}=w_{L}r_{L}-w_{S}r_{S}+w_{S}r_{reb},\quad R_{net}=R_{g}-f-p\max(R_{g}-f-h,0)
long-short-fund-net-return.text: Gross exposure = long weight + short weight; Net exposure = long weight - short weight; Gross return = long weight x long return - short weight x short stock return + short weight x interest on short proceeds; Fund return after management fee = gross - fee; Incentive fee = share x amount above the hurdle; Net return = after management fee - incentive fee
long-short-fund-net-return.when: Use it to read what a long/short fund does and what it costs. Net exposure is the market bet; the gap between the long and short books is the manager's skill. Fees take a fixed slice plus a share of gains, so investors keep much less than the gross figure. This sketch has a one-year view and no high-water mark, so multi-year fees may differ.

duration.text: Macaulay duration = sum of (time x present value of each cash flow) / Price; Modified duration = Macaulay duration / (1 + yield / payments per year)
duration.when: Use it to measure a bond's sensitivity to interest rates. A bond with a duration of 7 loses about 7% in price if yields rise by 1 percentage point. A higher coupon and a higher yield lower duration, and a longer maturity raises it.

margin-analysis.text: Gross margin = (Revenue - COGS) / Revenue; Operating margin = Operating profit / Revenue; Net margin = Net income / Revenue; the change is shown in basis points
