margin-analysis.when: Use it to see how much of each unit of sales becomes profit at each stage, and how that changed. A falling gross margin points to pricing or input cost pressure, and a falling operating margin with a steady gross margin points to rising overheads.

margin-call-price.text: Margin call price = Start price x (1 - Initial margin) / (1 - Maintenance margin)
margin-call-price.when: Use it to know how far a stock can fall before a margin call on a long position. Your equity is the position value minus the loan, and the call comes when equity falls to the maintenance share of the position value.

market-manipulation-ratios.text: Order-to-trade ratio = orders entered / trades executed; Cancellation rate = orders canceled / orders entered; Self-trade share = volume where the same beneficial owner is on both sides / total volume; Very high ratios and quick cancellations are warning signs of spoofing or layering, and a high self-trade share of wash trading
market-manipulation-ratios.when: Use it to see how exchanges and regulators screen for manipulation. Placing large orders and canceling them before execution (spoofing) gives a false view of demand; trading with oneself (wash trades) gives a false view of volume. A high ratio is a flag to investigate, since market makers can also have high ratios for legitimate reasons.

market-ratios-pb-ps-ev.mathml: P/B=PBVPS,P/S=Market capSales,EVEBITDA=Market cap+Net debtEBITDAP/B=\frac{P}{BVPS},\quad P/S=\frac{\text{Market cap}}{\text{Sales}},\quad \frac{EV}{EBITDA}=\frac{\text{Market cap}+\text{Net debt}}{EBITDA}
market-ratios-pb-ps-ev.text: P/B = Price / Book value per share; P/S = Market cap / Sales; EV/EBITDA = (Market cap + Net debt) / EBITDA; P/E = Price / EPS
market-ratios-pb-ps-ev.when: Use it to compare what the market pays with what the company reports. P/E, EPS and dividend yield have their own entries. P/B suits asset-heavy firms and banks, P/S suits firms without profits, and EV/EBITDA compares firms with different debt.

market-value-added.mathml: MVA=Market value of the firm−Capital investedMVA=\text{Market value of the firm}-\text{Capital invested}
market-value-added.text: MVA = (Market value of equity + Market value of debt) - Capital invested
market-value-added.when: Use it to measure whether a firm has created or destroyed value for its investors. A positive MVA means the market values the firm above the capital invested in it.

cap-weighted-index.text: Index level = Starting level x (Total market value now / Total market value at the start)
cap-weighted-index.when: Use it for indices like the S&P 500 and FTSE 100, where each company counts in proportion to its size. A big company moves the index more than a small one.

martingale-check.text: Under risk-neutral probabilities the expected discounted future price equals today's price: e^(-rT) x [q x Su + (1 - q) x Sd] = S0
martingale-check.when: Use it to test a price model. A martingale is a fair game: its expected future value equals its current value. Discounted asset prices are martingales under the risk-neutral measure, which is the reason risk-neutral pricing works. Under real-world probabilities the discounted price is usually not a martingale, because investors earn a risk premium.

maximum-drawdown.text: Maximum drawdown = the largest fall from a previous peak, as a percentage of that peak
maximum-drawdown.when: Use it to see the worst loss an investor would have suffered by buying at a peak and selling at the next low. It shows pain that an average or a standard deviation hides.

mbs-pass-through-month.mathml: Investor cash flow=Interest at pass-through rate+Scheduled principal+Prepayment\text{Investor cash flow}=\text{Interest at pass-through rate}+\text{Scheduled principal}+\text{Prepayment}
mbs-pass-through-month.text: Investor cash flow = Balance x Pass-through rate / 12 + Scheduled principal + SMM x (Balance - Scheduled principal)
mbs-pass-through-month.when: Use it to see where the monthly cash from a mortgage pool goes. Borrowers pay interest at the WAC and a level payment. Servicers keep a fee, and investors get the pass-through interest, the scheduled principal and any prepayments.

ou-process-moments.text: Expected value at time t = Long-run mean + (Start - Long-run mean) x e^(-speed x t); Variance = sigma^2 / (2 x speed) x (1 - e^(-2 x speed x t))
ou-process-moments.when: Use it for quantities that wander but are pulled back to a normal level, such as interest rates, spreads and commodity prices. The expected value moves from the start toward the long-run mean, and the variance rises to a ceiling instead of growing forever, unlike a random walk. The half-life is the time to close half the gap.

mental-accounting-cost.mathml: Net gain=Pay×(rdebt−rsave),Pay=min⁡(D,  S−B)\text{Net gain}=\text{Pay}\times(r_{debt}-r_{save}),\quad \text{Pay}=\min(D,\;S-B)
mental-accounting-cost.text: Amount you could pay off = smaller of the debt and (savings - emergency buffer you decide to keep); Interest saved = amount x debt rate; Interest given up = amount x savings rate; Net gain per year = amount x (debt rate - savings rate)
mental-accounting-cost.when: Use it when you hold savings in one pot and costly debt in another. Money is fungible, so a pound in the savings account that earns 3% while a card charges 22% is costing you the difference. People often keep the pots separate, because the savings feel "safe" or have a label. Keep the buffer so you do not need to borrow again.

merchant-payment-cost.mathml: Cost=a×MDR+f,MDR=i+s+m,Effective rate=Costa\text{Cost}=a\times MDR+f,\quad MDR=i+s+m,\quad \text{Effective rate}=\frac{\text{Cost}}{a}
merchant-payment-cost.text: Merchant discount rate (MDR) = interchange (paid to the card issuer) + scheme fee (card network) + acquirer margin; Cost of one payment = amount x MDR + fixed fee per transaction; Effective rate = cost / amount; Break-even amount against a flat-fee method = flat fee / (MDR - 0)
merchant-payment-cost.when: Use it to see what accepting cards or a wallet really costs. The percentage is split between the issuing bank, the network and the processor, and the fixed fee makes small payments cost a higher percentage. Compare payment methods by their effective rate at your average basket size.

merton-model.mathml: E=V N(d1)−D e−rTN(d2),PD=N(−d2),s=−1Tln⁡V−ED−rE=V\,N(d_{1})-D\,e^{-rT}N(d_{2}),\quad PD=N(-d_{2}),\quad s=-\frac{1}{T}\ln\frac{V-E}{D}-r
merton-model.text: Equity value E = V x N(d1) - D x e^(-rT) x N(d2); Default probability = N(-d2); Credit spread = -(1/T) x ln[(Firm value - Equity) / Debt] - risk-free rate; d1 = [ln(V/D) + (r + sigma^2 / 2) x T] / (sigma x sqrt(T))
merton-model.when: Use it to see credit risk as an option. Equity holders own a call option on the firm's assets with the debt as the strike. The firm defaults if its assets are below the debt when it falls due. The model turns asset value, debt and volatility into a default probability and credit spread. The default probability is risk-neutral, so it overstates the real-world probability.

minimum-variance-hedge-ratio.text: Hedge ratio h = correlation x (Volatility of the exposure / Volatility of the hedge); Contracts N = h x Exposure / Contract size
minimum-variance-hedge-ratio.when: Use it to size a hedge when the hedging instrument is not a perfect match for the exposure. A lower correlation means the hedge removes less of the risk.

minimum-variance-portfolio.text: Weight in asset 1 = (s2^2 - rho x s1 x s2) / (s1^2 + s2^2 - 2 x rho x s1 x s2), and asset 2 gets the rest
minimum-variance-portfolio.when: Use it to find the mix of two assets with the lowest risk. It is the left-most point of the efficient frontier. A negative weight means that asset should be sold short, and this formula allows it.

model-error-metrics.mathml: Bias=Pmodel−Pmkt‾,MAE=∣Pmodel−Pmkt∣‾,RMSE=(Pmodel−Pmkt)2‾Bias=\overline{P_{model}-P_{mkt}},\quad MAE=\overline{|P_{model}-P_{mkt}|},\quad RMSE=\sqrt{\overline{(P_{model}-P_{mkt})^{2}}}
model-error-metrics.text: Bias = average of (Model - Market); MAE = average of |Model - Market|; RMSE = square root of the average of (Model - Market)^2; Largest error = max |Model - Market|
model-error-metrics.when: Use it to test a model against market prices. Bias shows if the model is consistently too high or low. RMSE penalizes large misses more than MAE does, and the largest error shows the worst case. A model that is accurate on average can still fail badly in one corner.

mirr.mathml: MIRR=(FV of inflows at reinvestment ratePV of outflows at finance rate)1/n−1MIRR=\left(\frac{FV\text{ of inflows at reinvestment rate}}{PV\text{ of outflows at finance rate}}\right)^{1/n}-1
mirr.text: MIRR = (FV of inflows at the reinvestment rate / PV of outflows at the finance rate)^(1/n) - 1
mirr.when: Use it when IRR is unreliable, for example when cash flows change sign more than once and give several IRRs. MIRR always gives one answer and assumes cash is reinvested at a realistic rate.

mmf-nav-break-the-buck.text: Net asset value per share = value of assets after losses / shares outstanding; If investors redeem a share fraction w at the stable price of 1.00 while the true value is lower, the NAV left for remaining holders = (assets after losses - w x shares x 1.00) / (shares x (1 - w)). The fund breaks the buck if NAV falls below 0.995
mmf-nav-break-the-buck.when: Use it to see why money funds and other shadow-bank vehicles are run-prone. Investors who redeem early get 1.00 while the true value is below it, so those who stay absorb the loss, which gives everyone a reason to leave first. That first-mover advantage turned small losses into a run in 2008. Rules since then allow fees and gates, and some funds now float their NAV.

money-multiplier.mathml: msimple=1rr,m=1+cc+rr+e,ΔD=ΔRrrm_{simple}=\frac{1}{rr},\quad m=\frac{1+c}{c+rr+e},\quad \Delta D=\frac{\Delta R}{rr}
money-multiplier.text: Simple deposit multiplier = 1 / reserve ratio; Money multiplier with leakages = (1 + currency ratio) / (currency ratio + reserve ratio + excess reserve ratio); Deposit expansion from new reserves = new reserves / reserve ratio
money-multiplier.when: Use it to see how banks create deposits by lending part of what they receive. Each loan becomes a deposit elsewhere, so a reserve injection supports several times its amount. Leakages into cash and extra reserves cut the multiplier. In practice, banks lend when they see good borrowers and capital allows, and are not limited by reserves, so this is a teaching model.

money-weighted-return.text: Money-weighted return = the IRR of the investor's cash flows, including the ending value
money-weighted-return.when: Use it to measure what the investor actually earned. It is affected by the size and timing of deposits, so it differs from the time-weighted return when money moves in or out.

monte-carlo-standard-error.mathml: V^=1N∑i=1NPVi,SE=sN,Nneeded=(starget SE)2\hat{V}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\text{PV}_{i},\quad SE=\frac{s}{\sqrt{N}},\quad N_{\text{needed}}=\left(\frac{s}{\text{target SE}}\right)^{2}
monte-carlo-standard-error.text: Price estimate = average of the discounted payoffs; Standard error = sample standard deviation / sqrt(N); Paths needed for a target error = (sample standard deviation / target error)^2
monte-carlo-standard-error.when: Use it to judge how accurate a simulated price is. The error shrinks with the square root of the number of paths, so halving the error needs four times as many paths. A 95% confidence interval is the estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors. Variance reduction tricks lower s without more paths.

two-stage-ddm.text: Price = PV of the high-growth dividends for n years + PV of the terminal value at year n
two-stage-ddm.when: Use it for a company expected to grow fast for a while and then settle at a steady rate. It splits the value into the growth stage and the stable stage after it.

multiple-testing-false-positives.mathml: FWER=1−(1−α)n,αadj=αn,E[false positives]=nαFWER=1-(1-\alpha)^{n},\quad \alpha_{adj}=\frac{\alpha}{n},\quad E[\text{false positives}]=n\alpha
multiple-testing-false-positives.text: If you test n unrelated ideas at significance level alpha, the chance of at least one false discovery = 1 - (1 - alpha)^n; Expected number of false positives = n x alpha; Bonferroni-adjusted threshold = alpha / n; A result is credible only if its p-value is below the adjusted threshold; Required t-statistic rises from about 2 to 3 or more when many strategies are tried
multiple-testing-false-positives.when: Use it to check research for data mining. If you try 40 signals and report the best one, a "significant" result at 5% is very likely by luck alone. State how many things you tried, adjust the threshold, and test on data not used in the search. The same issue applies to backtests where many rules and parameters were tried.

muni-tax-equivalent-yield.text: Combined tax rate = Federal rate + State rate x (1 - Federal rate); Tax-equivalent yield = Muni yield / (1 - Combined tax rate)
muni-tax-equivalent-yield.when: Use it to compare a tax-exempt municipal bond with a taxable one. The higher your tax rate the more the exemption is worth. The formula assumes that state tax is deductible on the federal return, which varies by country and year, so adjust the combined rate if your rules differ.

murabaha-implied-rate.text: Sale price = cost x (1 + mark-up); Installment = sale price / number of installments; Implied periodic rate i solves: cost = installment x (1 - (1 + i)^(-n)) / i; Effective annual rate = (1 + i)^12 - 1 for monthly installments
murabaha-implied-rate.when: Use it to compare an Islamic cost-plus sale with a conventional loan. The bank buys the asset and sells it to the customer at cost plus an agreed mark-up, payable in installments, so the price is fixed and does not accrue interest on a loan. The implied rate is a comparison tool only: the two contracts are structured differently and differ in legal treatment, risk and late-payment rules.

narrative-contagion-sir.text: Basic reproduction number R0 = contagion rate / forgetting (recovery) rate. If R0 > 1 the story spreads. Peak share actively spreading = 1 - (1 + ln R0) / R0; Share who ever hear and believe it, z, solves z = 1 - e^(-R0 x z). A story dies out if R0 is 1 or less
narrative-contagion-sir.when: Use it to think about how popular narratives, such as a boom story or a panic story, spread like an epidemic. The same mathematics as disease models gives the threshold for a story to take off and how many people it eventually reaches. Shiller argues such narratives drive markets. The parameters are not directly measured, so the model gives intuition about thresholds, not forecasts.

neobank-unit-economics.text: Margin per customer per year = fee and interchange income + net interest income - cost to serve; Payback in months = acquisition cost / (monthly margin); Lifetime value = yearly margin / yearly churn; Breakeven customers = fixed cost / margin per customer
neobank-unit-economics.when: Use it to judge whether an app-based bank can make money. Many customers hold small balances, so income per customer is low and many neobanks need years of scale to cover costs. Compare the margin per customer with the cost of acquiring one and the time a customer stays. Fraud losses and a lack of a main-bank relationship lower income.

net-advantage-to-leasing.text: NAL = Asset cost - PV of after-tax lease payments - PV of depreciation tax shields given up
net-advantage-to-leasing.when: Use it to decide whether to lease or buy an asset. The lessee gives up the depreciation tax shield but saves the purchase cost. This version has no salvage value and pays leases at the end of each year.

nav-per-share.text: NAV per share = (Fund assets - Fund liabilities) / Number of fund shares
nav-per-share.when: Use it to find the price at which a mutual fund buys and sells its shares. It is calculated once a day after markets close, and you trade at that price, not at an intraday price.

net-book-value.text: Net book value = Cost - Accumulated depreciation
net-book-value.when: Use it to find the value at which an asset is shown on the balance sheet. It is an accounting figure and can differ a lot from the asset's market value.

net-change-in-cash.text: Change in cash = CFO + CFI + CFF, and Ending cash = Beginning cash + Change in cash
net-change-in-cash.when: Use it to reconcile the cash flow statement. The three sections add up to the change in the cash balance on the balance sheet.

net-income.when: Use it to find a company's profit for a period, at the bottom of the income statement. A negative result is a net loss.

net-interest-margin.mathml: NIM=Interest income−Interest expenseEarning assetsNIM = \frac{\text{Interest income}-\text{Interest expense}}{\text{Earning assets}}
net-interest-margin.text: NIM = (Interest income - Interest expense) / Earning assets
net-interest-margin.when: Use it to see how much a bank or other intermediary earns from the gap between what it charges borrowers and what it pays savers.

cap-rate-valuation.text: Net operating income = potential rent x (1 - vacancy) - operating expenses (before debt service, tax and depreciation); Value = NOI / cap rate; Cap rate = NOI / value; Debt service coverage = NOI / annual loan payment
cap-rate-valuation.when: Use it for a quick market value of an income-producing building. Dividing a steady year of income by a yield gives the price, the property-world version of a perpetuity. Cap rates move with interest rates and risk, so a small change in the rate moves value a lot. It ignores growth, so it fits stable properties best.

npv.text: NPV = sum of CF_t / (1 + r)^t, for t = 0 to n
npv.when: Use it to decide whether a project or investment is worth doing. Accept it when NPV is above zero and reject it when NPV is below zero.

net-working-capital.when: Use it to see how much short-term resources a company has left after paying its short-term bills. A negative figure is a warning sign.

net-worth.text: Net worth = total assets - total liabilities; Debt-to-asset ratio = total liabilities / total assets; Solvency ratio = net worth / total assets
net-worth.when: Use it once or twice a year to see where you stand. Net worth is a snapshot, so watch the direction over time, not one number. A young person with student debt may start negative. Count assets at realistic sale value, not what you paid.

netting-efficiency.text: Each bank's net position = payments received - payments sent; Multilateral net settlement = sum of the positive net positions; Bilateral netting = for each pair, the difference between the two payments; Liquidity saving = 1 - settled amount / gross payments
netting-efficiency.when: Use it to see why clearing houses and central counterparties reduce the cash banks need. Instead of settling every payment separately (gross), obligations are offset, so only net positions move. Multilateral netting through a central party shrinks flows most, but concentrates risk in the center, which is why it requires collateral and a default fund. Enter the payments of three banks row by row.

newton-implied-vol.text: Next guess = Current guess - (Model price at the guess - Market price) / Vega at the guess
newton-implied-vol.when: Use it to see how a numerical solver finds an answer that has no formula. Newton's method follows the slope: from the current guess, move to where the tangent line would hit the target. It usually settles in three to five steps. The same idea drives optimization, where it is applied to the derivative.

noise-variance-share.mathml: Var(P)=Var(F)+Var(N)+2 Cov(F,N),R2=Cov(P,F)2Var(P) Var(F)Var(P)=Var(F)+Var(N)+2\,Cov(F,N),\quad R^{2}=\frac{Cov(P,F)^{2}}{Var(P)\,Var(F)}
noise-variance-share.text: Noise = price - fundamental value; Variance of price = variance of fundamental + variance of noise + 2 x covariance; Share of price variation explained by fundamentals (R-squared) = Cov(P, F)^2 / (Var(P) x Var(F))
noise-variance-share.when: Use it to ask how much of price movement is news about value and how much is noise from sentiment-driven trading. If prices move much more than fundamentals, noise is large, as in the excess-volatility tests. Fundamental value is estimated, so the split depends on the model, and a high noise share can also reflect errors in the value estimate.

non-gaap-reconciliation.text: Adjusted net income = GAAP net income + sum of the pre-tax add-backs x (1 - tax rate); Adjusted EPS = Adjusted net income / Shares
non-gaap-reconciliation.when: Use it to rebuild a company's adjusted figure from its reported one. Companies publish adjusted metrics that exclude items they call one-off. Check the size of the gap and whether the items recur year after year. A large, persistent gap means the adjusted number is flattering.

futures-hedge-contracts.text: Contracts = (Target beta - Current beta) x Portfolio value / (Futures price x Multiplier); a negative number means sell
futures-hedge-contracts.when: Use it to cut or raise a portfolio's market exposure with index futures instead of selling the shares. A full hedge sets the target beta to zero. A negative answer means selling futures, and a positive one means buying.

loan-term.text: n = -ln(1 - P x r / PMT) / ln(1 + r)
loan-term.when: Use it to find how long a loan takes to repay when you choose the payment, for example when you pay more than the minimum on a credit card.

solve-for-periods.when: Use it when you know the starting amount, the target and the rate, and want to know how long it will take.

okun-law.mathml: Δu=−β (g−g∗)\Delta u=-\beta\,(g-g^{*})
okun-law.text: Change in the unemployment rate = - beta x (real GDP growth - trend growth), with beta about 0.5 in the United States
okun-law.when: Use it as a rough rule linking growth and unemployment. Growth below trend raises unemployment and growth above trend lowers it. The coefficient and trend growth vary by country and period, so treat the output as a guide. It is a statistical regularity, not a law.

working-capital-analysis.text: Operating working capital = (Receivables + Inventory + Prepaid) - (Payables + Accrued liabilities); Intensity = OWC / Sales; Incremental intensity = Change in OWC / Change in sales
working-capital-analysis.when: Use it to see how much money the day-to-day business ties up as it grows. Operating working capital leaves out cash and financial debt, which are financing items. A company with a high incremental intensity needs more funding as it grows.

op-risk-capital-bia.text: Basic Indicator capital = 15% x Average of the positive annual gross income over three years; Expected annual operational loss = Number of loss events per year x Average loss per event
op-risk-capital-bia.when: Use it for a simple measure of operational risk capital. The Basic Indicator Approach ties capital to income as a rough proxy for size. Most banks also model the frequency and severity of internal loss events to find the expected annual loss.

tangency-portfolio-two-assets.text: Weight in asset 1 = [(m1 - rf) x s2^2 - (m2 - rf) x rho x s1 x s2] / [(m1 - rf) x s2^2 + (m2 - rf) x s1^2 - (m1 - rf + m2 - rf) x rho x s1 x s2]; weight in asset 2 = 1 - weight in asset 1
tangency-portfolio-two-assets.when: Use it to find the mix of two risky assets with the highest Sharpe ratio. It comes from an optimization: maximize the Sharpe ratio subject to weights adding to 1, and set the derivative to zero. For more than two assets the same solution is found with matrix algebra or numerical optimizers.

option-greeks.mathml: ΔC=e−qTN(d1), Γ=e−qTϕ(d1)SσT, ν=Se−qTϕ(d1)T, ρC=KTe−rTN(d2)\Delta_{C}=e^{-qT}N(d_{1}),\ \Gamma=\frac{e^{-qT}\phi(d_{1})}{S\sigma\sqrt{T}},\ \nu=S e^{-qT}\phi(d_{1})\sqrt{T},\ \rho_{C}=K T e^{-rT}N(d_{2})
option-greeks.text: Call delta = e^(-qT) x N(d1); Put delta = call delta - e^(-qT); Gamma = e^(-qT) x pdf(d1) / (S x sigma x sqrt(T)); Vega = S x e^(-qT) x pdf(d1) x sqrt(T); Call theta = [-S e^(-qT) pdf(d1) sigma / (2 sqrt(T)) - r K e^(-rT) N(d2) + q S e^(-qT) N(d1)]; Call rho = K T e^(-rT) N(d2)
option-greeks.when: Use it to measure how an option's price reacts to each input. Delta is the hedge ratio, gamma shows how fast delta changes, vega shows the volatility exposure, theta is the daily cost of holding, and rho is rate sensitivity. These are for European options under Black-Scholes.

option-intrinsic-time-value.mathml: Option price=Intrinsic value+Time value\text{Option price}=\text{Intrinsic value}+\text{Time value}
option-intrinsic-time-value.text: Intrinsic value of a call = max(Spot - Strike, 0), of a put = max(Strike - Spot, 0); Time value = Option price - Intrinsic value
option-intrinsic-time-value.when: Use it to split an option's price into what it is worth today and what is paid for future possibility. Time value is highest when the option is at the money and falls to zero at expiry.

option-price-bounds.mathml: C≥max⁡(Se−qT−Ke−rT,0),P≥max⁡(Ke−rT−Se−qT,0),PAmer≥K−SC\ge\max(S e^{-qT}-K e^{-rT},0),\quad P\ge\max(K e^{-rT}-S e^{-qT},0),\quad P_{Amer}\ge K-S
option-price-bounds.text: European call lower bound = max(S x e^(-qT) - K x e^(-rT), 0); European put lower bound = max(K x e^(-rT) - S x e^(-qT), 0); American put lower bound = max(K - S, 0)
option-price-bounds.when: Use it to test whether an option price is sensible, and to see if early exercise might be worth it. An American option can be exercised any time, so it is worth at least its intrinsic value. If a put's intrinsic value exceeds its European lower bound, early exercise can be optimal. A call on a share with no dividends is never exercised early.

oos-r-squared.text: Out-of-sample R-squared = 1 - (sum of squared errors of the model forecasts) / (sum of squared errors of a benchmark forecast, usually the historical average)
oos-r-squared.when: Use it to judge whether a model really forecasts, as opposed to fitting history. It compares the model to a simple benchmark on data the model never saw. Positive means the model beats the benchmark. Return forecasts usually score a tiny positive number or a negative one, and even 0.5% a month can be economically useful, so judge it against the benchmark and costs, not against 100%.

output-gap-annualized.text: Output gap = (actual real GDP - potential real GDP) / potential real GDP; Annualized growth = (1 + quarterly growth)^4 - 1
output-gap-annualized.when: Use it to place an economy in the cycle. A positive gap means demand is running above sustainable capacity, which tends to push inflation up and prompts central banks to tighten. A negative gap means slack. Potential output cannot be observed and is estimated, so the gap is uncertain, often revised by a full percentage point.

owner-earnings.text: Owner earnings = Net income + Depreciation and amortization - Capital spending needed to maintain the business - Increase in working capital
owner-earnings.when: Use it to estimate the cash a business generates for its owners. Buffett prefers it to reported profit because depreciation is not cash but maintenance spending is. Value the stream as a perpetuity to estimate what the business is worth.

dilution-from-new-issue.text: New shares = Amount raised / Issue price; Ownership after = Shares you hold / (Old shares + New shares)
dilution-from-new-issue.when: Use it to see how much your ownership share falls when a company sells new shares to others and you do not buy any.

pe-earnings-yield.text: P/E = Share price / Earnings per share; Earnings yield = Earnings per share / Share price
pe-earnings-yield.when: Use it as a quick check of how much investors pay for each unit of profit. The earnings yield is the same thing upside down and can be compared directly with a bond yield.

pairs-trade-sizing.text: z-score = (spread - mean spread) / sd of spread; Units of the pair = floor(capital / (price Y + hedge ratio x price X)); Profit if the spread returns to its mean = Units x |spread - mean|
pairs-trade-sizing.when: Use it to size a trade once a spread has been identified. When the z-score is large and positive the spread is rich: short Y and buy beta units of X. When it is large and negative, do the reverse. Profit assumes the spread fully reverts, and ignores costs, financing and the chance that the relationship has broken, so it is an upper bound, not a forecast.

payback-period.mathml: Payback=t−1+Unrecovered cost at start of year tCFt\text{Payback}=t-1+\frac{\text{Unrecovered cost at start of year }t}{CF_{t}}
payback-period.text: Payback = last full year before recovery + unrecovered cost / cash flow in the recovery year
payback-period.when: Use it as a quick measure of how fast a project returns its cost. It ignores cash flows after the payback and ignores the time value of money, so use it alongside NPV, not instead of it.

payment-rail-crossover.mathml: Ccard=a mc+fc,Crtp=a mr+fr,a∗=fr−fcmc−mrC_{card}=a\,m_{c}+f_{c},\quad C_{rtp}=a\,m_{r}+f_{r},\quad a^{*}=\frac{f_{r}-f_{c}}{m_{c}-m_{r}}
payment-rail-crossover.text: Cost on a card network = amount x percentage fee + fixed fee; Cost on a real-time (account-to-account) rail = amount x percentage fee + fixed fee (often a small flat fee or zero); Crossover amount a* = (flat fee on rail B - flat fee on rail A) / (percentage on A - percentage on B)
payment-rail-crossover.when: Use it to choose a rail by payment size. Card networks charge mostly a percentage; many real-time rails charge a small flat fee or nothing, so they are cheaper for large payments, while a flat fee can be worse for tiny ones. Some systems, such as UPI in India, are free to the user, which changes who bears the cost.

peer-relative-ratio.text: Z-score = (Company ratio - Peer mean) / Peer standard deviation; Premium to the median = Company ratio / Peer median - 1
peer-relative-ratio.when: Use it to see whether a company's ratio is unusually high or low against comparable firms. Use the median as well as the mean, since a single odd peer can distort the mean.

p2p-note-net-return.text: Net return = loan interest rate - platform servicing fee - (annual default rate x loss given default); Break-even default rate = (rate - fee) / loss given default; Investor with n equal notes loses 1/n of the money per default
p2p-note-net-return.when: Use it to judge whether lending to individuals or small firms through a platform is worth the risk. The headline rate is not what you earn; defaults and fees take a slice, and you cannot easily sell a note. Spread across many notes, the result moves toward the expected value, but defaults tend to rise together in a downturn.

peg-ratio.text: PEG = P/E ratio / Expected annual earnings growth rate (as a whole number, such as 15 for 15%)
peg-ratio.when: Use it to compare growth and value stocks on one scale. A fast-growing stock can deserve a high P/E, and the PEG adjusts for it. A value of 1 is often read as fairly priced, and below 1 as cheap for its growth.

brinson-attribution.mathml: Ai=(wp,i−wb,i)(Rb,i−Rb),Si=wb,i(Rp,i−Rb,i),Ii=(wp,i−wb,i)(Rp,i−Rb,i)A_{i}=(w_{p,i}-w_{b,i})(R_{b,i}-R_{b}),\quad S_{i}=w_{b,i}(R_{p,i}-R_{b,i}),\quad I_{i}=(w_{p,i}-w_{b,i})(R_{p,i}-R_{b,i})
brinson-attribution.text: Allocation = (Portfolio weight - Benchmark weight) x (Benchmark sector return - Total benchmark return); Selection = Benchmark weight x (Portfolio sector return - Benchmark sector return); Interaction = (Portfolio weight - Benchmark weight) x (Portfolio sector return - Benchmark sector return)
brinson-attribution.when: Use it to explain why a portfolio beat or lagged its benchmark. Allocation shows the effect of over- or underweighting sectors, selection shows the effect of picking better stocks within sectors, and interaction is the combined leftover.

perpetuity.when: Use it to value payments that continue forever and stay the same, such as a fixed dividend or a bond that never matures.

budget-net-worth-dashboard.text: Savings rate = (income - spending) / income; Net worth = total assets - total liabilities; Runway in months = liquid assets / monthly spending; Debt-to-assets = liabilities / assets; Change in net worth = savings + investment gains - debt interest and fees
budget-net-worth-dashboard.when: Use it as the monthly check on your finances. The savings rate shows how much you add, the net worth shows where you stand, and the runway shows how long you could cover costs without income. Update it once a month with real numbers, in the same categories each time, so the trend is clear.

pmi-surprise.text: Diffusion index (PMI) = % of firms reporting better + 0.5 x % reporting no change (above 50 means expansion); Surprise z-score = (actual - consensus forecast) / standard deviation of past surprises
pmi-surprise.when: Use it to read two things markets focus on. A diffusion index above 50 means more firms are improving than worsening. Prices react to the surprise (actual minus consensus), not the level, because the consensus is already in the price. Dividing by the typical surprise puts different indicators on the same scale.

policy-rate-pass-through.mathml: Δrloan=βL Δrp,ΔNII=βL Ars Δrp−βD Drs Δrp\Delta r_{loan}=\beta_{L}\,\Delta r_{p},\quad \Delta NII=\beta_{L}\,A_{rs}\,\Delta r_{p}-\beta_{D}\,D_{rs}\,\Delta r_{p}
policy-rate-pass-through.text: Change in loan rate = loan beta x change in policy rate; Change in deposit rate = deposit beta x change in policy rate; Change in bank net interest income = loan beta x rate-sensitive loans x change - deposit beta x rate-sensitive deposits x change; Extra annual interest for a floating borrower = loan rate change x balance
policy-rate-pass-through.when: Use it to follow a central bank's rate move through to the people it affects. Banks pass higher rates to borrowers faster than to savers, so net interest income often rises when rates rise, unless depositors move money to better rates, which pushes the deposit beta up over time. Borrowers on floating loans feel the change at once, which is how policy slows spending.

portfolio-esg-score.text: Portfolio ESG score = sum of (weight x ESG score) over holdings; Benchmark score = same with benchmark weights; Tilt = portfolio score - benchmark score; Share excluded by a screen = weight of holdings below a minimum score
portfolio-esg-score.when: Use it to describe how a portfolio compares on environmental, social and governance scores. A tilt toward higher-scoring companies or a screen that removes low scorers changes the holdings and may change risk and return. Scores differ between providers, so the same portfolio can look better or worse depending on the source.

portfolio-variance-matrix.text: Portfolio variance = w-transpose x Covariance matrix x w = sum over all pairs i, j of (w_i x w_j x sd_i x sd_j x correlation_ij)
portfolio-variance-matrix.when: Use it for portfolios of any number of assets. The two-asset formula is the special case. The matrix form is how optimizers and risk systems compute portfolio risk. Each weight pair contributes a term, so correlations between all pairs matter.

position-size-stop-loss.text: Shares = (Account size x Risk per trade) / (Entry price - Stop price)
position-size-stop-loss.when: Use it to decide how many shares to buy when you place a stop order. A stop turns into a market order once the price touches it, so the loss is roughly the gap between entry and stop times the shares. Gaps and fast markets can make it worse.

ppe-rollforward.text: Ending PP&E = Opening PP&E + Capex - Depreciation - Net book value of disposals; so Capex = Ending - Opening + Depreciation + Disposals
ppe-rollforward.when: Use it to build a forecast, with capex and depreciation as drivers, or to work out capex from two balance sheets when the cash flow statement is not available. A roll-forward ties each balance to the flows that changed it, and is the base of every supporting schedule in a model.

vc-post-money.text: Post-money = Pre-money + Investment; Investor ownership = Investment / Post-money
vc-post-money.when: Use it to work out how much of a startup an investor gets for their money. A higher pre-money valuation means less of the company is given away.

preferred-stock-value.text: Value of a preferred share = Fixed dividend per year / Required return
preferred-stock-value.when: Use it to price preferred stock, which pays a fixed dividend with no end date. It is a perpetuity. Common stock has no fixed dividend, so it needs a growth model instead.

pv-growing-annuity.when: Use it for a limited number of payments that grow at a steady rate, such as a salary that rises each year until retirement. With no growth it becomes the ordinary annuity formula.

pv-lump-sum.when: Use it to find what a single amount you will receive in the future is worth today, for example to compare it with an amount offered now.

pv-annuity-due.text: PV(due) = PMT x (1 - (1 + r)^-n) / r x (1 + r)
pv-annuity-due.when: Use it when the payments are made at the start of each period, such as rent paid in advance. It is the ordinary annuity value multiplied by (1 + r).

pv-ordinary-annuity.when: Use it to value a stream of equal payments received at the end of each period, such as a pension payout or the payments on a loan.

price-elasticity.mathml: Ed=(Q2−Q1)/Qˉ(P2−P1)/Pˉ,Qˉ=Q1+Q22,  Pˉ=P1+P22E_{d}=\frac{(Q_{2}-Q_{1})/\bar{Q}}{(P_{2}-P_{1})/\bar{P}},\quad \bar{Q}=\frac{Q_{1}+Q_{2}}{2},\;\bar{P}=\frac{P_{1}+P_{2}}{2}
price-elasticity.text: Elasticity = (change in quantity / average quantity) / (change in price / average price). Revenue = price x quantity
price-elasticity.when: Use it to see how sensitive buyers are to price. If the size of elasticity is above 1, a price rise cuts revenue because volume falls faster. Below 1 (inelastic), a price rise increases revenue. The midpoint method gives the same answer whichever direction the price moves.

price-improvement.text: Price improvement = (Best quoted price - Price you got) x Shares; for a sell it is (Price you got - Best quoted price) x Shares
price-improvement.when: Use it to judge the quality of a broker's execution. A wholesaler that pays for retail orders must usually fill them at or better than the best public quote, and the gain is price improvement.

price-target-upside.text: Target price = Forward EPS x Target P/E; Upside = Target price / Current price - 1
price-target-upside.when: Use it to understand how a research report arrives at a rating. The target price is only as good as the earnings forecast and the P/E assumption, so test how the answer changes when each is wrong.

price-weighted-index.text: Index = Sum of the share prices / Divisor; New divisor after a split = New sum of prices / Index level before the split
price-weighted-index.when: Use it for an index like the Dow, where a high-priced stock counts for more than a low-priced one, whatever the company's size. When a stock splits, its price falls, so the divisor is lowered to stop the index from dropping.

price-yield-approximation.mathml: ΔPP≈−Dmod Δy+12 C (Δy)2\frac{\Delta P}{P}\approx -D_{mod}\,\Delta y+\tfrac{1}{2}\,C\,(\Delta y)^{2}
price-yield-approximation.text: Percentage price change = -Modified duration x Change in yield + 0.5 x Convexity x (Change in yield)^2
price-yield-approximation.when: Use it to estimate how much a bond price moves when yields change, without repricing the bond. Duration alone is a straight-line estimate, so it is too low for a fall in yields and too high for a rise. The convexity term corrects most of that.

pca-variance-explained.text: Eigenvalues of the covariance matrix = (var1 + var2) / 2 plus or minus sqrt(((var1 - var2) / 2)^2 + cov^2); Share of variance explained by the first component = first eigenvalue / (sum of eigenvalues)
pca-variance-explained.when: Use it to find how many independent sources of risk drive a set of assets. The first component is the direction of largest variance, often a market or level factor. The eigenvalues add up to total variance, so each one divided by the sum is the share explained. This closed form is for two assets; larger sets use software but the reading is the same.

private-credit-net-yield.mathml: y=SOFR+s+OIDn,Rnet=y−PD×LGD−f,Rlev=Rnet+DE(Rnet−c)y=SOFR+s+\frac{OID}{n},\quad R_{net}=y-PD\times LGD-f,\quad R_{lev}=R_{net}+\frac{D}{E}(R_{net}-c)
private-credit-net-yield.text: All-in yield = base rate + spread + upfront discount spread over the life; Expected credit loss = probability of default x loss given default; Net return = all-in yield - expected loss - fund fees; Return with leverage = net return + (debt / equity) x (net return - cost of debt)
private-credit-net-yield.when: Use it to compare a direct loan with public debt. Private loans are floating-rate, so the coupon moves with the base rate, and they pay a spread for illiquidity and for lending to smaller or private-equity-owned companies. Defaults and fees reduce it. Leverage adds to the return only when the net yield is above the cost of debt, and it adds loss in bad years.

pe-carry-waterfall.mathml: Pref=C[(1+h)T−1],Catch-up=c1−c Pref,GP=Catch-up+c (Profit−Pref−Catch-up)\text{Pref}=C\left[(1+h)^{T}-1\right],\quad \text{Catch-up}=\frac{c}{1-c}\,\text{Pref},\quad GP=\text{Catch-up}+c\,(\text{Profit}-\text{Pref}-\text{Catch-up})
pe-carry-waterfall.text: Order of payment: (1) return of capital to investors, (2) preferred return, (3) catch-up to the manager until it holds the carry share of all profit, (4) remaining profit split with carry % to the manager. With full catch-up the manager ends with carry % x total profit once profits are large enough
pe-carry-waterfall.when: Use it to see how profits split between investors (LPs) and the manager (GP) under a European (whole-fund) waterfall. Below the preferred return the manager earns no carry. The catch-up then lets the manager earn carry on all profit, not only on the excess. Multiples show performance: DPI is cash returned per unit invested, and TVPI includes unrealized value. Terms differ by fund and the example uses a single investment and exit for simplicity.

fund-performance-metrics.mathml: DPI=∑D∑P,RVPI=NAV∑P,TVPI=DPI+RVPI,0=∑tDt−Pt+NAVT1t=T(1+IRR)tDPI=\frac{\sum D}{\sum P},\quad RVPI=\frac{NAV}{\sum P},\quad TVPI=DPI+RVPI,\quad 0=\sum_{t}\frac{D_{t}-P_{t}+NAV_{T}\mathbb{1}_{t=T}}{(1+IRR)^{t}}
fund-performance-metrics.text: DPI = total distributions / total paid-in capital (cash actually returned); RVPI = remaining net asset value / paid-in capital (value still held); TVPI = DPI + RVPI (total value per unit paid in, also called the net multiple); IRR = rate that sets the net present value of calls, distributions and final NAV to zero
fund-performance-metrics.when: Use it to read a private fund report. TVPI shows total value created but part of it is only a valuation, so DPI is the part already in your hands. IRR depends on timing and can look high early on; a multiple (MOIC, TVPI) ignores time. Read all three together and be careful comparing a fund with unrealized value to a finished one.

normal-probability.text: P(X <= x) = Phi((x - mean) / standard deviation)
normal-probability.when: Use it to estimate how likely an outcome is, assuming returns follow a bell curve, for example the chance that a fund loses money in a year.

profit-margins.text: Gross margin = (Revenue - COGS) / Revenue; Operating margin = (Revenue - COGS - Opex) / Revenue; Net margin = Net income / Revenue
profit-margins.when: Use these to see how much of each unit of sales is kept as profit at three levels. Compare them over time or against other companies in the same industry.

profitability-index.mathml: PI=PV of future cash flowsInitial investmentPI=\frac{PV\text{ of future cash flows}}{\text{Initial investment}}
profitability-index.text: PI = PV of future cash flows / Initial investment
profitability-index.when: Use it to rank projects when money is limited. A PI above 1 means NPV is positive. Choose the projects with the highest PI until the budget runs out.

income-tax-brackets.mathml: Tax=∑krk[min⁡(Y,Uk)−Lk]+,Effective=TaxY\text{Tax}=\sum_{k}r_{k}\left[\min(Y,U_{k})-L_{k}\right]^{+},\quad \text{Effective}=\frac{\text{Tax}}{Y}
income-tax-brackets.text: Tax = for each bracket k, bracket rate x the part of taxable income that falls inside that bracket (between its lower and upper limits), added up; Effective rate = tax / taxable income; Marginal rate = rate of the bracket the last unit of income falls in
income-tax-brackets.when: Use it to find tax on a progressive scale. Each rate applies only to the income inside its own bracket, so moving into a higher bracket does not tax all your income at the higher rate. The marginal rate is the one that matters for the next decision, such as extra income or a deductible contribution. The brackets below are illustrative, so replace them with the schedule for your country and year.

project-operating-cash-flow.text: OCF = (Sales - Cash costs) x (1 - T) + Depreciation x T
project-operating-cash-flow.when: Use it to turn a project's sales, costs and depreciation into the cash flow you discount. Depreciation is not cash, but it lowers tax, so the formula adds back the tax it saves.

promised-return-reality-check.text: Equivalent annual rate = (1 + monthly return)^12 - 1; Value after n years = Principal x (1 + monthly return)^(12 x n); Months to double = ln 2 / ln(1 + monthly return)
promised-return-reality-check.when: Use it to turn a promise into the annual return it implies and compare that with what markets deliver. A promise of steady, high, guaranteed returns with little risk is a classic warning sign, as no legitimate investment offers all three together. This does not prove an offer is a scam, but if the numbers are far above market returns, check the seller's registration with your financial regulator and be wary of pressure to act fast or to bring in friends.

coinsurance-penalty.mathml: Payout=min⁡ ⁣(max⁡ ⁣(L×Kc V−D, 0), K)(K<cV)\text{Payout}=\min\!\left(\max\!\left(L\times\frac{K}{c\,V}-D,\,0\right),\,K\right)\quad(K<cV)
coinsurance-penalty.text: Required cover = coinsurance % x property value; If cover carried is below that, Payout = Loss x (cover carried / required cover) - deductible, capped at cover carried; otherwise Payout = Loss - deductible, capped at cover carried
coinsurance-penalty.when: Use it when a property policy has a coinsurance clause. If you carry less than the required share of the property's value, the insurer pays only the same share of every loss, even a small one. The fix is to insure to value and update the value as building costs rise. Not all policies have this clause, so check yours.

prospect-theory-value.mathml: v(x)={xαx≥0−λ(−x)βx<0,w(p)=pγ[pγ+(1−p)γ]1/γv(x)=\begin{cases}x^{\alpha}&x\ge0\\-\lambda(-x)^{\beta}&x<0\end{cases},\quad w(p)=\frac{p^{\gamma}}{\left[p^{\gamma}+(1-p)^{\gamma}\right]^{1/\gamma}}
prospect-theory-value.text: Value of an outcome x: gains = x^alpha; losses = - lambda x (-x)^beta... precisely: gain value = x^alpha, loss value = - lambda x |x|^beta, with typical alpha = beta = 0.88 and loss aversion lambda = 2.25; Decision weight of a probability p = p^gamma / (p^gamma + (1 - p)^gamma)^(1/gamma), gamma about 0.61 for gains and 0.69 for losses; Prospect value of a gamble = w(p) x v(gain) + w(1 - p) x v(loss)
prospect-theory-value.when: Use it to see why people turn down favorable gambles and why they buy lottery tickets and insurance. Losses are felt about twice as strongly as equal gains, so a gamble with a positive expected value can have a negative prospect value. The parameters are averages from experiments with wide variation between people, so treat the result as a model of tendencies, not a prediction for one person.

psa-prepayment.text: CPR = PSA speed x 6% x min(month / 30, 1); SMM = 1 - (1 - CPR)^(1/12)
psa-prepayment.when: Use it to describe how fast borrowers prepay. The benchmark starts at 0.2% CPR in month one and rises 0.2 points each month to 6% CPR at month 30, then stays there. Faster speeds shorten the life of the security (contraction risk) and slower speeds lengthen it (extension risk).

purchasing-power.when: Use it to see what a future sum of money will really buy in today's prices once inflation has pushed prices up.

ppp-expected-rate.text: Absolute PPP rate (foreign currency per 1 domestic) = foreign price of a basket / domestic price of the same basket; Misvaluation = spot / PPP rate - 1; Relative PPP: the foreign currency per domestic unit changes by (1 + foreign inflation) / (1 + domestic inflation) each year
ppp-expected-rate.when: Use it as a long-run anchor for exchange rates. The same goods should cost the same everywhere after conversion; if a basket is cheaper abroad, that currency looks undervalued. Relative PPP says the currency of the higher-inflation country should weaken by the inflation gap. PPP holds poorly in the short run and for non-traded goods and services, and it can take years to correct.

put-call-parity.text: Call price - Put price = Spot x e^(-dividend yield x T) - Strike x e^(-r x T)
put-call-parity.when: Use it to check whether option prices are consistent, or to build one instrument from the others: a call equals a put plus the stock minus a bond. If the two sides differ, there is an arbitrage. It holds only for European options.

quantity-theory-of-money.mathml: MV=PY,V=PYM,1+π=(1+gM)(1+gV)1+gYMV=PY,\quad V=\frac{PY}{M},\quad 1+\pi=\frac{(1+g_{M})(1+g_{V})}{1+g_{Y}}
quantity-theory-of-money.text: Money supply x velocity = price level x real output (= nominal GDP); Velocity = nominal GDP / money supply; Inflation = (1 + money growth) x (1 + velocity growth) / (1 + real output growth) - 1
quantity-theory-of-money.when: Use it to see the link between money and prices. If velocity and output growth are steady, inflation roughly equals money growth minus real growth. In practice velocity is unstable, especially after financial crises or when interest rates change, so the link is loose in the short run and clearer over long periods and in high-inflation countries.

quick-ratio.text: Quick ratio = (Cash + Marketable securities + Receivables) / Current liabilities
quick-ratio.when: Use it as a stricter test of short-term liquidity than the current ratio. It leaves out inventory, which can take time to sell.

r-squared.when: Use it to say how much of the movement in one series lines up with another. A high R-squared shows a strong link but does not prove that X causes Y.

raroc-limit-utilization.text: RAROC = (Revenue - Costs - Expected loss) / Economic capital; Limit utilization = Risk used / Limit
raroc-limit-utilization.when: Use it to compare businesses by return per unit of risk, and to track a limit set by the risk appetite. A business is creating value if RAROC beats the hurdle rate. Utilization near 100% means the desk has little room left.

fed-funds-futures-probability.text: Implied average rate for the month = 100 - futures price; Rate after the meeting = (implied rate x days in month - current rate x days before the meeting) / days after the meeting; Probability of a move = (rate after meeting - current rate) / size of the move
fed-funds-futures-probability.when: Use it to read what the market expects from the central bank. The futures price embeds an average expected rate for the month, and removing the days before the meeting isolates the post-meeting rate. A data release that changes the probability moves bonds and currencies. Assumes only two outcomes (no move or one move of the stated size), and ignores small risk premiums.

rational-bubble-growth.mathml: g=1+r1−π−1,P(survive n)=(1−π)n,Bn=B0(1+g)ng=\frac{1+r}{1-\pi}-1,\quad P(\text{survive } n)=(1-\pi)^{n},\quad B_{n}=B_{0}(1+g)^{n}
rational-bubble-growth.text: If a bubble bursts with probability pi each period, holders require the bubble part of the price to grow, while it survives, at g = (1 + r) / (1 - pi) - 1 so that the expected return stays at r; Chance it survives n periods = (1 - pi)^n; Bubble size after n periods if it survives = B0 x (1 + g)^n
rational-bubble-growth.when: Use it to see why bubbles are explosive. A price above fundamental value can persist if holders believe it will keep rising fast enough to pay for the burst risk. The required growth is high, so the bubble component becomes large the longer it lasts, while the chance of surviving falls. It shows that a bubble can be consistent with rational expectations, not that it is likely.

news-move-significance.mathml: z=rσd,P(∣Z∣≥∣z∣)=2 (1−Φ(∣z∣)),Days per event≈1Pz=\frac{r}{\sigma_{d}},\quad P(|Z|\ge|z|)=2\,(1-\Phi(|z|)),\quad \text{Days per event}\approx\frac{1}{P}
news-move-significance.text: Size of the move in standard deviations = daily return / typical daily volatility; Chance of a move at least this large in either direction under a normal distribution = 2 x (1 - normal cumulative of |z|); About how many trading days between such moves = 1 / that chance; Real markets have fatter tails, so large moves happen more often than a normal curve suggests
news-move-significance.when: Use it to put a dramatic headline in context. A fall of 3% may be an ordinary week for one stock and a rare event for another. Compare the move with the asset's own typical swings. Be careful: the normal curve understates how often extreme days occur, so treat the frequency as a lower bound.

real-return.when: Use it to see how much an investment really grows your buying power once rising prices are taken out. The quick shortcut nominal minus inflation is close but slightly off.

real-value-of-savings.text: Real value = Balance x (1 + interest rate)^n / (1 + inflation)^n; Real interest rate = (1 + interest rate) / (1 + inflation) - 1
real-value-of-savings.when: Use it to see what savings will actually buy later. When inflation is above the interest rate the real rate is negative and the balance grows on paper but shrinks in purchasing power. Cash at zero interest loses about the inflation rate each year, which is why long-term savings are usually invested, accepting risk, not left in cash.

rebalancing-trades.text: Trade for asset i = Target weight x Total portfolio value - Current value of asset i
rebalancing-trades.when: Use it to bring a portfolio back to its target mix after market moves have pulled it away. The trades sum to zero, because what you sell funds what you buy.

recovery-rate.text: Recovery rate = Amount recovered / Claim; Loss given default = 1 - Recovery rate
recovery-rate.when: Use it to measure what lenders get back when a borrower fails. Senior secured creditors usually recover more than junior or unsecured ones.

regression-line.mathml: y^=α+βx,β=Cov(x,y)Var(x),α=yˉ−βxˉ\hat{y}=\alpha+\beta x,\quad \beta=\frac{Cov(x,y)}{Var(x)},\quad \alpha=\bar{y}-\beta\bar{x}
regression-line.text: y-hat = alpha + beta x, with beta = Cov(x,y) / Var(x) and alpha = mean y - beta x mean x
regression-line.when: Use it to fit a straight line through paired data, for example to estimate a stock's beta against the market and its alpha, the return not explained by the market.

sinking-fund-payment.when: Use it when you have a savings goal and a deadline and want to know the regular deposit that gets you there. It is the future value of an annuity formula turned around.

reinsurance-recoveries.text: Quota share: the reinsurer takes a fixed share q of every loss and premium; Excess of loss: the reinsurer pays the part of a loss above the retention R, up to the limit; Net retained loss = gross loss - recovery
reinsurance-recoveries.when: Use it to see how reinsurance changes the loss an insurer keeps. A quota share reduces every loss in proportion and gives capital relief. Excess of loss protects against large single losses and leaves small ones with the insurer, and a loss beyond retention plus limit comes back to the insurer. Real programs add reinstatement premiums and exclusions.

reit-ffo-affo.text: FFO = net income + depreciation and amortization - gains on property sales; AFFO = FFO - recurring maintenance capital spending - straight-line rent adjustments; Price / FFO = share price / FFO per share; Payout ratio = dividend per share / AFFO per share
reit-ffo-affo.when: Use it to assess a REIT instead of ordinary earnings. Accounting depreciation falls on buildings that often hold or gain value, so net income understates the cash a REIT earns. FFO adds it back; AFFO goes further and removes the spending needed to keep the properties let. The payout ratio against AFFO shows whether the dividend is covered.

rsi.mathml: RSI=100−1001+RS,RS=Average gainAverage lossRSI=100-\frac{100}{1+RS},\quad RS=\frac{\text{Average gain}}{\text{Average loss}}
rsi.text: RSI = 100 - 100 / (1 + RS), where RS = average of the up-moves / average of the down-moves over the period
rsi.when: Use it as a gauge of recent momentum. Chartists use 70 and 30 as warning levels. This is the simple version with plain averages. Wilder's original smooths the averages over time, so values can differ a little.

relever-beta.text: Levered beta = Unlevered beta x (1 + (1 - T) x D/E)
relever-beta.when: Use it to rebuild a beta for the capital structure of the company you are valuing, after averaging unlevered betas from comparable firms.

loan-balance.text: Balance after k payments = P x (1 + r)^k - PMT x ((1 + r)^k - 1) / r
loan-balance.when: Use it to find how much of a loan is still owed part-way through, for example how much of a mortgage remains after 5 years.

rent-vs-buy-user-cost.mathml: Cost of owning=P[i(1−d)+o d+τ+m−g],Price-to-rent=P12R\text{Cost of owning}=P\left[i(1-d)+o\,d+\tau+m-g\right],\quad \text{Price-to-rent}=\frac{P}{12R}
rent-vs-buy-user-cost.text: Annual cost of owning = Price x [mortgage rate x (1 - down payment share) + opportunity return x down payment share + property tax rate + maintenance rate - price growth rate]; Price-to-rent ratio = Price / (12 x monthly rent)
rent-vs-buy-user-cost.when: Use it for a first comparison of renting and buying. Owning costs interest, tax, upkeep and the return lost on the down payment, offset by price growth. If the annual cost of owning is below annual rent, buying looks cheaper, but price growth is uncertain. It leaves out buying and selling costs, tax relief and how long you will stay, which matter a lot over short stays.

replicating-portfolio.mathml: Δ=Cu−CdS(u−d),B=Cu−ΔSu1+r,C=ΔS+B\Delta=\frac{C_{u}-C_{d}}{S(u-d)},\quad B=\frac{C_{u}-\Delta S u}{1+r},\quad C=\Delta S+B
replicating-portfolio.text: Shares held (delta) = (Option value if up - Option value if down) / (Stock price up - Stock price down); Bond holding B = (Option value if up - Delta x Stock price up) / (1 + r); Option value = Delta x S + B
replicating-portfolio.when: Use it to price an option by copying it. Hold delta shares and borrow or lend cash so the portfolio pays exactly what the option pays in both outcomes. The portfolio's cost today is then the option's price, with no probabilities needed.

repo-interest.mathml: Cash=V(1−h),Interest=Cash×r×d360,Repurchase price=Cash+Interest\text{Cash}=V(1-h),\quad \text{Interest}=\text{Cash}\times r\times\frac{d}{360},\quad \text{Repurchase price}=\text{Cash}+\text{Interest}
repo-interest.text: Cash lent = Collateral value x (1 - Haircut); Interest = Cash x Repo rate x Days / 360; Repurchase price = Cash + Interest
repo-interest.when: Use it to price a repo, which is a short-term secured loan. One side sells securities and agrees to buy them back later at a higher price. The difference is the interest. The haircut protects the lender if the collateral falls in value.

repricing-gap.text: Repricing gap = rate-sensitive assets - rate-sensitive liabilities (those that reset within the horizon); Change in net interest income = gap x change in interest rates
repricing-gap.when: Use it to see how a rate change affects income over the next year. A negative gap (more liabilities than assets repricing) means a rate rise cuts income, because funding costs go up faster than yields. It assumes every item reprices fully and by the same amount, which is not true of deposits, so use the pass-through version for a more realistic picture.

reserve-adequacy.text: Import cover (months) = reserves / (annual imports / 12); Short-term debt cover = reserves / short-term external debt (Greenspan-Guidotti: at least 1); IMF reserve adequacy metric (fixed exchange rate) = 5% of exports + 5% of broad money + 30% of short-term debt + 15% of other liabilities (weights for a fixed regime; floating regimes use lower ones)
reserve-adequacy.when: Use it to judge whether a country can defend its exchange rate regime. A peg or tightly managed rate needs reserves to meet capital outflows and pay for imports; a floating rate needs less. Three common tests are months of imports covered, cover for short-term debt, and the IMF composite metric (a ratio of 100% to 150% of the metric is regarded as adequate). The weights shown are the fixed-regime weights, and the IMF publishes different ones for other regimes.

reserve-requirement-cost-of-funds.text: Domestic bank's effective cost per dollar it can lend = (deposit rate + insurance fee) / (1 - reserve requirement); Offshore bank's cost = deposit rate (no reserve requirement or insurance); Wedge = domestic cost - offshore cost
reserve-requirement-cost-of-funds.when: Use it to see why offshore markets such as the eurodollar market exist. Banks outside the home regulator's reach avoid reserve requirements and insurance charges, so they can pay depositors a bit more and charge borrowers a bit less than domestic banks. The gap is the reason depositors and borrowers use them. The wedge shrinks when reserve requirements are low or zero, as they are in many countries now.

residual-income.text: Residual income = Net income - Required return x Opening book value; Value = Book value + RI next year / (r - g)
residual-income.when: Use it to value a company from its accounting numbers. Value is today's book value plus the present value of profits above the required return. It is useful when dividends and free cash flow are hard to forecast.

retained-earnings.text: Ending RE = Beginning RE + Net income - Dividends
retained-earnings.when: Use it to see how profits kept in the business build up over time. It links the income statement to the balance sheet.

retirement-nest-egg.text: Nest egg needed at retirement = first-year income / (r - inflation) x [1 - ((1 + inflation) / (1 + r))^L]; Yearly saving needed = (nest egg - current savings x (1 + g)^N) x g / ((1 + g)^N - 1)
retirement-nest-egg.when: Use it to turn a retirement income goal into a savings target. Income rises with inflation in retirement, and the account is assumed to run to zero at the end of the planning age. It uses end-of-year amounts and a fixed return, so test lower returns and a longer life. State or workplace pensions and other income would reduce the need, so subtract them from the goal.

margin-return.text: Return on equity = (Shares x Price change - Loan x Interest rate x Years) / Your own money; Loan = Shares x Start price - Your own money
margin-return.when: Use it to see how borrowing magnifies results. A gain is multiplied by the leverage, and so is a loss, and the interest cost is charged either way.

return-on-assets.text: ROA = Net income / Average total assets; Unlevered ROA = (Net income + Interest x (1 - tax rate)) / Average total assets
return-on-assets.when: Use it to see how well a company turns its assets into profit. Net income is after interest, so a heavily indebted firm looks worse. The unlevered version adds back after-tax interest to compare firms with different debt levels.

return-on-equity.text: ROE = (Net income - Preferred dividends) / Average common shareholders' equity
return-on-equity.when: Use it to measure the return earned for common shareholders. A high ROE can come from good operations or from heavy borrowing, so check it with the DuPont breakdown. Average equity is better than year-end equity when equity changed during the year.

percentage-of-completion.mathml: Revenue to date=Contract price×Costs to dateEstimated total costs\text{Revenue to date}=\text{Contract price}\times\frac{\text{Costs to date}}{\text{Estimated total costs}}
percentage-of-completion.text: Revenue to date = Contract price x (Costs to date / Estimated total costs)
percentage-of-completion.when: Use it for long contracts such as construction, where revenue is recognized as the work progresses rather than all on completion.

rights-issue-terp.mathml: TERP=NP+nSN+n,Value of a right=P−TERPTERP=\frac{N P+n S}{N+n},\quad \text{Value of a right}=P-TERP
rights-issue-terp.text: TERP = (N x P + n x S) / (N + n), and Value of a right = P - TERP
rights-issue-terp.when: Use it to see what a rights issue does to the share price and what a right is worth. Shareholders who neither buy nor sell their rights lose out, so rights are usually sold or exercised.

portfolio-variance-two-assets.text: Portfolio variance = w1^2 x s1^2 + w2^2 x s2^2 + 2 x w1 x w2 x rho x s1 x s2
portfolio-variance-two-assets.when: Use it to see how combining two assets changes risk. When the correlation is below 1, the portfolio is less risky than the weighted average of the two risks. That gap is the benefit of diversification.

risk-parity-weights.text: Weight of asset i = (1 / its volatility) / sum of (1 / volatility) across all assets
risk-parity-weights.when: Use it to build a portfolio where each asset contributes about the same amount of risk, instead of the same amount of money. This simple version assumes the assets are uncorrelated. The full version also uses correlations.

risk-premium.text: Risk premium = Expected return - Risk-free rate
risk-premium.when: Use it to see how much extra return an investment offers for taking on risk. A higher premium is the reward for accepting more uncertainty.

risk-neutral-pricing.text: Risk-neutral probability of the up state = (Spot x e^(rT) - Down price) / (Up price - Down price); Value = e^(-rT) x [q x Payoff if up + (1 - q) x Payoff if down]
risk-neutral-pricing.when: Use it to price a derivative without knowing investors' risk preferences. Pretend the world is risk-neutral, so the stock earns the risk-free rate, compute the expected payoff and discount at the risk-free rate. The real-world probability and expected return do not enter the price.

rule-of-40.mathml: Rule of 40 score=Revenue growth+Profit margin\text{Rule of 40 score}=\text{Revenue growth}+\text{Profit margin}
rule-of-40.text: Rule of 40 score = Revenue growth rate + Profit margin (often free cash flow or EBITDA margin)
rule-of-40.when: Use it as a quick check on high-growth software and similar firms. A score of 40% or more suggests a healthy balance between growth and profit.

rule-of-72.text: Years to double = 72 / r, with r as a percentage
rule-of-72.when: Use it for a quick mental estimate of how long money takes to double at a given yearly rate. For exact answers, use the periods formula.

sahm-rule-indicator.text: Sahm indicator = latest 3-month average unemployment rate - the lowest 3-month average of the previous 12 months. A reading of 0.5 percentage points or more has signaled the start of past US recessions. Yield curve spread = 10-year yield - 3-month yield (negative means inverted)
sahm-rule-indicator.when: Use it as one warning sign, alongside an inverted yield curve and falling surveys. The Sahm rule picks up a quick rise in unemployment, which has historically happened early in recessions. Neither signal is a forecast: they have had false alarms and different lags, and the rule was fitted to US data. Enter at least 15 monthly readings, oldest first.

sample-size-mean.text: Sample size = (z-value for the confidence level x standard deviation / margin of error)^2, rounded up
sample-size-mean.when: Use it before collecting data, to know how many observations you need. To halve the margin of error you need four times the sample. Use an estimate of sigma from a pilot or from history. For small samples or unknown sigma the exact answer needs the t-distribution, so treat this as a good first estimate.

sanctions-ownership-aggregation.mathml: O=∑j∈blockedoj,O≥50%⇒treated as blockedO=\sum_{j\in\text{blocked}}o_{j},\quad O\ge 50\%\Rightarrow\text{treated as blocked}
sanctions-ownership-aggregation.text: Under the US Treasury (OFAC) 50 percent rule, an entity owned 50% or more in total by one or more sanctioned persons is itself treated as sanctioned; Add up the stakes of all sanctioned owners (each stake alone can be below 50%); Total = sum of the stakes of blocked owners; Check whether total is 50% or more
sanctions-ownership-aggregation.when: Use it to screen customers and counterparties. A company with no sanctioned person above 50% can still be blocked if two sanctioned owners together reach 50%. This rule covers ownership only; control without ownership can also matter, and other regimes (EU, UK, UN) apply their own tests that should be checked.

sdr-basket-value.text: Value of 1 SDR in dollars = sum over the basket currencies of (fixed amount of the currency in the basket x its dollar exchange rate); Weight of currency i = its dollar value in the basket / total value
sdr-basket-value.when: Use it to see how the IMF's unit of account is valued. The SDR is a basket of five currencies with fixed amounts, so its value moves with the exchange rates, and the weights drift between reviews. It is a reserve asset the IMF allocates to members and is used for IMF loans. The amounts shown are believed to be those set at the 2022 review and the exchange rates are illustrative, so check the IMF's current published values before relying on the result.

secondary-purchase-irr.mathml: P=NAV(1−d),0=−P+∑tDt−Ut(1+IRR)t,MOIC=∑DP+∑UP=NAV(1-d),\quad 0=-P+\sum_{t}\frac{D_{t}-U_{t}}{(1+IRR)^{t}},\quad MOIC=\frac{\sum D}{P+\sum U}
secondary-purchase-irr.text: Price paid = reported NAV x (1 - discount); Buyer cash flows = distributions received - further capital the buyer must fund (unfunded commitment); Buyer IRR solves NPV = 0; Buyer multiple = total distributions / (price + unfunded capital called)
secondary-purchase-irr.when: Use it to judge a secondary purchase: buying an existing stake in a private fund from a seller who wants cash. The buyer pays a discount to NAV and receives the fund's distributions from then on, so the investment is already partly mature and the J-curve is shorter. The buyer still takes on any unfunded commitment, and the NAV may itself be too high.

securities-lending-income.text: Income = Collateral x (Reinvestment return - Rebate rate) x Days / 365 x (1 - Agent share)
securities-lending-income.when: Use it to see what an owner earns by lending shares to short sellers. The borrower pays by accepting a lower rebate on its cash. The harder a stock is to borrow, the lower (or more negative) the rebate.

security-market-line.text: Required return = rf + beta x (E(Rm) - rf); alpha = forecast return - required return
security-market-line.when: Use it to check whether a stock looks cheap or expensive. A stock plotting above the line (positive alpha) offers more return than its beta requires, so it looks undervalued, and below the line it looks overvalued.

segment-analysis.text: Segment margin = Segment profit / Segment revenue; Revenue share = Segment revenue / Total revenue; Profit share = Segment profit / Total profit
segment-analysis.when: Use it to see which parts of a group earn the profit. A segment can be a large share of sales but a small share of profit, or loss-making and hidden in a total. Compare margins between segments and across years.

seigniorage.mathml: S=ΔM0,Sinterest=i M0,Inflation tax=π M0PS=\Delta M_{0},\quad S_{interest}=i\,M_{0},\quad \text{Inflation tax}=\pi\,\frac{M_{0}}{P}
seigniorage.text: Seigniorage from base growth = change in the monetary base; Interest saved = nominal interest rate x monetary base (the base is a free loan from the public); Inflation tax = inflation rate x real money balances
seigniorage.when: Use it to see how central banks earn from issuing money. Holders of cash are lending to the central bank at zero interest, and inflation erodes their balances. Central banks usually return profits to the government, so this is public revenue. Reliance on money creation to fund spending leads to high inflation.

share-repurchase-eps.text: Shares bought = Amount spent / Price; New EPS = Net income / (Shares before - Shares bought)
share-repurchase-eps.when: Use it to see how a buyback raises earnings per share by shrinking the share count. This simple version ignores the interest lost on the cash spent, so it overstates the benefit.

sharpe-ratio.text: Sharpe ratio = (Portfolio return - Risk-free rate) / Portfolio standard deviation
sharpe-ratio.when: Use it to compare investments by return earned for each unit of total risk. Use it for a whole portfolio, or when the portfolio is someone's only investment, because it counts all risk.

short-sale-return.text: Profit = (Sale price - Buy-back price) x Shares - Dividends owed - Borrow fee; Borrow fee = Sale value x Fee rate x Days / 365
short-sale-return.when: Use it to work out the result of betting against a stock. You gain if the price falls and lose if it rises, with no upper limit on the loss. Dividends and borrow fees are costs on top.

short-swing-profit-16b.text: For a company insider, a purchase and a sale of the company's stock within six months can be matched; the profit to be paid back to the company is calculated by matching the lowest-priced purchases with the highest-priced sales; Recoverable profit = sum over matched shares of (sale price - purchase price) x shares matched; Losses on other matches cannot be used to offset it
short-swing-profit-16b.when: Use it as an example of how the 1934 Act limits profits by insiders (officers, directors, holders of more than 10%) from quick in-and-out trading. Liability does not depend on whether the insider used secret information. This simplified version matches the lowest purchase with the highest sale and does not include the full rules on derivatives or exemptions.

simple-interest.text: I = P x r x t
simple-interest.when: Use it when interest is paid only on the original amount and never on interest already earned. Common for short loans and some bonds.

moving-average.text: SMA = (sum of the last k values) / k
moving-average.when: Use it to smooth out day-to-day noise in a price or other series so the trend is easier to see.

simple-vs-log-return.text: Simple return R = P1 / P0 - 1, and log return r = ln(P1 / P0)
simple-vs-log-return.when: Use simple returns to describe a single period and to combine investments in a portfolio. Use log returns when adding returns across time, because log returns add up while simple returns do not.

gbm-step.mathml: St+Δt=Stexp⁡ ⁣[(μ−σ22)Δt+σΔt z]S_{t+\Delta t}=S_{t}\exp\!\left[\left(\mu-\tfrac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\right)\Delta t+\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,z\right]
gbm-step.text: S(next) = S x exp((mu - sigma^2 / 2) x dt + sigma x sqrt(dt) x z)
gbm-step.when: Use it as one step of a Monte Carlo simulation. Repeating it many times with different random z values produces thousands of possible price paths, from which you can estimate risks and option values.

skewness.text: Skewness = average of ((Ri - mean) / standard deviation)^3
skewness.when: Use it to see whether big moves tend to be gains or losses. Negative skewness means occasional large losses, which a standard deviation alone would hide.

sofr-futures.mathml: Price=100−Implied rate,Value of 1 bp=Notional×312×0.0001\text{Price}=100-\text{Implied rate},\quad \text{Value of 1 bp}=\text{Notional}\times\frac{3}{12}\times 0.0001
sofr-futures.text: Futures price = 100 - Implied rate (in %); Value of 1 basis point = Notional x 0.25 x 0.0001
sofr-futures.when: Use it to read the market's expected short-term rate from a futures price, and to hedge short-term interest rate risk. The price moves opposite to the rate. A long position gains when rates fall.

solow-steady-state.mathml: k∗=(sAδ+n)11−α,y∗=A (k∗)α,c∗=(1−s) y∗k^{*}=\left(\frac{sA}{\delta+n}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}},\quad y^{*}=A\,(k^{*})^{\alpha},\quad c^{*}=(1-s)\,y^{*}
solow-steady-state.text: Steady-state capital per worker k* = (s x A / (depreciation + labor force growth))^(1 / (1 - alpha)); Output per worker y* = A x k*^alpha; Consumption per worker c* = (1 - s) x y*. Consumption is highest when the saving rate s equals alpha
solow-steady-state.when: Use it to see why economies converge to a level of income per worker, not to ever-faster growth. Saving more raises the level of income but not its long-run growth rate; only productivity growth lifts that. Consumption is maximized at the golden-rule saving rate, and saving above it is wasteful. It is a stylized model.

sortino-ratio.text: Sortino = (Average return - MAR) / Downside deviation, where Downside deviation = square root of the average of min(Ri - MAR, 0)^2
sortino-ratio.when: Use it like the Sharpe ratio when only losses are the real concern. It ignores upside swings, which investors do not mind, and measures return per unit of downside risk.

debt-restructuring-haircut.mathml: hNPV=1−PV(new bonds at exit yield)Face of old bonds,hnominal=1−FnewFoldh_{NPV}=1-\frac{PV(\text{new bonds at exit yield})}{\text{Face of old bonds}},\quad h_{nominal}=1-\frac{F_{new}}{F_{old}}
debt-restructuring-haircut.text: Nominal haircut = 1 - new face value / old face value; NPV haircut = 1 - present value of the new bonds' payments, discounted at an exit yield, / face value of the old claim. A bond's PV = coupon x annuity factor + face / (1 + y)^n
debt-restructuring-haircut.when: Use it to judge how much creditors lose in a restructuring. The nominal haircut ignores the lower coupon and longer maturity of the new bonds, which are worth less. The NPV haircut counts them, so it is larger than the nominal cut. It depends on the exit yield, which is chosen by the analyst, so test several yields, because different yields give very different losses.

swf-permanent-income.text: Total wealth = present value of the remaining resource revenue (R each year for N years) + current fund; Sustainable spending (permanent income) = real return x total wealth; Amount to save each year = resource revenue - (permanent income - return on the fund)
swf-permanent-income.when: Use it to decide how much of a finite resource windfall can be spent without making future generations worse off. Treat the resource as part of wealth and spend only its return, saving the rest in a fund. This is the idea behind spending rules that cap withdrawals at an expected real return of the fund. It depends on assumptions about the price path and the real return.

srisk.text: SRISK = max[ Capital ratio x Debt - (1 - Capital ratio) x (1 - LRMES) x Market value of equity, 0 ]
srisk.when: Use it to estimate how much capital a financial firm would be short if the whole market crashed. A firm with a large SRISK would need rescuing at the worst moment, when no one else has capital to give, which is what systemic risk means. The figure is the sum across firms of the expected shortfalls.

stablecoin-reserve-income.text: Backing ratio = reserve assets / coins in circulation; Buffer = reserves - coins in circulation; Issuer income per year = government bills held x yield (holders usually receive none); Run loss = coins redeemed in a run that cannot be paid from cash = max(0, redemptions - cash)
stablecoin-reserve-income.when: Use it to judge how safe a fiat-backed stablecoin is and how the issuer makes money. Full backing in cash and short bills should let every holder redeem at par, but a run on redemptions can exceed the cash on hand. The issuer earns interest on reserves, which is why the business is profitable when rates are high.

stock-split.text: New shares = k x Old shares; New price = Old price / k, for a k-for-1 split
