stock-split.when: Use it to see what a split changes: the number of shares and the price per share. The total value of your holding stays the same. A reverse split uses k below 1.

sbc-adjusted-fcf.text: Adjusted FCF = Free cash flow - Stock-based compensation; Dilution yield = SBC / Market cap
sbc-adjusted-fcf.when: Use it when a company pays its staff in shares. Cash flow statements add SBC back, so free cash flow looks higher than it is. Treating SBC as a real cost shows what is left for owners after paying staff in the only currency that costs the firm nothing today: ownership.

straddle-strangle.text: Straddle (buy a call and a put at the same strike): Profit = |ST - K| - total premium; Strangle (put at a lower strike, call at a higher strike): Profit = max(Kp - ST, 0) + max(ST - Kc, 0) - total premium
straddle-strangle.when: Use it when you expect a big move but not its direction. Both strategies lose the premium if the price stays near the strikes, and profit from a large move either way. A strangle costs less than a straddle but needs a bigger move.

straight-line-depreciation.mathml: Annual depreciation=Cost−Salvage valueUseful life\text{Annual depreciation} = \frac{\text{Cost}-\text{Salvage value}}{\text{Useful life}}
straight-line-depreciation.text: Annual depreciation = (Cost - Salvage value) / Useful life
straight-line-depreciation.when: Use it to spread the cost of an asset evenly over its useful life, so the same expense appears on the income statement each year.

stress-test-loss.text: Scenario loss = Portfolio value x sum of (Weight of asset i x Shock to asset i); Multiple of the shock that exhausts capital = Capital / Loss
stress-test-loss.when: Use it to see what happens in a specific bad scenario, such as an equity crash or a credit shock, without relying on a statistical model. A reverse stress test works the other way: it asks how large the shock must be to wipe out capital.

student-loan-capitalization.text: Interest accrued while studying = Principal x annual rate x years; if added to the balance (capitalized) the new principal = Principal + accrued interest; the payment on it = i x New principal / (1 - (1 + i)^(-N)), with i the monthly rate and N the number of payments
student-loan-capitalization.when: Use it for loans that charge interest while you study (many unsubsidized loans). If you do not pay it, it is typically added to the principal and then earns interest itself. Paying the interest as it accrues keeps the repayment payment lower. Rules differ by country and loan type; some loans are interest-free during study, so check your terms. Repayment here uses standard level payments.

sum-of-the-parts.text: EV = sum of (Segment EBITDA x Segment multiple); Equity = EV x (1 - Conglomerate discount) - Net debt
sum-of-the-parts.when: Use it for a group with several businesses that deserve different multiples. It shows whether the whole is worth more or less than the parts.

sum-of-years-digits.text: Depreciation in year t = (Cost - Salvage) x (L - t + 1) / (L x (L + 1) / 2)
sum-of-years-digits.when: Use it when you want more depreciation early in an asset's life, but less sharply than double-declining balance. The yearly amounts fall in equal steps.

sustainable-growth-rate.text: Sustainable growth rate g = ROE x Retention ratio
sustainable-growth-rate.when: Use it to estimate how fast a firm can grow using only its retained profits. It is also a common way to set the growth rate in a dividend discount model.

swap-comparative-advantage.text: Total gain from the swap = (Fixed-rate gap between the weaker and stronger borrower) - (Floating-spread gap between them); each side saves half of what remains after the dealer's fee
swap-comparative-advantage.when: Use it to see why two firms might swap. The weaker borrower pays a much bigger penalty in the fixed market than in the floating market. The firms borrow where they have an advantage and swap, and the total saving is the gap between the two penalties.

money-market-yields.text: Discount yield = (F - P) / F x 360 / days; Money market yield = (F - P) / P x 360 / days; Bond equivalent yield = (F - P) / P x 365 / days
money-market-yields.when: Use it to compare short-term instruments that pay no coupon, such as T-bills, commercial paper and many CDs. The quoted discount yield understates the true return because it divides by the face value, not the price paid.

t-statistic.when: Use it to test whether an average is really different from a chosen value or just random noise. As a rough rule, a t value beyond about 2 (in either direction) is unlikely to be chance at the 5% level for a reasonable sample size.

cornish-fisher-var.text: Adjusted z = z + (z^2 - 1) x Skew / 6 + (z^3 - 3z) x Excess kurtosis / 24 - (2z^3 - 5z) x Skew^2 / 36; VaR = V x (adjusted z x sd - mean)
cornish-fisher-var.when: Use it to correct a normal VaR for fat tails and negative skew. Financial returns usually have both, so the normal VaR understates the true tail loss. This is an approximation that works for moderate skew and kurtosis. It cannot predict events with no precedent in the data, which is the black swan problem.

taylor-rule.mathml: i∗=r∗+π+0.5(π−π∗)+0.5 gap,it=ρ it−1+(1−ρ) i∗i^{*}=r^{*}+\pi+0.5(\pi-\pi^{*})+0.5\,\text{gap},\quad i_{t}=\rho\,i_{t-1}+(1-\rho)\,i^{*}
taylor-rule.text: Prescribed policy rate = neutral real rate + inflation + 0.5 x (inflation - target) + 0.5 x output gap; With smoothing, rate = rho x last rate + (1 - rho) x prescribed rate
taylor-rule.when: Use it as a benchmark for where policy might be. The rule raises rates when inflation is above target or the economy is running hot. Central banks do not follow it mechanically, and inputs such as r* and the gap are uncertain, so compare it with the actual rate to judge how tight or loose policy is. QE and QT are used when the rate is near zero or to unwind that.

terminal-value-exit-multiple.text: Terminal value = Final-year EBITDA x Exit multiple; Implied g = (TV x WACC - FCFF) / (TV + FCFF)
terminal-value-exit-multiple.when: Use it to set the terminal value from market multiples. Always check the growth rate it implies. A multiple that implies growth above the economy's long-run rate is too high.

terminal-value-growth.text: Terminal value = Final-year FCFF x (1 + g) / (WACC - g)
terminal-value-growth.when: Use it to capture all the value after the forecast period. It is usually a large share of a DCF value, so choose g carefully and check the implied exit multiple.

accounting-equation.when: Use it as the basic check behind every balance sheet. If you know two of the three, you can find the third.

time-weighted-return.text: Time-weighted return = (1 + R1) x (1 + R2) x ... x (1 + Rn) - 1
time-weighted-return.when: Use it to judge a manager, because it removes the effect of when clients added or withdrew money, which the manager does not control. GIPS standards require it.

token-nav-and-fees.text: Value per token = (asset value - annual fees x years) / tokens issued; Premium or discount = market price / value per token - 1; Cost to buy and sell = 2 x trading fee + bid-ask spread; Minimum investment = value per token
token-nav-and-fees.when: Use it to check what a token is really worth. A token represents a legal claim to an asset; its price can differ from the value of the asset if few people trade it. Fees, the law that gives the claim force and the chance to redeem determine whether the token tracks the asset. Fractions lower the minimum ticket but do not by themselves create liquidity.

trade-off-value.text: Value of levered firm = Unlevered value + Tax shield - (Probability of distress x Cost of distress)
trade-off-value.when: Use it to see why firms do not borrow without limit. The tax shield adds value, but more debt raises the chance and cost of distress, so there is an ideal mix of debt and equity.

traditional-vs-roth.text: Traditional (tax-deferred) after-tax value = Pre-tax contribution x (1 + growth)^n x (1 - tax rate at withdrawal); Roth (tax-free) value = Pre-tax contribution x (1 - tax rate now) x (1 + growth)^n
traditional-vs-roth.when: Use it to compare saving before tax with saving after tax. The growth factor is the same in both, so the answer depends only on whether the tax rate now is above or below the rate in retirement: pay tax at the lower rate. If the rates are equal, the two are the same. Real accounts differ by country, with limits, match rules and withdrawal rules, so this shows the principle, not a prediction.

tranche-loss.text: Share of the tranche lost = min( max(Pool loss - Attachment point, 0), Detachment point - Attachment point ) / (Detachment point - Attachment point)
tranche-loss.when: Use it to see who bears credit losses in a securitization. Losses hit the lowest (equity) tranche first, then the middle (mezzanine), and the senior tranche last. A tranche is like a slice of the pool, so it only loses when pool losses pass its attachment point.

treasury-stock-method.text: If options are in the money, Net new shares = Options x (1 - Strike / Share price); Diluted shares = Basic shares + Net new shares
treasury-stock-method.when: Use it to count the extra shares from stock options in diluted EPS and valuation. It assumes the exercise proceeds are used to buy back shares at the market price, so only the net new shares count. Options with a strike above the share price are ignored.

trend-index-analysis.text: Index = Value in year t / Value in the base year x 100; Year-on-year growth = Value in year t / Value in year t-1 - 1; CAGR = (Last / First)^(1 / years) - 1
trend-index-analysis.when: Use it to follow a figure across years on one scale. An index shows the total change since the base year, and growth rates show the pace. Comparing the indexes of revenue and profit shows if profit is keeping up.

treynor-ratio.text: Treynor ratio = (Portfolio return - Risk-free rate) / Portfolio beta
treynor-ratio.when: Use it to compare portfolios that are part of a larger, diversified holding, because it counts only market risk (beta) and ignores risk that diversification removes.

hypothesis-test-two-means.text: z = (average of group 1 - average of group 2) / sqrt(sd1^2 / n1 + sd2^2 / n2); two-sided p-value = 2 x (1 - N(|z|))
hypothesis-test-two-means.when: Use it to judge whether two averages really differ or the gap is plausibly noise, such as two funds, two strategies, or two periods. It assumes independent groups and large samples (roughly 30 or more each). A small p-value says the gap is hard to explain by chance; it does not say the gap is large or that it will persist. Testing many strategies and reporting the best inflates false positives.

uncovered-interest-parity.text: Uncovered parity: the expected future spot equals today's spot x (1 + domestic rate) / (1 + foreign rate), so the higher-rate currency is expected to weaken; Unhedged return in domestic currency = (1 + foreign rate) x (future spot / spot) - 1
uncovered-interest-parity.when: Use it as a benchmark for currency forecasts. If uncovered parity held, there would be no gain from holding a high-yield currency, because it would fall by the interest advantage. In the data, high-yield currencies have on average not fallen as much as parity says, which is why carry trades have earned a premium, with sharp losses in crises. The unhedged return shows what depends on the future spot.

labor-market-rates.text: Unemployment rate = unemployed / labor force, where labor force = employed + unemployed; Participation rate = labor force / working-age population; Employment-population ratio = employed / working-age population
labor-market-rates.when: Use it to read a jobs report. The unemployment rate can fall because people find jobs or because they stop looking (they then leave the labor force). The participation rate and employment-population ratio reveal which. Markets watch both along with wage growth, since a tight labor market can push inflation up.

units-of-production-depreciation.text: Depreciation = (Cost - Salvage) / Total expected units x Units used this period
units-of-production-depreciation.when: Use it when an asset wears out by use rather than by time, such as a machine rated for a number of hours or a vehicle rated for a number of kilometers.

unlever-beta.text: Unlevered beta = Levered beta / (1 + (1 - T) x D/E)
unlever-beta.when: Use it to strip the effect of debt out of a comparable company's beta, so that the business risk of different firms can be compared or averaged.

utility-risk-aversion.text: Utility U = E(r) - 0.5 x A x variance
utility-risk-aversion.when: Use it to score how attractive a risky investment is to a particular investor. The score is the guaranteed return that would make the investor equally happy, so compare it with the risk-free rate.

precedent-transactions.mathml: Deal multiple=EVdealEBITDAtarget,EV=EBITDA×Median deal multiple\text{Deal multiple}=\frac{EV_{deal}}{EBITDA_{target}},\quad EV=EBITDA\times\text{Median deal multiple}
precedent-transactions.text: Deal multiple = Deal EV / Target EBITDA for each past deal; Implied EV = Your EBITDA x Median deal multiple
precedent-transactions.when: Use it to value a company as if it were being bought. Past deal multiples include a control premium, so they are usually higher than trading multiples.

trading-comparables.text: Implied value = Target metric (such as EBITDA) x Median multiple of peer companies
trading-comparables.when: Use it to value a company by what the market pays for similar ones. Pick peers with similar size, growth, risk and business, and prefer the median to the average.

valuation-multiples.text: EV/EBITDA = Enterprise value / EBITDA; EV/Sales = Enterprise value / Sales; P/E = Share price / Earnings per share
valuation-multiples.when: Use them to compare what the market pays for a company's earnings and sales. EV multiples suit comparing firms with different debt levels, and P/E is a quick measure of what investors pay for each unit of profit.

var-historical.text: VaR = - Portfolio value x the (1 - confidence) percentile of past returns
var-historical.when: Use it when you do not want to assume a normal distribution. It uses actual past returns, so it captures fat tails and skew in the sample, but the answer depends on the window used and cannot see a loss worse than any in the history.

var-parametric.text: VaR = Portfolio value x (z-score x Daily volatility x sqrt(days) - Daily mean return x days)
var-parametric.when: Use it for a quick estimate of the loss that should not be exceeded with a chosen confidence over a set period. It assumes returns follow a normal distribution, which understates the chance of extreme losses. Monte Carlo VaR simulates many random paths instead, and historical VaR (next entry) reads the loss from past data.

acquisition-npv.text: Acquirer NPV = Synergies - Premium, where Premium = Price paid - Stand-alone value of the target
acquisition-npv.when: Use it to check whether a deal creates value for the buyer. The seller's shareholders keep the premium, so the buyer only gains if the synergies exceed it.

mm-levered-value.text: Value of levered firm = Value of unlevered firm + Tax rate x Debt
mm-levered-value.when: Use it to see the value that tax savings on interest add to a firm. It assumes the debt is permanent and ignores the costs of financial distress, so it overstates the gain from heavy borrowing.

var-backtest-kupiec.mathml: LRPOF=−2ln⁡[(1−p)N−xpx]+2ln⁡[(1−xN)N−x(xN)x]LR_{POF}=-2\ln\left[(1-p)^{N-x}p^{x}\right]+2\ln\left[\left(1-\tfrac{x}{N}\right)^{N-x}\left(\tfrac{x}{N}\right)^{x}\right]
var-backtest-kupiec.text: Kupiec statistic = -2 x ln[(1-p)^(N-x) x p^x] + 2 x ln[(1 - x/N)^(N-x) x (x/N)^x]; compare with 3.84 (5% level, 1 degree of freedom)
var-backtest-kupiec.when: Use it to check whether a VaR model is calibrated. A 99% VaR should be exceeded about 1 day in 100. Too many exceptions means risk is understated, and too few means capital is wasted. The Basel traffic light for 250 days at 99% is green for 0 to 4 exceptions, yellow for 5 to 9 and red for 10 or more.

variance-sd.text: s^2 = sum of (Ri - mean)^2 / (n - 1), and s = square root of s^2
variance-sd.when: Use it to measure how widely returns vary around their average. A larger standard deviation means a riskier, more volatile investment.

variance-of-distribution.text: Variance = sum of pi x (xi - E(X))^2
variance-of-distribution.when: Use it to measure risk when you have scenarios with probabilities, rather than a history of past returns. It uses probability weights, so it divides by nothing.

variance-ratio.text: Variance ratio = Variance of q-period returns / (q x Variance of 1-period returns)
variance-ratio.when: Use it to test whether prices follow a random walk. In a random walk the variance grows in proportion to time, so the ratio is about 1. Below 1 suggests returns reverse (mean reversion), and above 1 suggests they trend.

vasicek-zero-bond.mathml: P(0,T)=A e−Br0,  B=1−e−κTκ,  A=exp⁡ ⁣[(θ−σ22κ2)(B−T)−σ2B24κ]P(0,T)=A\,e^{-B r_{0}},\; B=\frac{1-e^{-\kappa T}}{\kappa},\; A=\exp\!\left[\left(\theta-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2\kappa^{2}}\right)(B-T)-\frac{\sigma^{2}B^{2}}{4\kappa}\right]
vasicek-zero-bond.text: Bond price = A x e^(-B x r0), where B = (1 - e^(-kappa T)) / kappa and A = exp[(theta - sigma^2 / (2 kappa^2)) x (B - T) - sigma^2 x B^2 / (4 kappa)]
vasicek-zero-bond.when: Use it to price bonds when the short rate is mean reverting with normal (Gaussian) shocks. It gives a full yield curve from three parameters. Its known weakness is that rates can go negative. The yield is a weighted mix of today's short rate and the long-run mean.

vc-dilution-exit.mathml: Stake=IVpre+I,sexit=s0∏(1−dk),Vreq=M×Isexit\text{Stake}=\frac{I}{V_{pre}+I},\quad s_{exit}=s_{0}\prod(1-d_{k}),\quad V_{req}=\frac{M\times I}{s_{exit}}
vc-dilution-exit.text: Post-money value = pre-money value + investment; Ownership bought = investment / post-money; Each later round dilutes existing holders by (new investment / new post-money value); Stake at exit = initial stake x product of (1 - dilution) x (1 - option pool share); Exit value needed for a multiple M = M x investment / stake at exit
vc-dilution-exit.when: Use it to judge what a venture investment must return. Early stakes shrink with each round and employee option pool, so a 20% stake can end at 10% or less. Because most startups fail, the winners must return many times the fund, so the exit value needed is large. Work it backwards from the multiple you need.

vc-method-ownership.mathml: Required stake at exit=I×MVexit,Stake today=Required stakeRetention\text{Required stake at exit}=\frac{I\times M}{V_{exit}},\quad \text{Stake today}=\frac{\text{Required stake}}{\text{Retention}}
vc-method-ownership.text: Required stake at exit = Investment x Target multiple / Exit value; Stake needed today = Required stake / Retention
vc-method-ownership.when: Use it to find the stake a venture investor needs today to reach a target return, allowing for dilution from future funding rounds.

vix-variance.text: Variance = (2 / T) x sum of [ (Strike gap / Strike^2) x e^(rT) x Option price ] - (1 / T) x (Forward / K0 - 1)^2; Index = 100 x square root of variance
vix-variance.when: Use it to see how a volatility index is built. The VIX does not use a Black-Scholes model. It weights the prices of out-of-the-money options across all strikes to read off the market's expected variance of the index. The real VIX blends two expiries to reach a constant 30 days. This is the one-expiry calculation.

warrant-value-dilution.text: Warrant value = Number of shares outstanding / (Shares outstanding + New shares created if all warrants are exercised) x Value of an ordinary call with the same terms
warrant-value-dilution.when: Use it to value a warrant, which is a call option issued by the company itself. When it is exercised the company creates new shares, so the stock price is diluted and the warrant is worth less than an ordinary call. This is a simple approximation. It uses an option value computed first, for instance with Black-Scholes.

wacc.text: WACC = E/V x re + D/V x rd x (1 - T) + P/V x rp
wacc.when: Use it as the discount rate for a firm's overall cash flows (FCFF) and for projects that have the same risk as the firm. Use market values for the weights, not book values.

weighted-average-cost.mathml: Average cost=Total cost of goods availableUnits available\text{Average cost} = \frac{\text{Total cost of goods available}}{\text{Units available}}
weighted-average-cost.text: Average cost per unit = Total cost of goods available / Units available
weighted-average-cost.when: Use it to value inventory and cost of goods sold at one average price when units were bought at different prices over time.

weighted-average-life.text: Weighted average life = Sum of (time x principal repaid at that time) / Total principal
weighted-average-life.when: Use it to describe how long the money in an amortizing or securitized bond is outstanding. Unlike duration it uses only principal, not interest, and it shortens when prepayments speed up. Tranches of securitized deals are often compared by WAL.

yield-curve-slope.text: Slope = 10-year yield - 2-year yield; Curvature (butterfly) = 2 x 5-year yield - 2-year yield - 10-year yield
yield-curve-slope.when: Use it to describe the shape of the curve. A positive slope is normal, a flat curve means little extra reward for lending long, and an inverted (negative) curve has often come before recessions because it signals that rates are expected to fall.

ytm.text: Find the yield y that makes the present value of all coupons and the face value equal to the price. Approximation: y = [C + (F - P) / n] / [(F + P) / 2]
ytm.when: Use it to find the return you earn if you buy at the current price, hold to maturity, and reinvest every coupon at the same yield. It has no direct formula, so it is found by trial and error, which the calculator does for you.

z-score.when: Use it to see how unusual a value is. A z-score of 0 is average, and values beyond about 2 or below -2 are unusual in a normal distribution.

zero-coupon-bond.text: Price = Face value / (1 + yield / payments per year)^(years x payments per year)
zero-coupon-bond.when: Use it to price a bond with a single payment at the end, including STRIPS, which are the coupons and principal of government bonds sold separately. Interest accrues as the price rises toward face value, and holders are often taxed on that accrual each year even though no cash arrives. Its duration equals its maturity.
